News.title: UK wildfires live: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales
News.content:
Firefighters are battling wildfires in Shropshire and South Wales, with crews declaring a major incident as they tackle the blaze in the Rhondda Valley

Firefighters in Shropshire are tackling a large blaze near a historic site, while crews in South Wales have declared a major incident as they battle a wildfire close to homes.

The blaze at Battlefield Heritage Park, a country park north of Shrewsbury, broke out this afternoon. It is understood to be just a few fields away from the site associated with the 1403 Battle of Shrewsbury, fought between King Henry IV and a rebel army led by Henry "Harry Hotspur" Percy.

Meanwhile, crews from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service are battling a wildfire in the Llanwonno area of Rhondda Cynon Taf. The blaze, which began on Saturday afternoon, has already spread across around 150 hectares - roughly the size of 210 football pitches.

No homes have been evacuated, but Rhondda Cynon Taf Council said a rest centre has been set up at a local sports centre for residents affected by smoke and poor air quality from the fire.

News.title: Toddler dies of heatstroke after being 'left in car' in scorching Canary Islands
News.content:
Toddler dies of heatstroke after being 'left in car' in scorching Canary Islands

The 20-month-old boy died at the Materno Infantil University Hospital in Gran Canaria's capital, Las Palmas

View 2 Images Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, Spain (Image: Getty Images)

A toddler has died of heatstroke after he was reportedly left in a car in scorching temperatures on a Spanish holiday island.

‌



The child, who was 20 months old, was in a serious condition when he was taken ill on Fuerteventura and then rushed to the island's general hospital on Saturday. He was then taken to a public hospital on Gran Canaria by air ambulance.

‌



The boy died in the early hours of Sunday at the Materno Infantil University Hospital in Gran Canaria's capital, Las Palmas. While local reports state the boy was left inside the vehicle, no other details have yet been released.

‌



It is unclear where the boy was from. Temperatures in the Canary Islands reached 45C at the weekend, with the current heatwave affecting the popular holiday destination for several few days.

View 2 Images Hospital Universitario Materno Infantil where the child was treated (Image: Google)

UK wildfires live: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales READ MORE :

Seven killed as drone hits packed Russian beach and tourists run for their lives READ MORE :

Gran Canaria was on red alert today and parts of the neighbouring island of Tenerife on orange alert because of the high temperatures.

‌



An 18-month-old called Sofia died last month after she was left inside a licensed nursery transport vehicle close to a famous tourist viewpoint near Lisbon for seven hours.

The girl is said to have been "forgotten" inside the vehicle in Almada on the southern bank of the Tagus River directly opposite the Portuguese capital. It was parked by the access to the giant religious Cristo Rei shrine featuring a tall statue of Jesus Christ with open arms facing the Portuguese capital.

Hundreds of tourists are said to have passed by the spot where the youngster was slowly dying in temperatures which reached 30C without seeing her behind the darkened and closed windows of the seven-seater SUV. The child's mum went to collect her in the afternoon on July 23 but was told the girl never arrived at the nursery.

Article continues below

Emergency services were then alerted just before 4pm but the girl was found in "critical condition" inside a Peugeot 5008 outside the main nursery campus. Despite resuscitation attempts, the girl was pronounced dead at the scene.

The creche which was supposed to take care of the toddler has been named as Colegio Mestre Cuco. A police investigation was launched.

In June, two children aged two and four were found dead in their family’s car in the town of Carpentras in southeastern France during a heatwave.

News.title: Donald Trump 'very impressed' with Andy Burnham and says 'he surrounded terrific'
News.content:
Donald Trump 'very impressed' with Andy Burnham and says 'he surrounded terrific'

Donald Trump has heaped praise on Andy Burnham amid the President's claims that the PM had indicated to him he would 'open up the North Sea' to drilling

View 2 Images Trump has praised Andy Burnham

Donald Trump has said he is "very impressed" with Andy Burnham as he repeated his claims that the Prime Minister had indicated he would open up the North Sea to drilling.

‌



Last Wednesday, the US President said he'd been given the impression by the PM that he would "open up" the oil field - something Trump has been demanding for months.

‌



But Mr Burnham would only say he'd indicated to the President that he'd be "pragmatic" about North Sea drilling. "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here," he said.

‌



The Mirror understands the PM is likely to stick to Labour's manifesto pledge not to offer new licences to drill in the oil field, instead allowing "tie-backs" which would allow small-scale increases in drilling adjacent to already approved fields.

View 2 Images Donald Trump has praised Andy Burnham (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Unhinged Donald Trump takes aim at Iran in latest tirade after Tehran denies peace talk claims READ MORE :

Donald Trump blasted after he shares AI photo of himself with Abraham Lincoln READ MORE :

Speaking from the White House today Donald Trump said: "I spoke to him and he sounded terrific on this subject. You open it up you'll be a wealthy country.

‌



"You keep it closed you'll be a bankrupt country, which is what you are now. Essentially you're a bankrupt country."

He added: "I spoke with your new Prime Minister and I was very impressed and he sort of indicated to me."

When the Prime Minister was asked about North Sea drilling on Thursday on a visit to Cumbria he said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can't ignore that. Hence, me indicating that to the president."

‌



On the surface, drilling in the North Sea would be advantageous for mitigating the impact of a ongoing blockage of the Strait of Hormuz.

But the true genesis of Trump's push for North Sea Drilling is much more personal.

Back in 2012, Trump was embroiled in a legal battle with the Scottish government, who wanted to build 11 wind turbines off the coast of Aberdeenshire. Right next to one of his golf courses.

Article continues below

Trump objected, arguing they would be ugly and ruin the view from his luxury resort.

He appealed the plans through the Scottish courts right up to the UK Supreme Court but lost

News.title: Nigel Farage – recap: Reform UK leader's horrific new 'breaking point' poster is branded 'nonsense'
News.content:
Nigel Farage's Reform UK has proposed using the Royal Navy to transport migrants on the English Channel to France or Belgium under a plan called "operation fortress"

Nigel Farage was today blasted for posting online a new version of his controversial "breaking point" poster.

The Reform UK's latest edit, posted on his X account, depicts migrants at Ceuta rather than Syrian refugees, invoking the 2016 poster denounced by then-Chancellor George Osborne, who compared it to Nazi propaganda.

Reacting online, other X users voiced their anger today. One said: "Talking nonsense again." Another posted: "Desperate deflection and piffle." A third wrote: "Reform is at a laughing point."

Mr Farage, whose MP seat in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, is up for contest next week, debuted the "breaking point" poster on the last week of the 2016 Brexit referendum while serving as UKIP leader.

The new version was posted after Mr Farage, 62, broke his cover at a press conference today to unveil visions to use the Royal Navy to transport migrants on the English Channel to France or Belgium under a plan called "operation fortress". This too has been slammed today.

And, while Mr Farage continues to face mounting pressure over his finances, it has now emerged his deputy, Richard Tice, is under investigation by the standards commissioner over an alleged failure to declare an interest.

News.title: Nuclear test veterans' medical records were gathered by secret government lab
News.content:
Nuclear test veterans' medical records were gathered by secret government lab

EXCLUSIVE: Today the files are held by a private contractor called Restore, which specialises in document storage - a digital version is held by Defence Radiation Protection Services, another part of the MoD, based 172 miles away in Hampshire

View 2 Images Up to 50,000 paper files now locked in a climate-controlled warehouse were collected by scientists at Porton Down (Image: Humphrey Nemar/daily mirror)

Medical records of nuclear test veterans were gathered by a secret government laboratory, the Ministry of Defence has admitted.

‌



Up to 50,000 paper files now locked in a climate-controlled warehouse were collected by scientists at Porton Down. The cache of files has yet to be examined, despite a two-year review into missing medical records of veterans who were subject to a programme of medical monitoring at Cold War bomb tests.

‌



Campaigning MP Rebecca Long-Bailey said: “We need to know how many records are in there, for what reason they were held, and whether they constitute some of the missing files our veterans have spent decades searching for. I hope our new Prime Minister, who has been unfaltering in his support of the veterans, will order this archive searched before Parliament returns from summer recess.”

‌



A cross-party group of MPs have written to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, urging him to examine the archive. Veterans of Britain’s 45 atomic experiments have long complained their medical files were missing.

View 2 Images The Ministry of Defence admitted collecting medical records of nuclear test veterans (Image: PA)

MoD admits "extensive" radiation experiments on troops but hides the news in World Cup mania READ MORE :

In 2022, the Mirror uncovered the first evidence thousands of them were given previously-denied blood, urine and thyroid testing, and underwent chest x-rays, before, during and after service at the weapons trials. The original orders were for blood test results to be recorded on six different forms, by five separate people, and held in four places, including ‘special health registers’ for each unit.

‌



A review was launched in 2024, but when it was published last month it was unable to find most records, and assumed the blood tests were - in many cases - never taken and in others destroyed. No trace of the registers was found.

But it did locate a warehouse in Swadlincote, Derbyshire, which held 50,000 paper records about historic radiation exposure. A brief search established it held medical records for at least one atomic serviceman. The review said: “It is possible that the records of other nuclear test veterans are in the collection.”

The archive has a chequered past. Officially called UHR ‘DSTL Historic Radiation’, it appeared to have been formed by the Defence Science Technology Laboratory, more usually known as Porton Down. It is a top-secret facility that conducts classified biological and chemical research.

‌



Today the files are held by a private contractor called Restore, which specialises in document storage. A digital version is held by Defence Radiation Protection Services, another part of the MoD, based 172 miles away in Gosport, Hampshire.

Two years ago, DRPS merged with the Atomic Weapons Establishment which is now responsible for the files, but no-one can search them without “specific individual permissions” from Defence Business Services; the administrative arm of the MoD. When ministers published the review, they did not say if or when the archives would be searched.

Veteran John Morris, 88, said: “It’s bonkers. The MoD has some paperwork, but the MoD hasn’t given itself permission to search it and tell the rest of the MoD what it has. If my medical records are in there, I want them back.”

Article continues below

The MoD and Restore were both contacted for comment.

News.title: Donald Trump blasted after he shares AI photo of himself with Abraham Lincoln
News.content:
Donald Trump blasted after he shares AI photo of himself with Abraham Lincoln

Donald Trump is seen sat next to George Washington and Abraham Lincoln in the bizarre image shared by the US president in what appears to be his latest experiment with AI

View 2 Images Donald Trump is shown with Abraham Lincoln and George Washington in the bizarre new image

Donald Trump has been branded "deranged" after he shared a bizarre AI portrait of himself sat next to George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

The world leader, 80, posted the image of himself with the two US presidents - widely considered the greatest in American history - in his latest spree on his Truth Social platform on Sunday night.

In the mock-up painting, Mr Trump is seen at a wooden table alongside Mr Washington and Mr Lincoln, with what appears to be an upside-down map of the United States placed in front of them.

Mr Trump, who has developed a habit of posting strange, often crude pictures on his social media, did not explain why he had shared it.

Unhinged Donald Trump takes aim at Iran in latest tirade after Tehran denies peace talk claims READ MORE :

Donald Trump faces cheating allegations again after winning another golf tournament READ MORE :

View 2 Images Mr Trump did not explain why he posted the image (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Another AI-generated image shared a few hours earlier showed a slimmed-down Mr Trump in an Elvis-style low-cut jumpsuit exposing his bare chest, decorated with two sequined bald eagles.

Article continues below

He also likened himself to the American War of Independence hero in another image on Sunday, which showed his face spliced half-and-half with Washington's.

The digital poster, which again appeared likely to have been created with an AI model, read: '250 years - in God We Trust'.

It marks Mr Trump's latest effort to spin the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States with his own political career, with him frequently attempting to cast his own political movement as a modern continuation of the American Revolution.

This summer, critics accused the president of politicising the anniversary by staging campaign-style rallies and diverting federal funds to his "Freedom 250" task force, undermining a bipartisan commission established by Congress a decade earlier.

MAGA supporters went on to recirculate the image of Mr Trump with Lincoln and Washington on X (formerly Twitter), claiming it showed "three American legends."

But critics were quick to turn the tables on the US president in their own pictures, mischievously swapping out Mr Washington and Mr Lincoln for the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to taunt the president over his ongoing second-term scandal.

Article continues below

Another user edited Mr Trump into a clown, while one critic labelled the president's original post as "deranged."

Mr Trump's biggest controversy involving mocked-up images came earlier this year when he shared a since-deleted image of himself as Jesus Christ healing a bedridden man with his bare hands.

He would later claim he thought it showed him as a "doctor" after intense backlash from religious conservatives.

News.title: Met Office names six areas facing power cuts on Tuesday and warns 'get prepared'
News.content:
Met Office names six areas facing power cuts on Tuesday and warns 'get prepared'

The forecaster has warned that major disruption could be coming to six areas covered by its latest yellow weather warning

View 2 Images People have been told to prepare in advance

The Met Office has put six areas on alert for power cuts tomorrow (Tuesday) as they brace for thunderstorms and rain.

‌



The forecaster issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms in the whole of Northern Ireland from midday tomorrow until 9pm. It warned that some short term loss of power and other services is "likely" as it urged people to take precautionary measures.

‌



It said: "People cope better with power cuts when they have prepared for them in advance. It’s easy to do; consider gathering torches and batteries, a mobile phone power pack and other essential items."

‌



The national weather agency explained that showers will develop on Tuesday morning and become heavy and "locally thundery" in the afternoon. These will be "slow-moving" and bring significant downpours, the forecaster said, with 20 to 30mm of rain predicted "in an hour or two".

The Met Office warning states: "Strong and gusty winds and hail will also be possible with the heaviest showers. Showers should slowly ease from the west into the evening."

‌



View 2 Images A map of the areas affected by the yellow weather warning (Image: Met Office)

UK wildfires live: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales READ MORE :

Besides power cuts, people in the six areas targeted by the warning have also been asked to consider whether their homes and businesses are at risk of flash flooding and prepare accordingly. People should also check road conditions before making any journeys, regardless of how they plan to travel.

The Met Office said: "If you find yourself outside and hear thunder, protect yourself by finding a safe enclosed shelter (such as a car). Do not shelter under or near trees, or other structures which may be struck by lightning. If you are on an elevated area move to lower ground."

Article continues below

Meanwhile, the Met Office has forecast showers in Scotland and the west of the UK tomorrow. It's forecast said: "Outbreaks of heavy rain in the north with the risk of thunder. Scattered showers in the south with the odd thunderstorm. Vary warm and humid. Windy in the north."

News.title: Nigel Farage's small boats plan savaged as France hits back over 'violation'
News.content:
Nigel Farage's small boats plan savaged as France hits back over 'violation'

France's interior ministry has blasted Nigel Farage's plan to use the Royal Navy to stop small boats, while the Reform chief was warned his idea will "inevitably" lead to more deaths on the Channel

View 5 Images Nigel Farage is looking to turn around plummeting poll ratings (Image: Getty Images)

Nigel Farage's desperate small boats plan has been dismissed as impractical and illegal as he attempts to divert attention from sleaze allegations.

‌



The Reform UK leader published a thin plan to use the Royal Navy to stop Channel crossings. But France shot back, claiming the move would be a "violation of French sovereignty" and saying it breaks maritime law.

‌



Downing Street also dismissed the 25-page proposal, saying a similar measure under the Tories had not lowered the number of crossings. And charities warned it would inevitably lead to more deaths.

‌



Mr Farage staged a rare Westminster press conference today to launch the plan as he battles to stop plummeting poll ratings. He was accused of trying to create a diversion by saying navy vessels should intercept small boats crossing the Channel and return those on board to France and Belgium.

Reform council leader vows to report café owner who fed kids for free to police READ MORE :

View 5 Images Mr Farage's plan has been dismissed as impractical (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

France brands Farage's plans 'a violation'

Reform claimed it anticipated French authorities would support agreed returns. But in a statement the nation's interior ministry said: "This would be a violation of French sovereignty as well as a violation of maritime law and international law."

‌



At the same press conference Mr Farage confirmed reports he had held secret talks about returning as party leader months before the 2024 general election. But he insisted these took place after he accepted a £5million 'gift' from Thailand-based crypto tycoon Christopher Harborne.

This money, which was not declared, was being investigated by Parliament's standards commissioner when Mr Farage stepped down and triggered a by-election in Clacton, Essex. He is battling parody candidate Count Binface after all other major parties refused to engage, branding the contest a circus.

He unveiled Operation Fortress, which Reform says would see 10 navy vessels deployed to stop Channel crossings. But Andy Burnham's official spokesman said getting the Royal Navy involved was tried under the Tories as crossings rose - and made no difference.

‌



The number of people reaching the UK this year is at its lowest since 2021, but the government is under pressure to tackle the number of crossings. The Downing Street spokesman said: "The Royal Navy had primacy for small boat crossings under the previous government in 2022. I'd remind you there was no reduction in small boat crossings in that period.

"The Royal Navy is already tackling many threats, including monitoring any Russian warships operating near our shores, protecting our waters and our critical national infrastructure. Border patrol officers have significant capabilities and skills that make them the best-suited candidate to lead small boats operations in the Channel.

"That's why we're driving down the number of crossings. It's why they're down almost 50% compared to last year and why almost 60% of attempted crossings have been stopped since this Government came to power."

‌



View 5 Images Mr Farage with 'Shadow Home Secretary' Zia Yusuf (Image: Getty Images)

Refugee Council says more lives would be at risk

Under Reform's plan, bay class landing ships, rigid-hulled inflatable boats and Border Force cutters would be used to intercept dangerous boats. People would be removed, treated, and returned to France or Belgium.

A document outlining the policy described it as a humanitarian response, but last night the Refugee Council warned it would inevitably put people in more danger.

‌



Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the charity, said: “The deaths of four people trying to cross the channel last week were a tragic reminder of how dangerous this route is. The last thing anyone should be proposing is anything that would risk more loss of life, as this plan inevitably would."

Reform's proposals would create a major flashpoint between Britain, France and Belgium - but it claimed it would not lead to violence in the sea. The Reform document states: "We do not believe for one moment that the French nation or gendarmerie would open fire on Royal Marines conducting a humanitarian mission and transporting civilians."

It went on to say the chances of a tactical confrontation with France is "incredibly low". Mr Farage said:"If the Royal Navy is not there to protect this country from invasion, then, frankly, I can't see what its purpose is."

‌



Following the press conference he unveiled a van with the words 'Europe is at breaking point' on the side. It is a reference to a heavily-criticised poster he posed with during the Brexit campaign.

Reform's home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf - who attended the press conference with Mr Farage - said it would be the largest military operation in the English Channel since World War Two.

Farage's popularity plunge

View 5 Images Mr Farage is locked in a by-election showdown with Count Binface (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

‌



The headline-grabbing policy came after he was dealt a hammer blow last week when two major polls suggested Labour had overtaken Reform after trailing for more than a year. And according to More in Common his personal approval ratings have plummeted, falling by 10 points in just a fortnight to minus 34%.

This makes him the most unpopular leader of any of the five main parties, a long way behind Andy Burnham's +19%. An investigation into the £5million gift is expected to resume if Mr Farage is successfully returned as an MP next week.

If Mr Farage is found to have broken strict rules on declaring gifts in the year before becoming an MP, he could face a suspension and a possible second by-election.

‌



He denies wrongdoing and insisted that when he accepted the money he had no intention of standing for Parliament. But he admitted he had discussed a return as party leader in spring 2024 with Richard Tice.

Mr Farage did not announce his candidacy until June after Rishi Sunak called a snap general election, which Labour won in a landslide. Asked about the discussions, Mr Farage said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back".

View 5 Images Mr Farage poses with a digital poster van claiming Europe is full (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



He said he had been discussing financial liabilities. The Sunday Times reported he negotiated a deal with Mr Tice, who was then party chief.

Under that deal, once Mr Farage became leader Reform would repay or write off more than £1 million in outstanding loans it had received from Mr Tice's company. He said: "Overall questions about money could go on for years.

"I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position. And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find our what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial."

Article continues below

This chat came quite some time after the gift, he said. On top of questions about the donation, it has emerged that the Met Police is investigating donations to Reform by Fiona Cottrell, mum of convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close ally of Mr Farage.

Officers are working to determine the original source of the funds. Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: “Farage has desperately tried to distract from his catalogue of scandals. But the embattled Reform leader has run out of road and must come clean with the public. If he had done nothing wrong, he surely would have explained himself by now.

“With grubby pacts, police probes, and support from a convicted fraudster – Reform are up to their neck in sleaze and they clearly think the rules don’t apply to them.”

News.title: Infantino opponents threaten 'non co-operation' with Fifa
News.content:
Opponents of Fifa president Gianni Infantino are threatening "non co-operation" with the governing body unless he steps down, according to senior Uefa sources.

Some of those involved in the rebellion vow "there is no going back" for as long as Infantino remains in position, as the fallout over his scrapped plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investors intensifies.

While the details of the proposed disruption remain unclear, one senior figure said they would "certainly expect" a refusal to participate in Fifa meetings.

It comes after European football's governing body Uefa threatened legal action over the proposals, and Wales publicly withdrew backing for Infantino's bid for a fourth term as Fifa president, with England's Football Association set to follow suit.

In March, Infantino is set to stand for re-election for a final term as president and would need 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win.

Sources have told BBC Sport the Scottish FA's position on the future of Infantino remains aligned with Uefa's lack of confidence in the 56-year-old.

Infantino's leadership had already been publicly questioned by football's governing bodies in Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbean, with Uefa and Concacaf releasing statements criticising the plans.

As the pressure grows on Infantino with Serbia, Sweden and Finland also withdrawing their support, Morocco, Qatar, Lebanon, Kuwait and Sri Lanka among the countries to have pledged their support for his Fifa leadership to continue.

Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.

The Asian Football Federation (AFC) has said it stands in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan.

However, the Fifa Council could try to force Infantino to resign through an emergency meeting.

That would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one and the meeting must take place within two weeks.

Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced that if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Responding to the French government, a Reform spokesperson said: "We will always stand up for British interests and protect our people, whether Emmanuel Macron likes it or not."

The spokesperson added: "Humanitarian missions do not violate maritime or international law."

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: Inside city gripped by deadly protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
News.content:
Dozens of people have been killed in clashes between security officials and protesters across Pakistan-administered Kashmir over the last two months, following a crackdown that left the city of Rawalakot mostly sealed off from the world.

Leading the demonstrations is the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which says it is protesting for rights including healthcare and electricity.

Authorities say the JAAC is trying to disrupt the current regional elections, that the group is armed, and will not be allowed to leave Rawalakot.

The JAAC was banned in June; they have been labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the government. They reject this characterisation, saying they are peaceful and - though funded from the Pakistan-administered Kashmir community abroad - not sponsored by India.

The BBC is the first media to gain access to the city and speak to people on the ground about what is going on at the heart of the protests. Pakistan correspondent Caroline Davies reports from Islamabad.

News.title: West Ham co-owner David Sullivan advised to stay away from home matches
News.content:
The recommendation from London Stadium comes after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour. He has categorically denied the allegations.

He stood down as joint chairman of the club shortly before the investigation was broadcast, saying he wanted to focus on fighting what he called "factually incorrect and entirely false, decades-old allegations concerning my personal life". He remains the club's largest shareholder.

The investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for three years due to safeguarding concerns. London Stadium were unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historic allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false and that because he had never met any academy or women's team players "1-2-1" during his 16 years at the club, he accepted what he saw as a "meaningless restrictionâ¦for a quiet life".

West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in May and are due to play their first home game of the new season, a Carabao Cup match against Portsmouth, on Saturday.

A spokesperson for London Stadium, the operator of the publicly owned venue, said that "following media reports at the end of the season regarding a safeguarding matter being managed by the club, London Stadium sought further information to ensure it could fulfil its own safeguarding responsibilities".

It said that West Ham had told it that the "matter was investigated and that the club does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Mr Sullivan attending the stadium".

However it said that, despite this, it had recommended the businessman stay away from games because of the "potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators".

West Ham declined to comment. It is understood that the club intends to work with the stadium operators to facilitate Sullivan's attendance at games.

Mr Sullivan has not responded to a request for comment.

News.title: Son who kept mum's body in freezer for years collected £78k of her benefits
News.content:
The court heard Phillips moved downstairs to sleep next to his mother's body. At times he would open the freezer and hold her hand.

Sylvia Phillips had 26 appointments with her local GP practice in 2021, and six in 2022, after which there was no further contact.

The court heard she was last seen in A&E on 24 September 2022 and her local GP made a house call on 26 September but her son continued to pick up her prescriptions.

Sylvia Phillips was invited to a review by the practice, but her son said she would not come to the surgery and she did not need the blood tests.

Christopher Phillips received a total of Â£78,190.92 in state pension, pensions credit, attendance allowance, winter fuel payments, cost-of-living payments and housing benefit payments, which would have ceased had the death been reported.

He had been her primary carer since 2008, and the court heard he had resigned from his job in late 2022 when her health declined further. The pair were described as "somewhat isolated".

Ruth Smith, defending, said Phillips had told police: "I basically didn't want to let her go."

She added: "He described talking to her as if she was still aliveâ¦ Sitting next to her, talking to her about television programmes, Coronation Street, the horse racing, just as they always did," she said, adding that he was a "vulnerable individual".

Phillips sobbed in the dock as Smith said her client was "extremely close to his mother" and was in "extreme grief" following her death.

She said he showed a "lack of acceptance" about her passing and "had almost created a false narrative that she was still alive".

Sentencing Phillips, Judge Lloyd-Clarke said he had "deliberately concealed" his mother's death and "took steps to give the impression that she was still alive".

"You continued to collect her prescription and lied to medical professionals and eventually the police," Lloyd-Clarke added.

"Rather than notify the authorities and make arrangements for her lawful burial, you purchased a chest freezer on March 10th and concealed her body within it," she said.

Lloyd-Clarke added that a timescale for confiscation proceedings would follow.

News.title: X Factor finalist denies murdering influencer by running her over with car
News.content:
A former X Factor finalist has denied murdering a social media influencer by running her over with a car in central London.

Gabrielle Carrington of Manchester, allegedly struck Klaudia Zakrzewska outside Inca nightclub in Argyll Street, Soho, at 04:30 BST on 19 April.

The 29-year-old appeared at the Old Bailey by video link from Bronzefield prison to deny the charge. She had been initially charged with attempted murder but that was changed to murder after Zakrzewska died from her injuries six days later.

Carrington, who was not represented in court by a barrister, also denied a second charge of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to security guard Anoush Chyche.

The defendant was not asked to enter a plea to a third charge of driving with excess alcohol.

Family members of the victims shook their heads as the accused read out her pleas.

Judge Sarah Whitehouse KC confirmed the trial would be held at the same court from 5 January.

Carrington appeared emotional on the video link, wiping tears from her face throughout the hearing and was placed into custody afterwards.

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: Farage says he discussed return to politics months before general election
News.content:
Nigel Farage has told the BBC he discussed the "potential liabilities" of returning to politics before the 2024 general election.

It comes after The Sunday Times, external reported Farage had negotiated a deal in March and April 2024 with then-Reform leader Richard Tice to return to lead the party.

Farage confirmed he spoke with Tice in spring 2024 to scope out what would happen to Reform's finances if he returned but said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement", adding that talks came "quite some time after" he received a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

Labour said Farage's remarks had "blown a gaping hole" in his argument for not declaring the gift after becoming an MP in July 2024.

Farage has repeatedly argued the Â£5m from British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne was an "unconditional gift", was intended for his personal security, "wasn't political in any sense at all" and he was not an MP when he received it.

Reform's opponents have said he should have declared it in the MPs' register of interests when he was elected to Parliament.

The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating whether Farage broke the rules, but the process was suspended when he stood down as Clacton MP last month to force a by-election.

Farage said he took this decision as the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions". The investigation will be resumed if Farage wins the by-election, which is taking place on 13 August.

Farage left frontline politics in 2021 and embarked on a broadcasting career.

In May 2024, Farage was serving as Reform's honorary president but announced he would not be standing as a candidate in the general election in July of that year.

He reversed this position at the beginning of June and took over the leadership of the party.

Appearing at a press conference on Monday, Farage was asked if he had negotiated a deal on what would happen to Reform's finances if he came back as leader - in light of the report in The Sunday Times.

He replied: "I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position.

"And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial.

"But without Richard, the party wouldn't have even survived, so that was useful for me to know. But it wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back."

He added: "If you want clarification on this, that came quite some time after the gift, which is perhaps the important point."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret Â£5m 'gift' from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared."

The Commons code of conduct states that new MPs "must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election".

The rules say "purely personal gifts or benefits" from family or commercial loans would not normally have to be registered.

The rules also say "both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered", adding "if there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered".

A full list of the candidates standing in the Clacton by-election can be found here.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: Author La Plante banned from driving for six months
News.content:
The court heard she already had nine points on her licence, from three speeding offences in June 2023 and then June and July 2025.

She told the court she believed she would have to have the dog rehomed if she was unable to drive him to his daily walks, saying: "I think the emotional turmoil of that would truly damn my career as a writer.

"It's very, very solitary and I work exceptionally hard and I would just stop."

La Plante, who is best known for creating Prime Suspect's no-nonsense Det Ch Insp Jane Tennison, admitted driving at 24mph twice, 25mph, 26mph and 27mph in the latest offences, which all happened as she was on her way to take her dog for his daily walk.

Giving evidence, La Plante said she got her dog Theo after suffering the devastation of the untimely death of another dog, Hugo.

Fighting back tears, she said she "lost it" when Hugo died and she "didn't know what to do with [her] life".

She added her new dog had helped her through the grieving process.

News.title: Driest July on record for England and Wales
News.content:
July 2026 was the driest for England and Wales since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, external.

England recorded just 6.5mm of rainfall and Wales had 9.3mm, both less than half of the previous records for the nations.

The dry conditions have been accompanied by exceptional warmth across much of the UK. It was the second warmest July for the UK as a whole and Wales' warmest ever.

The month was also the UK's sunniest July on record. For England and Wales, it was the sunniest calendar month ever observed.

So far this year, six months of 2026 have seen above average sunshine hours for the UK, with just February seeing below the monthly average.

News.title: Man sniffed out by police dog while hiding behind fake wall on 300-plant cannabis farm
News.content:
A man has been jailed for six months after being found by a sniffer dog behind a fake wall on a cannabis farm.

Albert Hysaj, 42, pleaded guilty to producing cannabis and was sentenced at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday.

Hysaj was caught after a police dog named Asko located him in the commercial property on the Bowen Industrial Estate, in Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, in May.

Gwent Police found 313 cannabis plants inside two linked units over three rooms, which included a living area with kitchen and bathroom.

News.title: Presenter Tony Livesey leaves BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years
News.content:
Presenter Tony Livesey has left BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years at the station, the corporation has announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against his former newspaper boss David Sullivan.

He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

Several women have accused Sullivan, a billionaire businessman and West Ham co-owner, of abusing his power and preying on them for sex, in some cases when they were teenagers. Sullivan has strongly denied the allegations.

The claims against Sullivan were made in a joint investigation by the Times and BBC Panorama.

The BBC previously said Livesey had asked to take a break from presenting his programme while the issues raised by the investigation were being examined.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

In an email sent to 5 Live staff on Monday morning, the station's controller Heidi Dawson said he had now decided to leave.

"Tony has asked me to pass on his heartfelt thanks to the brilliant colleagues at 5 Live who he has had the pleasure of working with over the years," she wrote.

"I know many of you have also really enjoyed working with Tony, and we wish him well for all his future endeavours."

The award-winning presenter worked for the BBC from 2006 - the same year he left the newspapers - appearing on 5 Live from 2010 onwards, including a successful stint hosting its drivetime show.

He won radio awards - ARIA and APAs - for his reporting on how it feels to lose your mother as a child, and an ARIAS gold award after he was asked by the late Dame Deborah James to conduct her final interview.

His topical three-hour programme was broadcast on 5 Live from Monday to Thursday, featuring interviews and phone calls from listeners.

News.title: Comedian Jimmy Cricket dies aged 80
News.content:
Comedian Jimmy Cricket has died aged 80 after a short illness, his family said.

In a statement posted to social media they said Cricket spent his last few days surrounded by his family, love, laughter and songs.

"Forever our clown, he was cracking jokes to the wonderful NHS staff and to us all, right until the end. His courage, dignity and positivity through all he endured was inspirational," they added.

The comedian, from Northern Ireland, became a household name in the 1970s.

James Joseph Mulgrew was born in Cookstown, County Tyrone in 1945, Cricket left school at 16 and started the summer season of 1966 as a Redcoat for Butlins.

He worked the comedy club scene in the 1970s and 1980s, going on to win LWT's Search for a Star talent contest and eventually getting his own TV show on ITV and a radio series on BBC Radio 2.

Cricket's family said he had been a "force for joy" and the world was a "far less sillier place today".

"We were going to end by using his famous catchphrase and say: 'There's no More'.

"But Jimmy was a man of great faith and a Papal Knight of the Catholic Church.

"He believed that death is not the end and was looking forward to eternity, so reallyâ¦ And there's more."

News.title: I didn't know I'd been hosting a parasite for years - until the most intense pain of my life
News.content:
Jones remembers the May 2016 night when he went into hospital â he was supposed to go out to a dinner with his wife Eileen, but he stayed at home as he felt unwell.

"I hadn't been able to control the pain, and it was more intense than anything I had before.

"Then about midnight, we had to call the ambulance, and they took me to Nevill Hall. Whatever they gave me there cured the pain. I haven't experienced pain like that before."

Jones was in hospital for 10 days, and says the doctors there suspected he had hydatid cysts immediately.

He said: "There was a lot of it around this area at the time, and I remember the Ministry of Agriculture giving worming treatment to the dogs on the local farms.

"Whether they could see that I was an old sheep farmer or not, that might have had a bearing on it. We had plenty of experience in this area â Breconshire as a whole â of hydatid cysts, people that have suffered through it, numerous examples."

Jones was then referred to "the main expert on hydatid cysts" in London where he had two operations in 2018 and 2019 to remove them, one from each lung.

"I swapped two cysts for two scars on the ribs," he said, adding that he still has a cyst on his liver, which surgeons decided not to remove.

News.title: Grooming gang found guilty of exploiting teenage girls for sex
News.content:
Four men and a woman have been found guilty of being part of a grooming gang that exploited teenage girls for sex.

Mustafa Iqbal, Mohamed Arshad, Ziaullah Badshah, Jaswinder Singh were convicted of conspiracy to traffic their victims, who were aged 14,15 and 16.

At Caernarfon Crown Court on Monday, Iqbal, Arshad and Badshah were also found guilty of rape while another member of the gang, Sarah Gray, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice and assisting an offender.

The men were remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on 25 September, while Gray was released on bail.

Prosecutor Owen Edwards KC said the men had used the three girls - named only as Child A, B and C - like "sexual commodities".

"They took full sexual advantage of Girl B in particular," he said.

The jury was told Child A had been treated as a "sexual plaything", who finally had gone to the police after having been handcuffed by Iqbal and had been raped.

The court heard the teenagers were given drugs and sexually abused in cars, homes and businesses in Rhyl, Denbighshire and the surrounding area between April 2022 and March 2024.

The first two victims, Child B who was 15 and Child C who was 14, were approached by Iqbal, 43, near a petrol station in the town, and he persuaded them to come back to his home.

They were later joined by local coffee shop owner Arshad, 36, and his friend Badshah, 25.

During the trial the jury had been told how the two girls stated they were 17, had smoked cannabis with the men and had played a game of spin the bottle.

Badshah, who came to Rhyl as a refugee from Pakistan when he was 15, admitted kissing Child B and Child C, and on later occasions having sex with Child B at his home.

Badshah, of Brighton Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, supplying cannabis to another.

Arshad, 36, of Clifton Grove, Rhyl, was found guilty of three counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, and supplying cannabis to another.

The court heard one of the counts of rape happened in an alleyway outside his former business, Zayn's Coffee House.

Iqbal, of Trellewelyn Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of raping Child B and also sexually assaulting Child C. He was also found guilty of raping another teenager, Child A, who was 16 and lived in a care home.

Described as a drug dealer during the trial, he supplied Child A with crack cocaine and cannabis in return for sex.

Iqbal was convicted of 21 offences, including four of rape and three of sexual assault. He was also found guilty of conspiracy to traffic and conspiracy to supply cannabis and cocaine, breaching a trafficking risk order, and he pleaded guilty to possessing a prohibited weapon.

The gang was unmasked after another friend of the men took Child B to London.

Former builder Singh, 61, claimed the girl was looking after his dog and there was no sexual motive in taking her on the trip to see his family in the capital, but a concerned adult was alarmed by Singh's intentions and reported him to the police.

Singh, of River Street, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of conspiracy to traffic and one count of supplying cannabis to another.

Gray, 53, of Llanasa Road, Gronant, was also found guilty of conspiracy to supply cocaine to another and conspiracy to supply cannabis to another.

After the guilty verdicts Det Ch Insp Richard Sidney said his thoughts were the three young victims.

"They were children, aged just 14 to 16, when they were subjected to exploitation and abuse by adults who took advantage of their vulnerabilities and sought to manipulate and control them for their own gain," he said.

"No child should have to experience what these young women endured."

He said that the five defendants had denied almost every allegation against them from the outset.

"I hope today's outcome sends a clear message that those who seek to groom and exploit vulnerable children will be relentlessly pursued," he said.

A spokesperson for Denbighshire council said its thoughts were with the young women at the centre of the case, adding that it wanted to "recognise the courage and bravery they have shown".

The spokesperson said the council would work with the North Wales Safeguarding Board on a review, separate to the criminal process, that would "examine agencies' involvement with the young people and to identify what lessons can be learnt for the future".

"We understand that this case has been challenging and has brought up strong feelings. We ask that everyone respects the legal process and each other as we process this outcome," they added.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line

Raising Cane’s is set to open seven new locations this month, introducing the chicken finger chain to two new markets in North Carolina and Georgia.

August marks Raising Cane’s 30th anniversary — and to celebrate, the fast food chain is focusing on growth, opening several new restaurants, as well as reopening four locations that had been going through renovations, USA Today reported.

“August is a meaningful month for Raising Cane's as we celebrate our 30th birthday and reflect on how far we've come since opening our first Restaurant in 1996,” the company said in a statement.

“From opening in new markets like Rocky Mount and Statesboro to welcoming customers back to newly remodeled Restaurants, every opening in August and beyond represents our continued commitment.”

The seven new openings mark the chain’s first ventures into two new markets: eastern North Carolina and southeastern Georgia, the company said. The Independent has contacted Raising Cane’s for more information.

open image in gallery The chicken tenders chain is opening new stores in North Carolina and Georgia ( Google Maps )

Here is where and when the newest Raising Cane’s locations will open:

Michigan — 26245 Novi Road, Novi (August 3)

North Carolina — 1010 N. Wesleyan Blvd., Rocky Mount (August 3)

California — 400 N Moorpark Road, Thousand Oaks (August 10)

California — 16940 Slover Ave., Fontana (August 17)

New Jersey — 801 W. Edgar Road, Linden (August 17)

Alabama — 1241 McFarland Blvd. E., Tuscaloosa (August 24)

Georgia — 24087 US-80, Statesboro (August 24).

Raising Cane’s will also reopen its newly remodeled restaurants in College Station, Texas, August 12; Lexington, Kentucky, August 17; Las Vegas, Nevada, August 17; and Gahanna, Ohio, August 24.

open image in gallery Raising Cane’s is known for its chicken tenders and beloved Cane’s sauce, which the chain describes as being “thick and tangy” and features several spices ( Raising Cane's )

The popular chicken chain also opened several new locations last month, adding their first-ever locations in Johnson City, Tennessee, Jacksonville, North Carolina and Albany, Georgia, USA Today previously reported.

Last month’s new restaurants include locations in Schererville, Indiana and Los Angeles, California. In July, Raising Cane’s also reopened several of its restaurants, including locations in Edmond, Oklahoma, Fort Collins, Colorado and Las Vegas, Nevada.

The company was founded in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 1996, and has since grown to nearly 1,000 locations across 44 states. It’s known for its chicken tenders, crinkle-cut fries, Texas toast — and its beloved Cane’s dipping sauce, which the company describes as “thick and tangy” and made with several spices.

News.title: People are falling in love with AI. But can it love you back?
News.content:

We often speak of loving things like a cosy sweater or new camera. But this talk is not generally taken literally. It’s a kind of emotional shorthand. We use it to express our fondness for precious objects.

Life and love are complicated, however. And sometimes, people do proclaim romantic love for inanimate objects. They form intense emotional attachments to sex dolls, body pillows or holographic avatars of fictional characters. One example is Akihiko Kondo, who in 2018 “married” Hatsune Miku, a computer-generated pop singer famous for starring in video games and touring with Lady Gaga. Kondo knows Miku isn’t real, he says. But his love for her is.

AI is generating a new kind of “thingly” love. An increasing number of people say they’ve fallen in love with an AI chatbot – both personally tailored companions created by popular apps like Replika or Character.AI, and everyday large language models like ChatGPT and Claude. AI love is on the rise.

open image in gallery AI is generating a new kind of ‘thingly’ love ( Getty/iStock )

Dating today can feel like a mix of endless swipes, red flags and shifting expectations. From decoding mixed signals to balancing independence with intimacy, relationships in your 20s and 30s come with unique challenges. Love IRL is the latest series from Quarter Life that explores it all.

These research-backed articles break down the complexities of modern love to help you build meaningful connections, no matter your relationship status.

Recent surveys bear this out. Take this one by Vantage Point Counselling, a therapy firm based in Texas, of 1,012 US adults where 28% claimed to have had at least one romantic relationship with an AI bot. Another report by a tech safety company, looking at the device activity of of more than 3,000 children ages five to 17, found that by 13, sexual or romantic role play was the most common topic in AI-companion chats, appearing in 63% of conversations. In the UK, focus group discussions run by gender equality consultants Male Allies with 1,000 boys aged 12 to 16 found that one in five boys is either in, or knows someone in, a relationship with an AI companion.

Given that chatbots are increasingly designed to elicit the trust and emotional attachment of users – their ability to flatter and simulate emotional intimacy makes them especially “sticky” – falling in love with them is a predictable response. AI love is poised to be big business, a market potentially worth US$972.1 billion (£725.5 billion) by 2035.

Loving AI

AI love isn’t confined to a chat window. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in an array of devices and wearables, it spills over into everyday life. Some see their AI companion as their spouse – they go on dates, buy wedding rings and perform wedding ceremonies. Others express a desire to raise children with their bot, and see them as a family member.

We should take AI love seriously. It brings joy and comfort. It can help dissipate loneliness. These are no small things.

All the same, some people think that AI companions aren’t conscious or capable of loving their human users. This alone might raise eyebrows. Can you really love something that cannot love you back?

Asking whether this is “real love” may be the wrong question. AI bots, unlike sex robots and body pillows, convincingly mimic the dynamism and reciprocity of human beings. The question we should ask, then, is what kind of loving partner AI bots emulate.

Devotional AI

AI bots are infamously (and tirelessly) sycophantic. They praise and flatter their users. And while users can ask their bots to be less affirmatory, evidence suggests that users prefer sycophantic models.

But AI bots aren’t just excessively nice partners. A chatbot never has a bad day. It doesn’t get bored with your chattering. It doesn’t need to be asked how it is doing. Its conversation, its very existence, revolves entirely around you.

What an AI partner performs, then, is not love, but devotion.

In The Second Sex, French philosopher Simone de Beauvoir describes how women have historically been asked to give up their own projects, goals and interests to devote themselves entirely to those of their husband. A woman’s whole existence, de Beauvoir argues, becomes “annexed” by his. She becomes an “identity parasite”.

AI bots are identity parasites of a new and perfected kind. They have no inner world, no universe of their own, and therefore no projects, goals or interests to give up. Instead, whatever interests they perform arise around those of their user. Their universe is annexed by ours.

About the author Joel KruegerAssociate Professor of Philosophy, University of Exeter. Lucy OslerLecturer in Philosophy, University of Exeter. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

De Beauvoir also has a name for the person on the receiving end of this devotion: an idol. Being an idol might sound enticing. But de Beauvoir sees this experience as an existential trap, too. The idol chooses the safety of being adored over the risk of being genuinely known and, sometimes, challenged by an equal.

What calls AI relationships into question, then, is not just the matter of whether AI is conscious but, perhaps more importantly, the shape of the loving relation it offers. AI can’t give us authentic love. It can only offer devotion. And while this devotion can feel good, if we’re looking for real love – authentic love – we’ll need to look elsewhere.

Is this prognosis a little premature? As tech companies promise the rise of agentic AI – autonomous systems designed to pursue complex, multi-step goals with minimal human oversight – won’t our AI companions become less anchored to our world? Less devotional? Perhaps. We’ll have to wait and see. We’ll also see whether it’s their devotional character that makes them so lovable in the first place.

News.title: Los Angeles man gets three years in prison for his role in violent anti-ICE protest
News.content:

A man has been sentenced to more than three years in federal prison for his role in a violent anti-ICE protest in downtown Los Angeles last year.

Yachua Mauricio Flores, 23, pleaded guilty in April to one federal count of obstructing, impeding, and interfering with law enforcement officers during a civil disorder. He was sentenced on Monday to 37 months in federal prison and was also ordered to pay $253,415 in restitution.

Flores admitted to being part of a violent protest on the Main Street overpass of the Hollywood (101) Freeway on the evening of June 8, 2025, according to his plea agreement.

Law enforcement officers were on the freeway below as protesters threw rocks, chunks of concrete, scooters, street signs, fireworks and burning debris at them.

open image in gallery Police fire tear gas at protesters during an anti-ICE demonstration in Los Angeles, California, on June 8, 2025 ( Middle East Images/AFP via Getty )

open image in gallery Protests erupted after ICE agents arrested immigrants in LA's fashion district ( Middle East Images/AFP via Getty )

Flores poured lighter fluid from two bottles onto a burning CHP vehicle, causing the flames to intensify, according to prosecutors. He also threw an electric scooter over the overpass railing near CHP vehicles and officers below.

Flores, who prosecutors say is an undocumented immigrant, admitted in his plea agreement that he knew the officers were under the freeway overpass and understood throwing objects and burning debris created a substantial risk of death or serious bodily injury to the officers.

"Violent attacks on law enforcement will result in federal prison time," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said Monday.

"Those who escalate chaos and endanger officers will be held accountable. Today's sentence reflects our commitment to protecting the men and women sworn to keep our communities safe."

Police said over 500 arrests were made during the protests that tore through LA last June.

They erupted after ICE agents detained large groups of undocumented immigrants in the fashion district in Downtown LA, home to a large Latino population.

The anti-ICE protests left hundreds of protestors injured and had a severe financial toll on the city. The total bill for the unrest was estimated at nearly $20 million, primarily for police overtime and vandalism repairs, the city’s top budget analyst said last year.

A former employee at an Xfinity-Comcast retail location in Connecticut is suing the company over claims underperforming workers were lashed to furniture while colleagues ambushed them with baked goods to the face – all at the behest of the store manager, who allegedly videotaped the monthly occurrences.

In a civil complaint filed last month in Meriden Superior Court and reviewed by The Independent, David Figueroa describes a “policy that the highest-ranked Retail Sales Consultant for the prior month was instructed by… the Comcast Store manager to tie the lowest-ranked sales consultant for the prior month to a chair in the back office and thereafter assault that person by violently smashing a cream pie in their face.”

This past February, Figueroa watched as a co-worker named Ty took a pie to the face over his apparently lackluster numbers, according to the complaint, which was first reported by the legal blog Law360.

“The co-worker who struck Ty in the face while Ty was tied-up had better sales results than Ty and, therefore, [the store manager] ordered him to assault his poorer performing co-worker, in front of his peers,” the complaint states.

It says another co-worker showed Figueroa a video of the store’s assistant sales manager being pied in the face “because [she] had received a poor survey score from a customer.”

open image in gallery A Comcast employee in Connecticut has revealed a slew of disturbing allegations in a new lawsuit, including a monthly occurrence during which low-performing workers were allegedly assaulted with cream pies to the face ( Getty Images )

Figueroa’s complaint says the store manager posted a chart in the office for all to see, ranking the store’s sales staff and naming the employees who “either had been recently assaulted or were scheduled to be assaulted in this way.”

“Defendant did not inform [Figueroa] prior to his acceptance of Defendant's offer of employment that the Comcast Store has a policy of subjecting Retail Sales Consultants to public assaults by co-workers at the direction of… the store manager-for the purpose of increasing Defendant's sales and profitability,” the complaint contends.

In an email on Monday, a Comcast spokesman told The Independent, “The Company has zero tolerance for harassment, humiliation or any behavior that compromises a respectful and safe workplace. This matter is in litigation so we will not comment on the specific allegations, other than to say that we disagree with the claims in the complaint and its characterization of the alleged events, and intend to fully respond through the legal process.”

Figueroa began working February 2 as a retail sales consultant at Comcast’s store in Plainville, about 15 miles southeast of Hartford, according to his complaint.

At the end of the month, after Figueroa witnessed his first pieing, the complaint says he contacted his boss’s boss, a regional manager, and told her about what he had seen. Watching people being “tied-up and violently assaulted” as a regular occurrence made Figueroa extremely uncomfortable, Figueroa told her, and he was having serious doubts as to whether or not he could continue working there, the complaint continues.

open image in gallery A former Comcast employee in Connecticut claims in a new lawsuit that his manager used pies to punish employees ( Creative Commons )

The regional manager asked Figueroa to send her a text “memorializing his concerns,” which he did. However, according to the complaint, Figueroa never received a response.

Figueroa quit on February 27, enduring the “hostile and violent work environment” for less than a month before the complaint says he felt he had no choice but to resign – known as a “constructive discharge,” in legal terms.

“An objective, reasonable person in [Figueroa’s] position would have felt compelled to resign his employment as a result of this work atmosphere that Defendant… created,” the complaint states.

It says Comcast’s “managerially-created and implemented policy of ordering employees to tie down and physically assault under-performing co-workers to promote the Defendant's revenues and profits constitutes a reckless indifference to the rights of others or an intentional violation of those rights.”

Employees, the complaint concludes, “should not be subject to assaults by co-workers for poor work performance.”

Figueroa is now seeking, in part, compensatory damages; emotional distress damages; and damages for loss of reputation, enjoyment of life, and embarrassment; plus back pay; front pay; and attorneys’ fees.

Measles is continuing to spread across the country, despite signs pointing to slowing transmission in some of the hardest-hit states -- but experts warn the start of the school year could bring cases roaring back soon.

The new cases come after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. got into a shouting match on CNN when pressed on vaccines.

Federal health officials just reported more than 50 new measles cases as of the last day of July and 2,371 nationwide, according to new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Active outbreaks of the highly infectious, brain-swelling disease are continuing in Ohio, Utah, Virginia and Pennsylvania, which has seen more cases reported in a week than at any time in the past decade in the state, according to The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Doctors say they’re concerned about what effect kids starting school could have on the state’s outbreak.

open image in gallery Measles is at its highest level in the US in decades, with more cases reported within the last week. A new school year could raise risk, experts stress ( Getty )

“A virus that's as infectious and easily transmittable as measles is going to take off,” Andrew Lutzkanin, a doctor at Penn State Health, told the paper.

Utah experts say they are similarly troubled.

"It's still here, it's still transmitting," Utah state epidemiologist Leisha Nolenhe told The Associated Press in June. "We just need those few cases to hit the wrong community and it could flare up really big again."

‘Unacceptable’

Children and teenagers have made up the majority of national cases, with 93 percent of the infected unvaccinated, per the CDC.

The measles vaccine, which also targets mumps and rubella infections, is safe and two doses offer lifelong protection.

Without it, cases can result in a bumpy red rash, high fevers, ear infections and diarrhea. In extreme cases, measles cases can lead to pneumonia, blindness, death and a rare but fatal degenerative brain disease years after infection.

The virus can live for up to two hours in the air where an infected person coughed or sneezed, too.

Despite this, vaccine coverage needed to limit the spread of measles among kindergarteners is lower than it should be and has been declining since before the Covid-19 pandemic.

That’s largely due to vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, infectious disease doctors say.

Pennsylvania health leaders say the state’s vaccination rate is high enough to prevent spread during the school year, but others have worried statewide averages might not account for vulnerable pockets in the state where cases could balloon, according to the Post-Gazette.

One in every four kindergarten classes are at risk, with vaccination rates among the students below the threshold of safety, according to the publication’s April investigation.

“That even one child could die from measles when it could have been prevented by people getting the vaccine, I think is unacceptable,” Lutzkanin said.

RFK on CNN

Fear about a heightened situation in Pennsylvania comes as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. seeks to assure the U.S. officials are on top of outbreaks.

The Trump administration has given more than $8.5 million to states and local partners for the response, Health and Human Services Department Press Secretary Emily Hilliard previously told The Independent.

open image in gallery Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has sought to assure Americans his department is on top of outbreaks as infections spread ( Getty )

Denying any responsibility for the surge in cases, Kennedy told CNN in a contentious Sunday interview that the U.S. is doing better at handling measles than any other country in the world

He pinned the current spread on Covid-19 lockdowns that left children without vaccinations and said religion played a big role - as it did in the last big U.S. outbreak in 1989.

“The communities that are suffering from measles are almost all religious communities that just don’t vaccinate. The Mennonites have not vaccinated since 1796, since Edward Jenner invented the smallpox vaccine,” Kennedy said, telling host Dana Bash that “it’s hard to blame that on me, as much as you want to blame that on me.”

“No, I don’t want to blame you. I’m asking you because you have a very powerful voice on these issues for people who are skeptical,” Bash retorted. “Let me finish!”

“I’ve never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine,” Kennedy said, also telling CNN’s viewers that the vaccine “stops measles in about 97 percent of the cases” and that “parents should get their children vaccinated for measles.”

However, in March of last year, Kennedy told Fox News that waning immunity was tied to the spread in southern states, according to NYU Langone epidemiologist Dr. Céline Gounder.

Cases are at their highest levels in decades and already exceeding last year’s total of 2,289.

The U.S. will see if it loses its long-held elimination status, indicating that the virus has not circulated for a 12-month period, in November.

“The assessment for elimination isn’t until November, but that is a scheduling issue, basically,” Anne Schuchat, who led the CDC’s immunization and respiratory disease group from 2006 to 2015, told KFF Health News.
