Colombian Gold Draws Crowds in Alicante

An exhibition of Colombian treasures, El oro y el universo. Saberes indígenas de Colombia, has drawn about 19,000 visitors during its first month at the MARQ, the Archaeological Museum of Alicante in Spain. The figure was reported by the museum and Spanish regional press.

The show is built around 291 archaeological objects, 157 of them gold and more than 2,000 years old, lent by the Museo del Oro of Colombia’s central bank. Many of the pieces are being shown in Spain for the first time, alongside works by present-day indigenous communities.

It is one of the largest loans the Museo del Oro has made to a Spanish museum in more than a decade, and its early attendance suggests strong appetite among Spanish audiences for Colombia’s pre-Columbian heritage.

What the 19,000 Figure Tells Us

Roughly 19,000 visitors in a single month is a robust number for a temporary archaeological show in a mid-sized Spanish city. More than 3,000 of those visitors chose a guided tour, offered in Spanish, Valencian, French and English by the C.V. MARQ Foundation.

The mix matters. A high share of guided visits points to an audience that wants context, not just a look at shiny objects — a sign the exhibition’s interpretive framing is landing with the public rather than being skipped.

For Colombia, the attendance is also soft-power currency. Cultural exports like this one raise the country’s profile abroad in a register far removed from the security and drug-war stories that dominate international coverage.

Inside the Exhibition: Objects and Ideas

The pieces on view include masks, pendants, nose ornaments known as narigueras and pectorals, along with depictions of hybrid beings such as the famous human-bat figures and shamans shown in flight. Many were prized as much for their ritual role as for their craftsmanship.

The exhibition’s guiding idea is an indigenous vision of a shared universe, one populated by both human and non-human beings. In that worldview the gold objects are not jewellery or treasure to be hoarded but active presences, meant to be given, shared and returned rather than accumulated.

That framing deliberately upends the old European fantasy of El Dorado as a hoard of loot. The curators present the metalwork instead as a body of knowledge about transformation, balance and reciprocity, blending archaeology and anthropology with biology and sustainability.

The Museo del Oro on the World Stage

The Museo del Oro in Bogotá, run by Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República, holds one of the world’s foremost collections of pre-Hispanic goldwork. Loaning a substantial part of it abroad is a calculated act of cultural diplomacy.

The Alicante show was organised with the University of Cambridge, the MARQ and the C.V. MARQ Foundation, under the provincial government of Alicante. That academic partnership lends the exhibition scholarly weight and helped shape its unusual interpretive approach.

It also fits a wider pattern of Colombian museums reaching international audiences. From gold collections to modern art, Colombian institutions have increasingly toured their holdings, and the country’s museum scene continues to expand at home as well.

An Immersive Design Beyond the Vitrine

The MARQ has staged the objects inside an immersive design rather than rows of glass cases. Visitors enter reconstructed environments — a maloca, or indigenous communal house, and the heat of a metalworking workshop — using architecture, video, sound and even scent based on recent research.

The soundscape was composed for the show by the Alicante musician Luis Ivars, weaving in melodies recorded on flutes and ocarinas between 600 and 1,000 years old, together with field recordings of the Andean páramo and the Caribbean lowlands.

The approach reflects a broader museum trend toward experience-led displays, especially for archaeology, where context can be as important as the artefacts. It aims to convey a worldview, not just exhibit precious metal.

Why It Matters and Where the Show Goes Next

The exhibition runs at the MARQ until 2 May 2027, an unusually long window that should let attendance build well beyond the opening month. After Alicante, the show is expected to continue on tour in Europe.

Reported next stops include the Gaiás museum at the Cidade da Cultura in Santiago de Compostela and the MAMUZ museum in Mistelbach, Austria, extending the reach of Colombia’s gold across the continent.

For expats and travellers, the takeaway is twofold. In Spain, El oro y el universo is a rare chance to see the Museo del Oro’s holdings without crossing the Atlantic; in Colombia, the museum in Bogotá remains one of the region’s essential cultural stops.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I see El oro y el universo?

The exhibition is on show at the MARQ, the Archaeological Museum of Alicante, in Spain, until 2 May 2027, before it continues on a European tour.

How many visitors has the Colombian gold exhibition drawn?

The MARQ reported about 19,000 visitors during the show’s first month, with more than 3,000 of them taking guided tours offered in Spanish, Valencian, French and English.

Where do the gold pieces come from?

The 291 objects, 157 of them gold, are on loan from the Museo del Oro of Colombia’s central bank in Bogotá, organised with the University of Cambridge, the MARQ and the C.V. MARQ Foundation.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Romería Closes With Zero Deaths and 1,772 Medical Cases
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Romería closed without a single reported death, ending a nine-day emergency operation in which the Costa Rican Red Cross treated 1,772 people along the roads into Cartago and moved 34 of them to hospitals. The count covers July 25 through August 2, the feast day of the Virgen de los Ángeles, and it climbed steadily through the final Sunday.

At midday the Red Cross reported 1,681 people treated — 1,477 medical cases, 164 trauma injuries and three burns — with 31 transfers to medical centers, of which 20 were classified urgent, six critical and five stable. The 1,772 figure released Sunday evening is the most recent tally and remains provisional until the institution issues its close-out report.

Milena Bogantes, regional operational sub-coordinator for the Red Cross, reviewed the pattern of cases as the operation wound down. Before the walking began, the organization had said the emergencies it sees most often on this route are heat-related illness and blood pressure episodes, and it had asked pilgrims to hydrate, wear broken-in shoes and reflective clothing, and carry any prescription medication with them. In the earliest cuts of the operation, most patients were over 40, with the single largest group aged 61 and up.

The scale of the response is hard to overstate. The Red Cross fielded more than 850 responders and over 145 emergency vehicles across eight aid stations strung between San Pedro, on the eastern edge of San José, and the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles. The busiest posts were at the basilica itself, at Ochomogo and at La Galera, with smaller volumes recorded at El Cristo, Conventillos and San Pedro.

Raúl Rivera Bonilla, director general of the Fuerza Pública, said officers seized small quantities of drugs and weapons over the course of the operation. Around 500 officers were assigned to the corridor from La Sabana to Cartago during the heaviest days, working alongside roughly 150 Traffic Police officers, municipal police units and a network of surveillance cameras along the route. Authorities have not announced charges arising from the seizures, and the Fuerza Pública said it would keep its deployment in place through Monday.

Mario Redondo, the mayor of Cartago, said municipal crews recovered 13 dogs found abandoned along the pilgrimage route and took them to the city’s animal care center, where they will receive veterinary attention and, where appropriate, be neutered. Redondo put the total municipal and interinstitutional deployment at roughly 3,000 people across police forces, the Red Cross and sanitation crews, and said they collected more than 34 metric tons (37 short tons) of solid waste.

The pilgrimage itself is a walk of about 22 kilometers (14 miles) from central San José to Cartago, though many people set out from far greater distances and walk for days. Church estimates put participation across the period at close to two million, and this year’s program carried additional weight as the centenary of the Virgin’s pontifical coronation, granted by Pope Pius XI in April 1926. The 2025 operation, by comparison, ended with 2,196 people treated, 47 transferred to medical centers and no deaths.

The observance is not quite finished. The traditional Pasada takes place Monday at 9 a.m., when the image of the Virgin is carried from the basilica to the Catedral Nuestra Señora del Carmen through streets covered in flower and sawdust carpets, accompanied by bands, mascaradas, oxcarts and boyeros. Roads through central Cartago close for the procession, and nine schools along the route switched to at-home learning for the day, returning to classrooms Tuesday. Anyone driving through the Cartago canton center Monday morning should expect closures and delays until the procession finishes and traffic is restored.

Since Costa Rica has just over five million people, moving a crowd on that scale along public highways for nine days and finishing with no fatalities is the number the institutions involved will point to. The operation has been refined over decades of repetition, and the outcome reflects that: the traffic plan staged months in advance, aid posts placed where the walking gets hardest, and thousands of volunteers standing on the shoulder of a highway at three in the morning handing out water.

World.title: CONCACAF Calls for Reckoning With Infantino’s FIFA Leadership
World.content:
North and Central American football’s governing body CONCACAF yesterday called for a “comprehensive reckoning with” Gianni Infantino’s leadership of FIFA after his aborted plan to allow private investment in the World Cup. “This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behavior,” CONCACAF said in a statement.

“A comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative.” Last week, world governing body FIFA had announced plans to create a commercial subsidiary which would run its biggest events, including the World Cup and Club World Cup. This body would be open to minority private investment, under a plan which Infantino said would “turbocharge the development of the game globally” by raising up to $4.2 billion.

On Friday, facing a fierce global backlash, Infantino pulled the plug on the plan. CONCACAF, which includes all three co-hosts of the recently concluded 2026 World Cup — the United States, Canada and Mexico — as well as Caribbean associations, yesterday welcomed the decision to scrap the divisive proposal.

It joined European organization UEFA in criticizing Infantino’s actions and expressing doubt over his suitability to continue in the role. “This concern is not CONCACAF’s alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game,” said the statement.

In defending his initial proposal, Infantino had said that it could provide each of FIFA’s 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027 and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million. But the CONCACAF statement noted that FIFA already has “vast reserves,” and said that its members would push for those finances to be disbursed “for football development across our region, without compromising our shared future.”

Infantino’s plan had “advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process,” it said. “A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first.”

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Attends the Basílica Mass for the First Time Since 2023
World.content:
President Laura Fernández attended Sunday’s solemn Mass for the Virgen de los Ángeles in Cartago, the first Costa Rican head of state to take part in the ceremony since 2023, and sat through a homily in which the officiating bishop named violence, crime, drug trafficking, corruption and poverty as problems the country could no longer afford to look past.

The Eucharist began at 9 a.m. on the plaza in front of the shrine and was presided over by Monsignor Mario Enrique Quirós Quirós, bishop of Cartago, with the homily delivered by Monsignor José Manuel Garita Herrera, bishop of Ciudad Quesada. Fernández arrived with her husband, Jeffry Umaña, and was seated to one side of the altar alongside representatives of the country’s supreme powers. Her attendance had been confirmed in advance by Luis Esteban Fernández, vicar and spokesman for the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles.

Garita told the congregation that the nation was living through a moment demanding responsibility from everyone, and that violence continued to sow pain in many households while criminality cut deeply into the social fabric. He said Costa Rica needed to rediscover the value of unity, and argued that the effort had to translate into a greater culture of encounter, with citizens and authorities willing to work alongside one another.

He stressed the importance of discerning the signs of the times with wisdom, and asked for illumination for those holding public office. The Church, through his homily, called for a dialogue in which people were capable of listening to and respecting one another. The message landed at the end of a novena in which clergy had already addressed national politics with unusual directness.

On July 30, celebrating a Mass at the basilica as part of the nine days of devotion preceding the feast, Monsignor Manuel Eugenio Salazar Mora, bishop of the Tilarán-Liberia diocese, told the congregation that Costa Rica was polarized and defended the Catholic Church’s right to speak on the country’s problems. He rejected dictatorships of both the left and the right, then closed with a prayer asking that Costa Ricans preserve democracy and find the capacity for dialogue needed to reach agreement.

It was not the only exchange of the week. On July 26, during a presidential visit to Guanacaste, the priest Jeison Víquez Acuña, also of the Tilarán-Liberia diocese, urged Fernández from the altar not to raise taxes on the goods that make up the basic consumer basket, and reminded her that freedom of thought was a treasure the country needed to protect. Fernández responded publicly afterward that she would neither raise taxes nor create new ones while she was president.

The gap in presidential attendance says less about Fernández than about the office. She took power on May 8, which made Sunday the first August 2 of her administration and the first opportunity she has had to attend. The last president at the solemn Mass was Rodrigo Chaves, in 2023 — the only one of four such ceremonies Chaves attended during his term. Chaves now serves as a minister in Fernández’s cabinet.

She has also been to the basilica twice this year in a political capacity: once as a candidate on election day in February, and again on May 9, when a thanksgiving Mass for her incoming government became her first public act as president. At that ceremony she symbolically offered the presidential sash to the Virgin, and Monsignor Javier Román Arias, president of the Costa Rican Bishops’ Conference, used his homily to call for national unity and to observe that the country was losing its capacity to listen.

Neither the basilica nor Casa Presidencial has characterized Sunday’s attendance as a response to any of the recent remarks from the pulpit, and the presidential palace had not answered questions about her participation as of late last week.

The Mass marked the 391st anniversary of the discovery of the image and fell within the centenary year of its pontifical coronation, celebrated under the theme “a woman clothed in the sun, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.” Church authorities had projected participation approaching two million people across the weekend, with some estimates reaching 2.5 million over the full twelve days of the festival.

Around 500 Fuerza Pública officers and roughly 150 traffic police were deployed across the peak days, alongside Red Cross crews and hundreds of surveillance cameras — an operation that also had to account for a president who has said she is the subject of several investigated threats against her safety.

Many in the crowd travelled a long way to be there. More than 800 pilgrims from Pérez Zeledón set out after a 4 a.m. Mass on July 29 for a four-day walk north. A group of over 150 from San Vito de Coto Brus, near the Panamanian border, arrived Saturday morning after nine days and roughly 270 kilometers (168 miles) on foot.

Among them was Ronald Monge Jiménez, completing his sixth pilgrimage, who said he had decided this year to stay at the back of the group to help companions who were struggling, and described the nine days as closer to a retreat than a walk.

The crowd is also less exclusively Costa Rican than it appears. The pilgrimage draws walkers each year from Nicaragua, Panama, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador, along with visitors from the United States, Canada and Europe and foreign residents of Costa Rica who join for some or all of the route.

The ceremony was carried live nationwide as the day’s principal broadcast and remains the single most-watched religious event on the Costa Rican calendar. The festival closes Monday at 9 a.m. with the Pasada, the procession carrying the Virgin from the basilica to Cartago’s Nuestra Señora del Carmen cathedral, a tradition observed since the late eighteenth century and a considerably smaller affair than the one that filled the plaza on Sunday morning.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Economy Slows as Central Bank Warns of El Niño Risk
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Central Bank has lowered its growth forecast for this year, pointing to a climate shock that has already begun to weigh on output and warning that a severe El Niño could push up the cost of food and electricity before the year is over. In its Monetary Policy Report, the Banco Central de Costa Rica projected the economy will expand 3.4% in 2026, down from the 3.5% it forecast in its previous report.

The 2027 projection was trimmed as well, from 3.6% to 3.5%. Róger Madrigal, president of the institution, attributed the revision to a climate shock together with a moderation in household consumption and in external demand, factors he said had already left their mark during the first months of the year.

The climate variable is no longer hypothetical. The Instituto Meteorológico Nacional has confirmed that El Niño has taken hold and is strengthening through the second half of the year, with its early-warning system for the phenomenon raised from surveillance to advisory — the threshold at which forecasters treat the event as effectively certain.

The institute’s seasonal outlook for August through October anticipates below-normal rainfall across most of the country and temperatures above average, with the Pacífico Norte facing a rainfall deficit of up to 60%. The strongest impacts are expected between October and March, with temperature anomalies of as much as 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal in the most exposed regions.

Among the risks it flagged as capable of altering its projections, the Central Bank identified the possibility that a very strong ENSO event could leave impacts greater than those recorded in previous episodes. The transmission channels are familiar ones for an economy that still draws the bulk of its electricity from reservoirs and grows a significant share of what it eats. Reduced inflows to hydroelectric reservoirs force greater reliance on thermal generation, which costs more, and dry conditions across the Pacific slope and Central Valley affect the agricultural calendar in regions already under water stress.

Electricity bills have not yet shown that pressure. Rates fell at the start of this year, with the Autoridad Reguladora de los Servicios Públicos approving reductions of between roughly 5% and 16% depending on the distributor, driven by a negative Variable Generation Cost of about ₡34.274 billion — close to US$75 million at the Central Bank’s reference selling rate of ₡454.44 on July 31 — the product of less thermal generation and higher electricity exports to the regional market.

The regulator has since signaled that the arithmetic reverses next year, with fuel costs for backup generation likely to push tariffs upward in 2027, and has said it will not be able to estimate the size of any increase until October. For households and businesses, that means the bill arrives with a lag, not an exemption. Grupo ICE has moved to rent additional thermal capacity and add solar generation to cover demand through the dry stretch.

On prices, the Central Bank expects inflation to run at averages above 2% in the coming months, still below its 3% target with a tolerance band of one percentage point on either side. That represents a normalization after an extended period of deflation, and it followed a decision by the bank’s board on July 23 to reduce the Monetary Policy Rate by 25 basis points to 3.00%. Madrigal noted that the rate remains out of step with levels in other countries, and the bank flagged as an internal risk that the pass-through from its rate cuts to market lending rates may be slower than historical evidence would suggest.

The external picture is the other half of the slowdown. Export momentum has faded sharply, with the contribution of exports to GDP growth falling from 3.1 percentage points in the final quarter of last year to 1.1 points in the second quarter of this one, according to figures presented with the report. Household consumption followed a similar path, dropping from a 2.7-point contribution to 1.7. Special-regime firms in the free trade zones have decelerated following the closure of the Intel and Qorvo plants in 2025, a gap the rest of the economy has not fully filled, though the definitive regime improved its pace from 2.3% to 3.3%.

Compounding that, the colón remains at its strongest levels in two decades. The Central Bank’s reference rate closed the week at ₡448.31 for purchase and ₡454.44 for sale, a level not seen since the modern exchange regime was established in 2006. Producers of coffee, bananas, pineapple and melon have spent much of the year warning that dollar revenues no longer cover colón-denominated costs, and the Central Bank has been explicit that its dollar purchases are intended to smooth volatility rather than defend any particular level.

Tourism sits at the intersection of both pressures. The Instituto Costarricense de Turismo reported 1,605,360 air arrivals between January and June, a 7.8% increase over the same period last year and a record for a first half. June broke the streak, falling 1.2% to 214,518 arrivals, which the institute attributed to the geopolitical context, higher jet fuel prices and the concentrating effect of the World Cup on North American travelers.

Executive president Marcos Borges said the institute projects between 2.7 and 2.9 million international arrivals for the full year, a forecast that depends on the colón not appreciating further and on new air routes holding their traffic. Tourism accounts for roughly 8.2% of GDP and close to a fifth of national employment, and it is exposed to water and electricity conditions in precisely the Pacific regions the forecast identifies as driest.

The labor and fiscal indicators in the report point in the same direction. Unemployment edged down from 6.9% in May of last year to 6.7% this May, but the improvement came alongside a fall in labor participation from 55.6% to 54.3% and in the employment rate from 51.8% to 50.7%, with a recent contraction in income levels. Central government debt rose from 57.3% of GDP to 61.1% over the same twelve months.

Not every sector is slowing. Construction grew 8.9%, financial and insurance activities rebounded 5.9%, and information and communications rose 4.4%. The Central Bank also noted that the country financed its current account deficit and accumulated reserve assets through external savings.

What happens next depends heavily on rainfall. ARESEP’s October tariff calculation will be the first hard number on what El Niño costs at the meter, IMN will continue updating its seasonal outlooks as ocean and atmospheric conditions evolve, and the Central Bank’s next Monetary Policy Report will show whether a 3.4% year holds or slips further.

World.title: La Negrita: Faith, Unity, and the Heart of Costa Rica
World.content:
Today, thousands of pilgrims from across Costa Rica are arriving at the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago. They come on foot, some from nearby towns and others from distant provinces, to honor the Virgin of Los Ángeles, affectionately known as La Negrita.

This annual pilgrimage, called La Romería, is one of Costa Rica’s most important religious and cultural traditions. It brings together people of all ages and backgrounds who share a common purpose: to pay tribute to our patron saint. The event is more than a religious obligation. It is an expression of faith, gratitude, and unity that has connected generations for nearly 400 years.

The Story Behind La Negrita and the Pilgrimage

Lindsay Fendt/The Tico Times

The story of La Negrita dates back to August 2, 1635. According to tradition, a woman named Juana Pereira discovered a small, dark-colored statue of the Virgin Mary holding the baby Jesus on a rock near a spring in Cartago. She took the statue home, but each time she placed it somewhere safe, it would vanish and reappear on the same rock where she had first found it.

Perplexed, she brought the statue to the local priest, but the same thing happened again. The community interpreted this as a sign that the Virgin wanted a temple built on that very spot. A small chapel was erected there, and over time, devotion to La Negrita spread throughout Costa Rica. By 1824, the Virgin of Los Ángeles was declared the nation’s patron saint. The current Basilica, built in the early 20th century, now stands on the site where Juana Pereira made her discovery.

Inside the Basilica, the small statue is displayed above the altar, while the original rock where it was found rests in a crypt below. Next to it, a spring flows with water that many believe has healing properties. Pilgrims often collect it in bottles or drink it as part of their visit.

Since the late 19th century, La Romería has drawn massive crowds. Each year, close to two million people—nearly half the population of Costa Rica—make their way to Cartago. Some walk from San José, a distance of about 22 kilometers. Others travel from as far away as Guanacaste or Puntarenas, often beginning their journey several days in advance.

Many pilgrims walk in groups with family and friends. Some come to give thanks for a blessing received, such as recovery from illness or the safe return of a loved one. Others walk with petitions, asking La Negrita for help in overcoming personal struggles. Along the route, strangers offer water, food, or words of encouragement to those passing by, turning the event into a national act of solidarity.

For some, the devotion is deeply personal. Many pilgrims enter the Basilica on their knees, covering the final stretch in a gesture of humility and reverence. Others leave behind small metal tokens called ex-votos, which are shaped like body parts to represent healed injuries or illnesses. The walls of the Basilica’s crypt are covered with these offerings, silent testimonies to generations of answered prayers.

The Romería begins in late July with a nine-day novena of prayers and religious services held in parishes across the country. As the days pass, the number of pilgrims on the road increases, with many choosing to walk at night to avoid the heat. By August 1, the roads leading into Cartago are filled with steady streams of people.

On the evening before the feast day, a special ceremony is held in the Basilica, during which the statue of La Negrita is dressed in a new gown. This ritual, performed annually, is one of the most emotional moments of the celebration. At dawn on August 2, the main Mass is held in front of the Basilica. Government officials, church leaders, and thousands of pilgrims attend, filling the plaza and surrounding streets.

Faith and Unity

Alberto Font/The Tico Times

Organizing an event of this scale requires extensive planning. The Catholic Church coordinates religious ceremonies, while government agencies handle logistics. The Red Cross sets up first-aid stations along the main routes to Cartago, offering medical care and water to exhausted pilgrims. Police and transit officers manage traffic and help keep the routes safe.

Trains and buses run special routes to bring pilgrims as close as possible to Cartago before they begin their walk. Portable restrooms, hydration stations, and designated rest areas are placed at key points along the way.

A key part of the pilgrimage experience is visiting the holy spring inside the Basilica. Many pilgrims believe the water from this spring has special properties, particularly for those who are ill or seeking comfort during difficult times. Collecting this water has become a symbolic act, one that connects the faithful to the original story of La Negrita.

Another important tradition takes place after the feast day. Known as the Pasada, this event occurs on the first weekend of September. The statue of the Virgin is carried from the Basilica to Cartago’s cathedral and then returned in a grand procession. Streets are decorated with colorful flower carpets and sawdust designs, and the procession is accompanied by music and community celebrations.

The Romería is as much about community as it is about faith. Along the route, volunteers offer coffee, meals, and a place to rest. Local businesses set up stands selling everything from rosaries to snacks, turning the pilgrimage into a mix of devotion and cultural tradition. Families often walk together, passing the tradition down to younger generations, who grow up watching their parents and grandparents make the annual trip.

Even for those who are not Catholic, the Romería holds cultural significance. It is one of the few moments each year when our country pauses and comes together in a single, shared purpose.

Despite its spiritual importance, the Romería is not without challenges. Pilgrims often walk long distances under difficult conditions. Some develop blisters, exhaustion, or dehydration. Health officials remind walkers to stay hydrated and use proper footwear. Yet, year after year, these hardships do little to deter the faithful.

Alberto Font/The Tico Times

The determination of the pilgrims reflects the deep roots of the tradition. For many, the act of walking itself is a form of prayer. Each step is a way of expressing devotion, gratitude, or hope for something better.

The Romería is not simply an event; it is a national moment of reflection and unity. It is a reminder of how a centuries-old story continues to inspire modern Costa Rica. Today, as the crowds pour into Cartago, the plaza of the Basilica once again becomes a living testament to the power of faith and the endurance of tradition.

For those arriving today, it is the end of a long walk, but it is also a new beginning. Many will leave with a renewed sense of purpose, their faith strengthened by the experience. And in the coming weeks, the image of La Negrita will remain at the center of daily life in Cartago, as it has for nearly four centuries.

World.title: BCCI reaffirms grave concerns over BTL’s proposed Speednet acquisition
World.content:
BCCI reaffirms grave concerns over BTL’s proposed Speednet acquisition

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry has publicly reiterated its firm opposition to the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited, operators of Smart, by Belize Telemedia Limited in its current form, warning that public resources and Belizean workers’ pension funds are directly at risk.

In a release issued Monday, the Chamber said that following its formal correspondence of July 30 and a response from BTL Chairman Markhelm Lizarraga dated July 31, its critical reservations regarding governance, financial due diligence, market competition and legal compliance “remain entirely unaddressed.”

According to the release, BTL has indicated its Board of Directors is satisfied with a targeted, risk-based valuation conducted by Moore Belize, premised predominantly on a single year’s revenues. The BCCI maintains that a transaction of this magnitude demands more, because BTL is majority state-owned and significantly financed by the Social Security Board.

The Chamber laid out four concerns. On financial transparency, it insists a second, fully independent valuation supported by no less than five years of audited Speednet financial statements is a prerequisite for fair market valuation. On market structure, it notes Belize lacks any comprehensive competition and merger control legislation, meaning the deal would create what it calls a state-backed telecom monopoly without legislative guardrails. On legal compliance, it says eliminating BTL’s only meaningful competitor raises severe issues under Section 42(4) of the Telecommunications Act, and that Public Utilities Commission oversight cannot replace market-driven competition. On consumers, it warns of higher prices, diminished service quality, reduced choices and slower innovation.

“As the representative of more than 6000 employers across Belize, the BCCI has a fiduciary and civic responsibility to safeguard the business environment and public investment,” said Chamber President Giacomo Sanchez. “Voluntary promises and contractual indemnity clauses cannot replace real market competition.”

The Chamber is urging BTL’s Board, the Government of Belize, the SSB and the PUC to halt the acquisition until the audited review and second valuation are provided, a national merger control framework is enacted, and compliance with the Telecommunications Act is independently verified. It says it remains open to constructive dialogue. BTL’s fuller response to the renewed statement was not available up to news time.

World.title: Belize Government Lotteries hiring a marketing assistant, applications close August 14
World.content:
Belize Government Lotteries hiring a marketing assistant, applications close August 14

Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Creative professionals, a new opportunity has opened at Belize Government Lotteries Ltd. The company is recruiting a Marketing Assistant to support its Marketing Consultant in creating and executing campaigns across digital and traditional platforms, with applications due by Friday, August 14, 2026.

The role is hands-on and content-heavy: creating graphics and marketing materials in Adobe Photoshop, developing infographics, live feed posts and short reels, scheduling content across social platforms, building and monitoring Google Ad campaigns, editing photos and videos, maintaining the asset library, and supporting marketing projects and events. The post also includes promoting BGLL on live television through pre-approved media appearances or in-content videos, and flexibility to work holidays or weekends for expos and night markets.

Qualifications offer two routes: a bachelor’s degree in marketing, communications, graphic design or a related field with a minimum of two years of marketing experience, or an associate degree in marketing with at least five years of experience. Photoshop proficiency is required, along with working knowledge of Meta Business Suite and Meta Ads Manager and familiarity with Google Ads. Canva, Adobe Illustrator, photography skills and a valid driver’s license are assets.

The Marketing Assistant reports to the Managing Director under the Marketing Consultant’s supervision. Resumes go to [email protected], attention Human Resource Manager, Belize Government Lotteries Ltd, before the August 14 deadline.

World.title: Belize Police Department concludes 27th annual Police youth cadet corp summer camp
World.content:
Belize Police Department concludes 27th annual Police youth cadet corp summer camp

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department concluded the 27th Annual National Police Youth Cadet Corps Summer Camp 2026 in Dangriga.

The youth cadet corps summer camp was a transformative week-long program that brought together 279 cadet members and 80 police and civilian instructors from across the country, including the Cayes.

The camp was held at Ecumenical High School Campus in Dangriga Town, from Saturday, July 25, to Saturday, August 1.

The camp embodied this year’s theme, “Command with Honor, Inspire Action, Teaching Young Minds for a Successful Tomorrow.”

The official featured addresses by Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado; Sr. Supt. Gerald Jones; Supt. Elroy Carcamo (Campground Commander); and other distinguished officials.

Sponsors and cadets received certificates of participation and appreciation, followed by a ceremonial march through the principal streets of Dangriga Town accompanied by the Belize Police Department Marching Band.

The Belize Police Department reaffirmed its unwavering commitment to strengthening the National Police Youth Cadet Corps and investing in the nation’s greatest resource—its youth.

World.title: UDP hosts party convention in Twin Towns, selects 5 councillor candidates for municipal elections
World.content:
UDP hosts party convention in Twin Towns, selects 5 councillor candidates for municipal elections

By Breaking Belize News Staff: On August 2, 2026, the United Democratic Party (UDP) selected its five councillor candidates as it gears up for municipal elections in San Ignacio and Santa Elena Town.

The party convention was held in the Twin Towns.

Lin Valentine secured the highest number of votes with 555, followed by Abdel Cowo with 429, Tosh Lanza with 411, Illiana Moreno with 379, and Kim Price with 349.

The five emerged victorious from eight candidates vying for spots on the party’s municipal slate.

The elected councillor candidates will now join mayoral candidate Earl Trapp and Councillor Leader Bernadette Fernandez to complete the UDP’s ticket for the upcoming municipal elections.

Following the convention, the UDP expressed gratitude to its candidates, delegates, volunteers.

World.title: Belize City Council hosts successful Ebo Town Festival 2026
World.content:
Belize City Council hosts successful Ebo Town Festival 2026

By Zoila Palma: On August 1, 2026, in celebration of Emancipation Day, the Belize City Council and partners hosted Ebo Town fest 2026.

It was a day filled with cultural entertainment, education, and community spirit, celebrating our heritage, reflecting on our history, and strengthening the bonds that define Belize City.

The festival featured beloved Belizean dishes and proudly showcased the African traditions deeply woven into our cultural identity.

The Belize City Council extended gratitude to the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History for their invaluable collaboration and support in making this event possible.

The Council says that it remains committed to supporting events that preserve our culture, educate future generations, and provide meaningful opportunities for residents to connect.

World.title: Beach, rainforest or culture? In Belize the answer is yes
World.content:
Beach, rainforest or culture? In Belize the answer is yes

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Every vacation begins with the same argument. The beach people want salt and sun. The adventure people want jungle and adrenaline. The culture people want food, music, and history you can touch. In most of the world, somebody loses that argument. In Belize, nobody does, because this small country delivers all three, often in the same week, sometimes in the same day.

Start with the beach, because the Caribbean here makes an unanswerable opening statement. The Belize Barrier Reef, second largest on Earth, runs the length of the coast, turning the sea into a living aquarium for snorkelers, divers, and fly-fishers. On the Placencia Peninsula, the beach vacation reaches its finest form at Chabil Mar Villas, the award-winning, guest-exclusive resort where the water begins where the veranda ends, and the hardest decision of the day is hammock or pool.

Then turn inland, where the second Belize waits under the canopy. The west is rainforest country, rivers, caves, waterfalls, and the ancient Maya sites that crown it all. Base yourself at Villa Massis Resort on the banks of the Mopan River near San Ignacio, and the jungle chapter organizes itself: Xunantunich and its towering El Castillo one day, Cahal Pech the next, the legendary ATM Cave for the brave, and the river itself for the lazy golden afternoons in between. Good food, good vibes, and howler monkeys for an alarm clock.

And through it all runs the third Belize, the one that lives in people rather than places. This is a nation of cultures side by side: Garifuna drumming and hudut on the southern coast, Maya villages where chocolate is still made from bean to bar, Mestizo towns fragrant with escabeche and corn, Creole rice and beans perfected in every kitchen, and market mornings in San Ignacio where the whole tapestry shops together. Cultural immersion here is not a scheduled excursion. It is simply what happens when you talk to people.

The practicalities seal the case. Belize speaks English, pegs its dollar two to one to the US dollar, and has never been easier to reach, with a record 1.4 million visitors, new nonstop routes connecting five more American cities this winter, and Canadian service growing from three cities. The world is discovering what a single small country can hold.

The only real challenge is logistics, stitching reef, rainforest, and culture into one seamless trip, and that is a solved problem too: Barefoot Services in Placencia, local travel experts who live the destination daily, build the whole route, transfers, tours, and hidden gems included.

So bring the beach people, the adventure people, and the culture people on the same plane. Belize ends the argument the only way worth ending it: everybody wins.

World.title: ‘Kimmy Boo’, in this trimester of pregnancy, found dead in advanced state of decomposition
World.content:
‘Kimmy Boo’, in this trimester of pregnancy, found dead in advanced state of decomposition

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the sudden death of 22-year-old Kimane Rosita Ashanti Garbutt, a pregnant woman also publicly known as “Kimmy Boo,” whose body was discovered inside an upstairs room in Belize City on Sunday morning.

Police were called to a building at the corner of Vernon Street and Amandala Drive at about 9:30 a.m. on August 2. Upon arriving, officers met a 44-year-old man, who escorted them to a room on the upper floor.

Inside, police found Garbutt’s motionless body in a seated position in a corner of the room. Her body was reportedly already in an advanced state of decomposition.

Moore told investigators that he went to check on Garbutt at about 9:00 that morning but found the door to the upstairs room locked. He forced the door open, found her motionless and immediately contacted police.

According to the police report, Garbutt had suffered from epileptic seizures for several years. She was also in the third trimester of pregnancy and had reportedly been experiencing complications. She had visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for a prenatal check-up approximately two weeks before her death.

Garbutt was last seen alive at about 7:00 a.m. on Saturday, August 1. At the time, she told him that she was not feeling well.

Garbutt had previously received public attention under the name “Kimmy Boo” through several Magistrate’s Court appearances. In October 2025, she pleaded guilty to a theft charge and was fined, and in December 2025, she was fined after pleading guilty to common assault.

Her body was transported to the National Forensic Science Service laboratory, where it awaits a post-mortem examination. The cause of death has not yet been determined, and police investigations continue.

World.title: Pregnant young woman found dead in Belize City room
World.content:
Pregnant young woman found dead in Belize City room

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A death investigation is underway in Belize City after a 21-year-old woman, in the third trimester of pregnancy, was found lifeless in an upstairs room, with a post mortem examination expected to determine how she died.

According to the Belize Police Department, information of a sudden death was received at about 9:30 a.m. on Sunday, August 2, 2026, directing police to a location at the corner of Vernon Street and Amandala Drive.

On arrival, officers met a 44-year-old man who escorted them to a room on the upper floor of a building, where they observed the motionless body of a young woman seated at a corner of the room. She appeared to have passed some time before she was found. The deceased was identified as a 21-year-old domestic of the area.

The man reported that at about 9:00 a.m. that morning, he went to check on the young woman and found the door to the upstairs room locked. He forced the door open to gain entry, and upon seeing her motionless, immediately called the police.

The circumstances of her health add layers of sorrow to the investigation. The young woman had been suffering from epileptic seizures for several years, and was in the third trimester of pregnancy with complications, having last been seen by medical personnel at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital about two weeks earlier for a prenatal checkup.

She was last seen alive at about 7:00 a.m. on Saturday, August 1, when she informed the man that she was not feeling well.

Her body has been transported to the National Forensic Science Service laboratory, where it awaits a post mortem examination. Police have given no indication of foul play, and the matter remains under investigation, with the examination expected to establish the cause of death.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
