World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Poland appeals €1.3B Pfizer vaccine ruling
World.content:
Warsaw says the end of the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine upended the deal.

Poland on Monday appealed a Brussels court judgment ordering it to take delivery of roughly 64 million unwanted Covid-19 doses and pay Pfizer about €1.3 billion. Warsaw also asked judges to freeze the ruling’s provisional enforcement while the challenge is heard.

“The decision of the court of first instance does not take into account all the relevant factual and legal circumstances of the case,” the Health Ministry said in a statement. It added that Poland would use “all legal means of defense,” but declined to disclose its arguments or evidence, citing the need to protect the state’s interests.

The ruling which Poland appealed relates to a 2021 agreement the European Commission negotiated with Pfizer on behalf of EU countries. Poland stopped accepting vaccine deliveries in 2022, citing collapsing demand and the impact of Russia's war against Ukraine. Pfizer sued Poland and Romania the following year. In April 2026, a Brussels court ruled that Warsaw remained bound by the contract and ordered it to pay roughly €1.3 billion, plus interest and legal costs, for the undelivered doses.

Pfizer defended the Belgian judgment, which it told POLITICO reflected “the importance of the contractual obligations that underpinned a successful European pandemic response, built on the principle of solidarity between Member States.” The company said it was taking “appropriate steps” to ensure compliance through “established legal enforcement mechanisms,” adding that those efforts followed “years of discussions and significant flexibility to accommodate Member States' circumstances.”

World.title: Farage needs the border to be the battle of the summer
World.content:
Under its proposals, an “integrated surveillance command” to track boats using drones, space satellites and infrared feeds would be established using the Royal Navy, Royal Air Force, Royal Marines and British Army.

Small boats would be intercepted at sea with their occupants detained, medically-assessed and given food and water before being returned on military inflatable boats to the country they came from, most likely France.

“I am entirely confident that under a Reform government, within a fortnight, there would be no more boats,” Farage — who took questions at a press conference for the first time since early May — told reporters.

“If the Royal Navy is not there to protect this country from invasion, then, frankly, I can’t see what its purpose is,” he added.

Seizing the agenda

The Reform announcement comes as the ruling Labour Party enjoys a modest bounce in opinion polls two weeks after swapping out Keir Starmer as prime minister for former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.

Burnham has seized the agenda, announcing a flurry of spending commitments in his first fortnight in charge, and struck a more optimistic tone than his predecessor.

World.title: Zelenskyy appoints chief negotiator as head of foreign intelligence
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed Kyiv’s chief negotiator and former Defense Minister Rustem Umerov as head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, according to a decree published by the presidential office on Monday.

Umerov’s current position as secretary of the National Security and Defense Council will be taken over by Ihor Klymenko, who was serving as minister of internal affairs, as announced in a separate presidential decree. Klymenko had been considered by lawmakers the leading candidate to replace ousted Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

Umerov’s appointment comes as part of a broader reshuffle of Ukraine’s security leadership that Zelenskyy announced in July. The overhaul included the dismissals of Fedorov, Commander-in-Chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi and others. Ukraine needed “more strength” in its wartime leadership, said Zelenskyy.

Umerov will now be in charge of a broader portfolio including “diplomacy, defense, negotiations with the U.S. and other designated partners, as well as talks on ending the war,” according to Zelenskyy’s announcement. A key participant in Ukraine-Russia negotiations, Umerov will also continue overseeing work on the EU–Ukraine Drone Deal.

World.title: Paris court rejects pro-Kremlin TV star’s appeal against expulsion
World.content:
A Paris court on Monday rejected Russian television star Xenia Fedorova’s appeal against a ruling that she must leave the country, a week after French authorities accused her of acting as “a conduit for disinformation campaigns” orchestrated by Moscow to “destabilize public order.”

The former head of Kremlin-backed RT France, who has been under house arrest in Paris since Wednesday, challenged three government measures: the expulsion order, a requirement that she remain in Paris and report to police daily, and a six-month asset freeze. But an administrative court ruled she had failed to demonstrate any of these measures caused her immediate and serious harm.

The former RT France chief was a regular commentator on media platforms owned by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bolloré — including CNews and Europe 1 — where her Russia-friendly views on Ukraine, NATO and European security had come under growing scrutiny ahead of the country’s 2027 presidential election.

World.title: Von der Leyen rallies to support Spain after Ceuta crisis
World.content:
Around 50,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco last week, with dozens dying in the attempt. Almost all those who entered have since returned to Morocco.

Von der Leyen on Monday praised the “swift handling” of returns by Spanish and Moroccan authorities, saying they had “successfully prevent[ed] illegal movement onwards to mainland Spain and Europe.”

The exchange followed a joint letter from 22 EU leaders at the weekend calling for an emergency meeting of interior ministers and a tougher, coordinated response to the crisis. That meeting will take place on Tuesday, with EU ambassadors discussing the situation on Monday afternoon.

The intervention by EU leaders opened a new political fight over Spain’s migration policy, including Madrid’s plan to regularize more than 1 million undocumented migrants. Some governments argued that the measure created a “pull factor” by encouraging people to believe that irregular entry could eventually lead to legal residency.

Sánchez rejected that criticism in his letter, accusing some EU countries of responding in a “selfish,” “polarizing” and unlawful manner. He argued that Spain needed European solidarity rather than blame after the deaths and the strain placed on Ceuta’s authorities. The Spanish government refused to comment for this article.

Von der Leyen’s letter offered that solidarity while making clear that the crisis would also have to prompt stronger EU action.

World.title: Spain’s politicians point finger at Morocco over Ceuta crisis
World.content:
That led many to suspect that such a large flow of people could hardly be masterminded without the acquiescence of Morocco, which claims the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla as occupied territories.

Diplomatic speculation has also centered on whether Rabat could be flexing its muscles over Spain’s recent rapprochement with Algeria, which supports self-determination in Western Sahara — a territory claimed by Morocco.

“Let’s call things by their name: Morocco is using human beings to attack our sovereignty,” said Eduardo Rubiño, lawmaker with the Sánchez-allied, left-wing Más Madrid party.

Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas from the conservative People’s Party on Monday said the situation could not be characterized as “a migration crisis” because “people have the perception that this, if not orchestrated, was encouraged or permitted” by Moroccan authorities.

Vivas conceded that Madrid had to do its utmost to continue working with Rabat, but also told Spanish newspaper El País that “Morocco has shown us that it is not reliable.”

Since the outset of the crisis, Spain’s Socialist-led government has prioritized smooth relations with Morocco, which will prove critical to resolving the crisis, rather than pinning the blame on Rabat.

World.title: France bolsters checks on ‘sensitive’ foreign investments
World.content:
Earlier this year, Lecornu asked three parliamentarians from his center-right coalition to report on France’s economic security. Obtained by POLITICO, the document called for a “radical change in posture” and urged the government to take “a holistic approach” to protecting strategic assets, securing critical supply chains, reducing dependencies and strengthening technological sovereignty.

In a press release on the threshold change, Lecornu’s office said the government would give its response on any proposed foreign investments within 10 days of notification to “avoid placing an undue burden on companies’ ability to raise capital in financial markets.”

The move is intended to “guard against opportunistic acquisitions by non-EU investors in French companies listed outside the EU that could pose risks to national security,” the statement noted.

France had previously set up a screening process for planned acquisitions of over 10 percent of shares in French companies listed on European markets during Covid-19, with the stated aim of “protecting strategic companies” in a time of crisis. The measure was later made permanent and is now being extended to French companies listed outside the EU.

The new rules will come into effect in the coming days.

Other EU countries, such as Germany and Spain, have similar foreign investment screening regimes that apply a 10 percent threshold to acquisitions in certain strategic sectors.

Paul de Villepin contributed to this report.

World.title: Iran signals no immediate U.S. talks after Trump says negotiations to resume
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would resume Monday, after scrapping a planned military strike over the weekend. Speaking on Sunday, the American leader also refused to set a deadline for reaching a broader deal with Tehran.

“They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming. Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon, and we’ll see,” said Trump, talking to reporters aboard Air Force One.

Asked whether he had imposed a deadline, the U.S. president responded: “Would I rather make a deal? I’m not looking to kill people because people die, a lot of people die, and we don’t want that.”

Trump’s remarks came on the heels of his early Sunday announcement on Truth Social that the U.S. was shelving a “massive attack,” after Iran and several Middle Eastern countries asked Washington to pause military action while negotiators worked toward an agreement. He said the framework under discussion included the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat, adding that Israel had also agreed to pause strikes.

Baghaei stated there would be “no significant change” in the situation in the Strait of Hormuz as long as Iran remained under what he described as U.S. military pressure.

World.title: Authorities probe boat and jet ski crossings from Ceuta to mainland Spain
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. World.title: Alleged operator of major darknet drugs platform charged in Germany
World.content:
More than a year after authorities took down the darknet marketplace “Archetyp Market,” German prosecutors have charged the alleged operator of the platform, which was reportedly used for the large-scale trading of illegal substances.

 

The 31-year-old suspect is accused of having run the platform since July 2020, facilitating the sale of narcotics and other illegal substances.

Prosecutors allege that, from June 2022 onward, he operated the marketplace as part of an organized criminal group involving at least two other people, generating around €20 million in revenue.

At the time it was shut down in June 2025, Archetyp was the world's largest darknet marketplace for illegal drugs.

The platform offered a wide range of substances, including cocaine, heroin, crystal meth, fentanyl, and crack cocaine. It also hosted listings for cannabis products, prescription drugs, performance-enhancing substances, and new psychoactive drugs.

Between November 2022 and June 2025 alone, around 2.3 million orders were processed on the platform, with an estimated turnover of about €330 million.

According to the indictment, the man set up and operated the platform's technical infrastructure. He is also alleged to have determined the marketplace's strategic direction and enabled vendors to trade in illegal goods.

More than 600,000 customer accounts were registered on the platform. The cryptocurrency Monero is said to have been used as a payment method, with the operator allegedly receiving a 5% commission on each sale.

The investigation took place as part of the international operation "Deep Sentinel", which was coordinated by the Central Office for Combating Cybercrime and the Federal Criminal Police Office. German authorities were supported by Europol and Eurojust.

As part of the investigation, authorities seized suspected criminal proceeds, including cryptocurrency, cash, and luxury vehicles, with a combined value of nearly €10 million.

If convicted, the suspect faces up to 15 years in prison, in addition to the confiscation of the seized assets. He was arrested at his home in Barcelona in June 2025 by a special unit of the Spanish National Police and was later extradited to Germany.

World.title: Thousands of migrants, including more than 860 minors, remain in Ceuta
World.content:
Authorities in Ceuta are struggling to cope with thousands of people that remain in the autonomous city following the mass arrival of migrants last week.

 

Security forces estimate that around 73,500 people have already left the North African exclave and returned to Morocco, while local authorities say up to 5,000 remain in the Spanish territory, including 862 minors.

The crisis has so far resulted in at least 88 confirmed deaths, according to Ceuta’s authorities, in addition to bodies recovered by Moroccan authorities in Moroccan waters.

Juan Vivas, the president of Ceuta, estimates that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the city four days after the mass influx from Morocco. He said the situation has not yet returned to normal and that Ceuta is still dealing with the aftermath of the incident.

Vivas added that between 1,800 and 2,000 people had already entered the city by swimming in the days before the mass crossing, a warning sign that he said showed the need for stronger border monitoring and better coordination to prevent another such crisis.

The Ceuta leader also highlighted the emotional toll of the crisis on residents, describing the fear, uncertainty, and sense of helplessness some had experienced. In an interview with Spanish newspaper El País, Vivas said: “Morocco has shown that it cannot be trusted; we must demand respect from it.”

More than 860 minors remain

Ceuta is seeking to expand its reception capacity to care for the 862 minors currently left under the city's watch.

Authorities say the figure could approach one thousand and admit that some may still be on the streets and unaccounted for.

While new facilities are being prepared, existing shelters are operating beyond their capacity. The Spanish territory is continuing to offer support for the minors and is preparing new reception measures while it processes possible transfers to mainland Spain.

City services have increased support, providing accommodation, food and clothing. Younger children have been placed in more suitable facilities, while older teenagers are being housed in temporary spaces until more resources become available.

Caring for minors has become one of the city's main priorities, with around 250 workers assigned to the task. Officials do not rule out further increases in the number of children under the city’s care. Drawing on the experience of the 2021 migration crisis, the Ceuta government estimates the figure could eventually reach between 1,000 and 1,100 minors.

The city’s reception system is completely overwhelmed. Its 29 standard places for minors are currently operating at almost 3,000% of their capacity. The local government is calling on the Spanish state to provide urgent assistance and additional funding, while preparing new facilities, including an industrial warehouse in El Tarajal, to cope with the arrivals.

Ceuta residents take action amid growing uncertainty

Fears of further incidents following the mass arrivals have prompted some residents of Ceuta to set up barriers in the territory, installing makeshift fences to restrict access to certain streets.

Tensions have risen in several parts of the city in recent days, with residents reporting isolated incidents and confrontations, according to El Faro de Ceuta. In one neighborhood, a resident claimed he was assaulted after refusing to give a cigarette, while some young migrants said they regretted that the actions of a small number of individuals were affecting the image of the wider group.

World.title: Ceuta explained: How Spain's biggest migration crisis unfolded
World.content:
An unprecedented migration crisis unfolded in Ceuta last Wednesday and escalated dramatically on Thursday, when tens of thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave illegally.

 

In the end, between 60,000 to more than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Cueta, marking the territory's largest migration crisis. Footage showed thousands of people swimming, navigating around breakwaters or climbing down steep areas in the autonomous city.

The influx prompted Spain to deploy its military and police to contain the situation. Most of those who had entered the North African enclave returned to Morocco within hours, largely due to a lack of accommodation and basic supplies.

Most of the new arrivals were young men, but the footage also showed women with children and entire families, on a journey fraught with the risk of drowning and exhaustion.

At least 88 people died, Spanish officials said on Monday, though Moroccan officials later presented a lower estimate.

Amid criticism from Ceuta's president, Juan Jesús Vivas, as well as growing calls to amend immigration laws to allow for immediate push backs of those who crossed by swimming, Spain and Morocco reached an agreement to speed up the repatriation of migrants.

Spanish army soldiers alongside migrants who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday 1 August 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

The Spanish government and Moroccan authorities have attributed the surge to rumours circulating on social media that falsely claimed a recent Supreme Court ruling prevented the immediate return of migrants, as well as to the activities of people-smuggling networks.

What neither side has adequately explained is why, according to reports from the area, Moroccan security forces initially allowed large crowds to advance towards the border unhindered, or how thousands of people from Casablanca, Rabat, Tangier and Marrakech were able to travel north without the closure of access routes.

The delayed intervention of Moroccan authorities only fuelled suspicions that the surge was coordinated from within.

Migrants who crossed into Spain are escorted by Spanish soldiers towards the Spanish-Moroccan border for their return to Morocco on 2 August 2026. AP PhotoFoto AP/Bernat Armangue

The New York Times reported accounts from several young men explaining how the country's authorities encouraged them to cross into the Spanish city.

Alaoui, 26, said that when his group approached the border on Thursday, several Moroccan police officers pointed them in the right direction, telling them to "go that way, go that way," the US outlet reported.

Spain's Civil Guard reportedly spotted Moroccan intelligence agents among the group of migrants

Sources within Spain's Civil Guard also claimed that officials from Morocco's intelligence service had infiltrated the crowds entering Ceuta.

According to 'El Español' (source in Spanish), they were able to detect so through a camera surveillance system installed at the Ceuta border. Civil Guard analysts identified several individuals operating on the ground, dressed in civilian clothes and mingling with groups of migrants, acting as guides, gathering information and coordinating the crossings.

A migrant who has crossed from Morocco into Spain drinks water distributed by Spanish soldiers in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Sunday 2 August 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

If accurate, these findings challenge the theory that the surge was a spontaneous phenomenon driven largely by social-media rumours and instead suggests a degree of cooperation involving state intelligence actors.

Who was pulling the strings inside Morocco?

According to Spanish newspaper 'The Objective' (source in Spanish), which cited Moroccan sources familiar with the kingdom's power structures, the man identified as the possible mastermind of the operation is Fouad Ali El Himma, a close friend and advisor to King Mohammed VI who is described in some circles as Morocco's 'viceroy'.

A former senior Interior Ministry official and founder of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) in 2008, El Himma is said to have sought to exploit the migration chaos for a dual purpose: to weaken the government of Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch and to strengthen PAM's position ahead of Morocco's general elections.

This timing would not be accidental. On Wednesday, Mohammed VI delivered a speech marking the 27th anniversary of his accession to the throne, projecting an image of stability and progress.

Hours later, thousands of Moroccans were attempting to reach Ceuta, highlighting the stark contrast between the speech and the scenes at the borders.

Supporters of this theory point to events of 2021, when about 10,000 people entered Ceuta after Moroccan forces relaxed border surveillance during the diplomatic crisis sparked by Spain's decision to admit Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali for hospital treatment.

This instance demonstrated Rabat's ability to control migration flows in ways that can exert political pressure on Spain.

Soldiers from the Spanish army travel in military vehicles after being deployed in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday 30 July 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

Migration as a bargaining chip and Pedro Sánchez's role in Spain's relations with Morocco

Spain has a long history of migration tensions along its southern border, but the Ceuta crisis cannot be understood without consiering the complex relationship between Madrid and Rabat, nor without the disagreements between Pedro Sánchez's government and several of its European partners over migration policy.

In 2022, Sánchez endorsed Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara, backed by the United States. The move—which marked a historic shift from Spain's traditional position of neutrality—was welcomed in Rabat and widely criticised in Spain, including by the Polisario Front and by some parties within the coalition government.

The mass regularisation of migrants driven by the Spanish government has also triggered an open conflict with leaders from 22 European Union countries, who signed a letter explicitly linking that policy to the so-called pull factor and to the Ceuta crisis.

From Italy, Meloni justified the joint letter by saying that "defending borders is a shared responsibility". Italy itself last week introduced stricter temporary Schengen controls for non-EU citizens travelling from Spain.

It is worth noting that the European Union offered to deploy the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in Ceuta, given the gravity of the situation, but the Spanish government rejected the offer.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the return to Morocco of most of those who crossed into Ceuta. However, tensions between Madrid and Brussels remain high.

Pedro Sánchez sent a letter to Brussels criticising the "lack of solidarity" of some EU partners. The letter contained no mention of Morocco's responsibility for the crisis. The Socialist leader also requested an emergency videoconference of EU interior ministers.

The Trump factor: facts and context behind Washington's role

Days before the Ceuta crisis, US President Donald Trump sent a message to Mohammed VI for the occasion of Throne Day, reaffirming Washington's recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and calling Morocco's autonomy proposal "the only basis for reaching a fair and lasting solution".

The message came just days after Morocco named one of its main motorways after the US president.

In April 2026, a Capitol committee approved a budget proposal that included a non-binding recommendation calling on the US diplomatic service to open discussions on Ceuta and Melilla, arguing that the two lie in "Moroccan territory". The proposal received 35 votes in favour, all from Republican members, and 27 against.

During the crisis in Ceuta, the Trump administration has used its platform to warn for the risks of illegal immigration and of laws that fail to curb migrant flows, blaming the "far left" for the situation. One of the few voices to focus on Morocco's responsibility was Anna Paulina Luna, a member of the House of Representatives for the Republican Party.

According to correspondent David Alandete (source in Spanish), the Republican Party's closer ties with Morocco responds to a clear strategic logic: Rabat has demonstrated its willingness to take significant steps to strengthen its relationship with Washington, from recognising Israel to allowing the port of Tangier to be used by arms-carrying ships, naming a road in Western Sahara after Trump and cooperating militarily when requested.

Meanwhile, Pedro Sánchez's government has increasingly become a more difficult partner for Washington, amid repeated disagreements over the war in Gaza, NATO defence spending and the recognition of Palestine.

According to Alandete, US officials don't doubt that Morocco has at times used irregular migration as a means of applying pressure, but there is little political appetite in Washington to back Sánchez against Rabat.

A historical footnote provides further context: in 1967, dictator Francisco Franco warned US President Lyndon B. Johnson in a letter about the risks of rearming Morocco, describing it as an "aggressive and destabilising" nation.

Decades later, former Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez responded to Moroccan threats to annex Ceuta and Melilla with a direct warning: "You know we can bomb Rabat within 48 hours". This approach to managing pressure from Spain's southern neighbour stands in stark contrast to the current government's stance.

The strategic position of Gibraltar: is the control of the Strait of Hormuz what is really at stake?

Several European geopolitical analysts, including French commentator Laurent Ozon (source in Spanish) and historian Édouard Husson, have recently argued that the Ceuta crisis goes beyond the question of migration or internal power struggles in Morocco.

Their main argument is that, with the Strait of Hormuz under growing strain following the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, as well as pressures on the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, the Strait of Gibraltar—whose territorial waters are under Spanish sovereignty—is gaining exceptional strategic value as the only secure access route to the Mediterranean for international shipping.

According to this interpretation, the United States and Israel would be seeking to establish an alternative corridor through Morocco that would not rely on Spain or, by extension, on the wider European alliance. Under this scenario, Ceuta would be a key asset: control over the city would enable Rabat, acting as a proxy power for the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, to challenge Spain's control of the gateway to the Mediterranean.

Spanish police officers intervene as migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday 30 July 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

Ozon also argues that European anti-immigration right-wing parties and certain media outlets are, consciously or not, helping to isolate Spain by framing the issue solely around migration policy while overlooking the wider European interest in preserving Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta.

However, this hypothesis, which is gaining traction in certain European geopolitical circles, is not currently backed by any official documentation. It should be read as an interpretative framework proposed by analysts.

A crisis contained but far from over

The Ceuta crisis cannot be viewed as an isolated event. It is the latest development in a broader sequence of events, which includes the 2021 migration incident, Spain's shift in position on Western Sahara, allegations that Pegasus spyware was used against Spanish government officials from Morocco, ignored warnings from the CNI intelligence service, mass migrant regularisation and the gradual deterioration of Spain's standing in its relations with Washington and Brussels.

But beyond the competing theories, several points remain clear: Morocco has once again demonstrated its ability to influence migration flows; that, according to police intelligence sources, Spanish authorities were warned and did not act; that at least 88 people have lost their lives attempting the crossing and that hundreds remain in Ceuta with no short-term solution in sight.

Many local residents have voiced their frustration over the government's response to a situation that is not new, and which they say makes them feel unsafe and unprotected.

Residents of Ceuta protest against the arrival of Spanish far-right politician Alvise Pérez in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday 1 August 2026. Foto AP/Bernat Armangue

Spain's King Felipe VI also sought to send a message of suppor to the people of Ceuta, expressing his "indignation" and recalling that "the state must safeguard the security of Ceuta and Melilla".

The question now facing Spain, is whether the country still has the capacity and political will to manage its southern border with relying on Morocco's cooperation, and whether the European bloc can maintain a united response when crises like last week's in Ceuta emerge again.

World.title: England and Wales record driest July on record, Met Office says
World.content:
England and Wales recorded their driest July on record this year, the UK's national weather agency has announced, citing provisional figures.

 

The Met Office described July as an "exceptional month" for the UK's weather books, with provisional statistics showing records were challenged or broken for temperature, sunshine, and rainfall.

According to the agency, England saw 6.5mm of rainfall over the month of July, 10% of its usual average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm, which was set in 1911.

Southern England also experienced its "driest month ever recorded" in July, the Met Office added, noting that records dated back to 1836.

In Wales, 9.3mm of rainfall was recorded in July, around 9% of the normal average and again less than half of the previous record of 22.6mm - also set in 1911.

Dr. Amy Doherty, a science manager at the Met Office, called July a "truly remarkable month in the UK's climate record."

“The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records," she said.

Europe's scorching summer

Much of Europe has sweltered under high temperatures this summer, with brutal heatwaves wreaking havoc across the continent - which has been battling devastating wildfires and severe droughts.

A pharmacy display shows a temperature of 43 degrees Celsius in Paris during a heat wave, Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Emergency services and hospitals have been pushed to their limits amid repeated surges in callouts linked to the hot weather, and many countries have reported increases in heat-related deaths. In July, the UK Health Security Agency said there were estimated to have been around 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during two hot spells in May and June.

Soaring temperatures are now also adding to concerns of an energy crisis in central Europe, where the Danube River has dropped to record-low levels.

In Hungary, a fresh heatwave almost forced the shutdown of the nation's only nuclear power plant for the first time in 44 years, although Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Monday that it was still in operation for the time being.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s military shake‑up continues – but Fedorov remains out
World.content:
Rustem Umerov, former secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council has been appointed as head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service on 3 August.

 

Umerov has also been a key member of Kyiv’s negotiating team in the US-led peace process and he will carry on with this task, according to Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Ukraine’s president explained as well that Umerov will also continue coordinating the Drone Deal initiative with foreign partners, including in the Middle East.

"He has greater capacity to deal with these issues simultaneously — diplomacy, defence, and the negotiations process with the US and some other partners," Zelenskyy said during an event with diplomats on Monday.

Former Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko will replace Umerov as secretary of the National Security and Defence Council.

The appointments come as part of Zelenskyy’s war-time government reshuffle launched in July, which triggered a self-inflicted political and military crisis.

FILE - Secretary of State Marco Rubio, left, and Secretary of the National Security of Ukraine Rustem Umerov shake hands, Nov. 30, 2025 AP Photo

Pro-Fedorov protests continue in Kyiv

Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service has been without a permanent chief since winter, a situation that has drawn far less attention than turmoil at another key institution - the defence ministry, which has now gone more than two weeks without a full‑time minister.

Ukrainians are still demanding that Zelenskyy reinstates former Mykhailo Fedorov after his dismissal triggered nationwide street protests.

On 31 July Kyiv saw what the organisers claimed was the “the largest protest since the Revolution of Dignity” in 2014.

Activists shout slogans during a thousands-strong rally to denounce Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to dismiss Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, Kyiv, Ukraine July 31, 2026. AP Photo

Ukrainian war veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi, one of the protest movement's public leaders, called on Zelenskyy to “give Mykhailo (Fedorov) a year to carry out the reforms, and then make decisions based on the results."

Koziatynskyi said even “during the air raid alert in Kyiv, the protesters refused to disperse and chanted: "We stand and we will keep standing.”

“Frustration and anger are building up in society, and it's currently completely unclear how such a disoriented state will enter the promised harsh winter.”

“You must end the protests by bringing Fedorov back to the Ministry of Defence,” he said calling on Zelenskyy to fulfil the last one of the protesters' original demands.

Earlier Ukraine’s president already dismissed Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander in chief and replaced him with Mykhailo Drapatyi, a widely respected commander.

But as the protesters vow to continue demonstrating, Zelenskyy has given no indication that he intends to return Fedorov.

World.title: Study shows why younger generations may be more cancer-prone
World.content:
Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.

Making cancer cell therapy affordable To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.

In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.

"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.

Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.

Here's what you need to know about breast cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.

There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.

An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.

Prostate cancer: The shift in early detection To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can I improve my biological age?

We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.

"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."

To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.

And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.

It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.

"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.

She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.

"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.

Could microrobots be used to zap cancer cells? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.

Can my doctor determine my biological age?

In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.

Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.

"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Dry Danube River threatens nuclear power in Romania, Hungary
World.content:
Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling riverwater. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.

Several central and eastern European countries are facing power shortages and impacts on industry amid prolonged hot and dry weather and record low levels on the Danube River and other waterways.

Hungary narrowly averted switching off its lone nuclear plant, but had still powered it down to a fraction of capacity. In Romania, the navy demolished a rocky outcrop exposed in the Danube's riverbed, trying to improve the water flow.

And in Serbia, hydroelectric power output was severely impacted by the dry conditions.

Continued hot and dry weather is forecast during the week, providing little sign of relief.

The Cernavoda nuclear plant draws its cooling water from the Danube Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

How did Romania try to feed the Cernavoda power plant?

Romania's military detonated a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels on a branch of the Danube, seeking to improve the flow of cooling water to the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which typically supplies about one-fifth of the country's power.

The plant draws all of its cooling water from the Danube.

Soldiers detonated a rock some 50 kilometers (roughly 30 miles) upstream. The debris would be taken to a strategic spot and sunk to help raise the water level.

Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the operation was a success, and also said the military had been waiting for a chance to access and demolish the rocks for decades.

Romania's navy was in action on the river on Monday Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

If the partial diversion of the water fails, Miruta said, the plant would likely have to shut down entirely by Thursday.

Caretaker Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said that carmakers Dacia and Ford had agreed to suspend production in Romania until August 19, following a crisis meeting with representatives of the energy-intensive industry. He said that other companies would be taking similar steps.

What was the situation at Hungary's Paks power plant?

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was possible to avoid the unprecedented total shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant on Monday that was originally announced last week.

But the four-reactor station that typically generates almost half of Hungary's electricity production and around a third of its consumption was running at little more than 10% capacity on Monday.

The four-reactor Paks plant is a key contributor to Hungary's energy output Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

Hungary had asked industrial users to curb consumption and households to make voluntary savings. Electric-powered freight trains were also stopped on Monday to reduce the load on the grid.

Magyar thanked people for their restraint on Monday evening.

"We have entered the critical period. The network is stable, consumption is currently well below planned levels, thanks to self-restraint. The last Paks turbine is operational. I will report back shortly from the (grid operator) MAVIR control room," he said.

Magyar also said slightly earlier on Monday that "water management forecasts for the coming days have become slightly more optimistic."

How power plant closure impacts Hungary's new government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How was Serbia affected?

In Serbia, the vast Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube was operating at only around one-fifth capacity on Monday.

Prime Miniser Djuro Macut convened an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss the energy problems.

He appealed to residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners," having described the situation as "serious an demanding" late on Sunday.

Shallower stretches and Danube tributaries have been reduced to a trickle in the heat Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

Far upstream in Bavaria, the Danube's levels were also affecting freight transport.

New German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the historic low levels on the Danube, and particularly the Rhine to the west — Europe's busiest inland freight waterway — were providing a first challenge for his tenure.

"It is indeed a very tense situation with the low waters," Bilger told Reuters TV on Monday, saying he would chair a crisis meeting on Thursday. "We are used to repeated low water situations, but this is really a very early point in the calendar year for problems of the kind we're currently experiencing."

Typically European rivers reach their lowest levels slightly later in the summer — it's entirely possible that several more weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather are yet to come.

Danube water levels far upstream in Bavaria are also well below even their seasonal expectations Image: Manfred Segerer/IMAGO
