Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: South Ossetia presidential election: Meet the seven contenders
World.content:
Presidential contenders in South Ossetia

Registration of candidates for South Ossetia‘s snap presidential election, scheduled for 18 September 2026, has closed, with seven contenders set to run.

Yet, even before the campaign has begun, many in South Ossetia believe the outcome is already decided. Most see acting President Marat Kambolov – a senior Russian official appointed from Moscow – as the clear frontrunner and the likely winner.

Candidates

Marat Kambolov

The initiative groups have nominated acting President and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov, former KGB officer Kazbek Kodoyev, and Eduard Gabarayev, a member of the extra-parliamentary Iron party and a former defence ministry official.

***

Murat Valiyev

Several political parties have also nominated their own candidates. Khoh Chochiyev, a former State Protection Service officer, has been nominated by the extra-parliamentary Iry Farn party. Another security official, Murat Valiyev – a serving officer in the presidential State Protection Service and a former KGB officer – has been nominated by the Patriots of Alania party.

***

Zurab Kokoyev, chairman of the Unity party, which has previously been in power, has also announced his intention to run, despite having earlier backed Kambolov’s nomination.

***

Fatima Khugayeva

Finally, the only woman in the race and a newcomer to South Ossetian politics is Fatima Khugayeva, a retired lieutenant colonel in Russia’s Interior Ministry – making her yet another candidate with a security background.

She has been nominated by the Development Party. Although she was born in Moscow, Khugayeva has South Ossetian roots. After retiring, she returned to her ancestral homeland, got married, and now works as a deputy headteacher while teaching history.

Dropouts

In a surprise development, Georgiy Kabisov, leader of the Iron party, a former head of the Information and Press Committee who previously served a prison sentence for fraud, abandoned his earlier plans to run for president. His party now appears set to throw its full support behind its other nominee, Eduard Gabarayev. Vladimir Kelekhsayev, leader of the Unity of the People party and a former member of parliament, has also decided not to run. His party is likely to back one of the remaining contenders.

Following the close of registration, the Central Election Commission will review the documents submitted by the registered contenders to ensure they meet all legal requirements. Only then will they officially acquire candidate status, allowing them to open campaign accounts and begin collecting signatures. Some contenders may still be eliminated at this stage if irregularities are found in their paperwork.

Frontrunner, ‘supporting cast’ and ‘independent players‘

Of the seven contenders, only Prime Minister Marat Kambolov appears to have a realistic chance of winning. A Moscow official dispatched from the Kremlin just a few months ago, he has no prior ties to South Ossetia but enjoys unprecedented political backing. Even the territory’s main opposition forces have effectively thrown their support behind him, opting not to contest the election so as not to stand in his way.

Zurab Kokoyev

Kazbek Kodoyev

Most of the remaining candidates are viewed by analysts as technical candidates whose role is largely to fill out the ballot rather than mount a serious challenge.

This includes Kazbek Kodoyev and Zurab Kokoyev.

***

Murat Valiyev is a political newcomer whom the Patriots of Alania party appears to have nominated primarily to give him electoral experience. The campaign will also provide the party, founded only in 2023, with an opportunity to raise its profile. At the same time, the party’s chairman, Dzambolat Tedeyev, has urged voters to back Marat Kambolov.

Khoh Chochiyev

Analysts regard Khoh Chochiyev and Eduard Gabarayev as the more independent contenders.

Eduard Gabarayev

In this context, “independent” means that neither politician is regarded as a technical candidate or as someone willing to run merely to benefit the frontrunner. However, both are backed by different groups of current and former officials, as well as opposition figures.

***

Fatima Khugayeva, meanwhile, is widely seen as a candidate backed by local business interests. The Development Party, which nominated her, is led by businessman and restaurateur Albert Valiyev, who is friends with Khugayeva’s husband, a producer of alcoholic beverages.

However, Khugayeva is not merely being put forward because of her husband’s connections. She has political experience of her own: she remains a member of the Russian party Communists of Russia and has frequently taken part in protest rallies.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

World.title: Ukraine drone strike on Russian holiday spot kills 11
World.content:
At least 11 people have died, and dozens are wounded after Ukraine launched strikes at a Russian Black Sea resort and the annexed peninsula of Crimea, according to officials.

A drone attack on Russia's seaside village of Arkhipo-Osipovka killed seven people, with three children among them, according to a post from the crisis task force for Russia's southern Krasnodar region on social media.

Venyamin Kondratyev, the governor for the region, confirmed the strike earlier, saying Ukraine had struck the Black Sea resort with a drone.

Unverified social media footage showed what appeared to be a drone crashing into a busy beach at Arkhipo-Osipovka, as tourists looked on from the shore and in the water.

Krasnodar region Governor, Venymin Kondratyev posted about the strike on social media. (Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP Photo)

The Russian health ministry said 21 people, including three children, had been rushed to hospital and that nine people were in a serious condition.

Specialist medical teams were dispatched to the resort region according to Russian authorities.

Four people were also killed in a Ukrainian strike on Russia-annexed Crimea, the Moscow-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov said in a post on Telegram.

Both locations are popular summer destinations among Russian tourists.

Increasing civilian deaths

The United Nations has reported an uptick in civilian deaths in the Russia-Ukraine conflict throughout 2026, as the four-and-a-half-year war grinds on with no sign of a peace deal.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine, which, like Russia, says it does not deliberately target civilians in the full-scale war which Moscow launched in 2022.

Russia last month accused Kyiv's forces of killing 11 people, including four children, in an attack on a holiday camp in a Russian-held part of Ukraine's ‌Zaporizhzhia region.

Russia itself has repeatedly struck targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, displacing millions and laying waste to swathes of Ukraine. Thousands of civilians have so far died in the war, most of ​them Ukrainians killed in Russian attacks.

Ukraine often fires hundreds of drones into Russia at night, in retaliation for Moscow's own barrage of drones and missiles against Ukrainian towns and cities.

Russia launched its full-scale offensive against Ukraine in February 2022, and has regularly struck its neighbour, including from the Crimean peninsula.

Ukraine has in recent months intensified its counter-strikes on Crimea — seized by Moscow in 2014 — leading to electricity and fuel shortages this summer.

Firefighters put out a fire at a petrol station following a Russian drone attack in Dnipropetrovsk region, (Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP Photo)

On Monday, a Russian attack on a petrol station in Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city — killed three people, the governor of Dnipropetrovsk region, Oleksandr Ganzha, said

Among the victims was an eight-year-old boy, he said.

In a picture he posted, firefighters could be seen dousing the flames near the charred shell of a car at a gas station.

Another Russian attack, on the southern Odesa region, wounded 13 people on Saturday, said governor Oleg Kiper.

AFP / Reuters

World.title: Neil the seal merch site taken down after questions about donation claim
World.content:
A website selling Neil the seal merchandise has been taken down after questions about claims it donates a percentage of profits to marine conservation.

The "Neil the seal official" website advertised merchandise including a $150 hoodie featuring a depiction of the popular elephant seal that visits beaches in Tasmania's south biannually.

The company stated it financially supported marine conservation.

"A portion of every purchase from the Neil the Seal Official store goes toward marine conservation work protecting seals, sea lions, and ocean ecosystems in Australia and beyond," it stated.

"We're building formal partnerships with conservation organisations.

"Direct donate links and clearer reporting on impact will be published here as those partnerships are confirmed — in the meantime, every order still contributes, and you can support the organisations below independently today."

The website was selling a hoodie for $150. (neilthesealofficial.com)

The website stated it "supports and recommends":

Australian Marine Conservation Society

WWF Australia

Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE), which was incorrectly referred to by its old name, DPIPWE

Marine Mammal Foundation

For each organisation, it stated "official partnership details" were coming soon.

But the three organisations and the government department told the ABC they had not had any contact with the company, nor had they received any donations from it.

The website said it donated to marine conservation efforts. (neilthesealofficial.com)

After the ABC contacted the website, it altered the section about its support for those organisations.

It changed "organisations we support and recommend" to "organisations we recommend" and removed the references to "official partnership details coming soon".

It also added links to donate directly to the organisations.

Shortly afterwards, the website was taken down.

The front page of the website, which was later taken down. (neilthesealofficial.com)

Artwork generated by OpenAI

The company claimed a sticker depicting Neil the seal it had for sale was designed by a "local artist".

"This beautiful die-cut vinyl sticker is custom designed by a talented local Tasmanian artist to celebrate Neil's famous seasonal return!" the website stated.

But OpenAI's tool to detect AI-generated images found the sticker "was generated using OpenAI tools".

"We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI," the tool reported.

OpenAI says the image of the hoodie contains a watermark meaning it was generated by AI. (OpenAI)

The plushie, T-shirt, mug and jumper for sale all revealed the same results.

While the website has been taken down, similar ones remain online.

A website called 'official Neil the seal' (rather than 'Neil the seal official') has been operating for a few weeks and also sells merchandise depicting Neil that appears AI-generated.

The ABC has not been able to determine who runs the second website.

The plushie also came up as AI generated. (OpenAI)

Corporate records reveal website owner

The first website, 'Neil the seal official', displayed an Australian Business Number (ABN) linked to New South Wales man Grant Vaby.

Mr Vaby told the ABC he had not intended to communicate he had an "official partnership" with the conservation organisations, but said he was going to donate a percentage of profits to them if the website made any money.

Neil the seal returned to the sea last month. (Supplied: Sam Volker Photography)

He said the website had made 10 sales. Asked if he had fulfilled any of those orders, he declined to comment.

Mr Vaby also said he could not comment on the artwork being AI-generated, and declined to name the "local artist", saying he did not want to involve them.

Misleading websites prolific in the age of AI

The Marine Mammals Foundation, which was named on the website as a supported organisation, said it was concerned by the messaging.

"As a not-for-profit charity organisation, we rely on the generosity of community members and work incredibly hard to build trust so they know their support is making a difference," founding director Kate Robb said.

"We utilise the donations we do receive for research, education and conservation of marine mammals."

Neil the seal is known to interact with traffic cones and signage when he visits Tasmania. (Supplied: Sam Volker Photography)

University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson, who specialises in consumer protection and the regulation of AI, said businesses could be fined for misleading consumers.

"If you're marketing that you're donating money to conservation groups and you're not, it's misleading — it's also morally repugnant," she said.

"And if you're saying this is a local product and it's not, again, it's misleading."

Jeannie Paterson says AI has made it easy to create misleading content online. (Australian Story: Simon Winter )

Professor Paterson encouraged consumers to be sceptical before buying from online stores.

"AI and the internet have made it really easy to make misleading conduct, scam conduct, untruthful conduct — and for the ordinary consumer, they have to remember to check carefully before they buy," she said.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is the regulator in charge of protecting consumers from misleading business practices, but Professor Paterson said it had its work cut out.

"The ACCC can't pick up every misleading website and nor can the state fair trading office, but the idea is that by prosecuting a few examples, they're sending a message that you can't engage in misleading conduct in Australia," she said.

The ACCC encouraged people concerned about misleading information to report it.

"Under the Australian Consumer Law, businesses should not engage in misleading or deceptive conduct or make false or misleading representations," a spokesperson said.

"This includes representations about affiliations with charities or other entities."

World.title: A stark warning from corporate watchdog on illegal prediction markets
World.content:
The corporate watchdog has issued its strongest warning yet about the risk of offshore prediction markets, cautioning users they are likely to lose money without consumer protections.

Prediction markets allow users to place money on yes-or-no questions covering a vast range of topics from speculation on the oil price, to global conflict and pop culture. They are illegal in Australia.

The popularity of these platforms has skyrocketed across the world, especially two of the largest firms Kalshi and Polymarket, worth about $US22 billion ($31 billion) and $US15 billion ($21 billion) respectively.

Kalshi is another major player in the prediction market industry. (AP Photo: Erin Hooley)

The rise is being felt in Australia too, forcing the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) to update its Moneysmart website with guidance and advice.

"If you are engaging their prediction market, you are doing so with an operator overseas and that means that you miss out on important protections that would apply to any other market you engage in within Australia," said ASIC's Commissioner Alan Kirkland.

It comes as FEX Global, a financial futures trading house, pitched what could become Australia's first regulated prediction market.

Loading...

'Akin to gambling'

At the heart of ASIC's warning is that while these markets are often promoted as sophisticated financial products, they are fundamentally speculative bets on the outcome of future events.

Alan Kirkland says the presence of Australian-specific markets like RBA decisions indicates a high likelihood of Australian users on offshore platforms. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"Whatever the legal definition of a prediction market, let's just focus on the substance and in all practical terms, it is akin to gambling," Mr Kirkland said.

He said while it's hard to tell how many Australians are using these illegal markets, the fact that local events are available to place bets on indicates Australians are participating.

"We do see prediction markets that offer the right to bet on outcomes of events within Australia, such as RBA rate decisions," he said.

"It is possible that Australians are engaging in these markets, but we think it's important that they understand that they come with risks."

Why ASIC is intervening

No prediction market is licensed to operate in Australia.

That means consumers who use offshore operators are doing so without the protections provided under Australian financial services laws, including safeguards such as formal dispute resolution processes and other oversight designed to protect investors.

Prices fluctuate as traders reassess the likelihood of an event occurring, creating a market where participants can buy and sell contracts before the final result is known.

Crypto platform marketing highlights regulatory gaps A major cryptocurrency platform is operating like "gambling" in Australia, according to experts, despite new regulatory laws.

Supporters argue prediction markets can provide an efficient way of aggregating information and forecasting future events, with markets often producing remarkably accurate estimates ahead of elections, economic announcements and other major events.

It has prompted debate internationally about whether they should be treated as financial markets, gambling products or something entirely new.

Widespread ad campaigns

Many Australians have been exposed to prediction markets through social media promotion, and international sporting events.

ADI PredictStreet's Ajay Bhatia (right) on stage alongside FIFA president Gianni Infantino. (X: ADI Predict Street)

This year FIFA signed a multi-year partnership with ADI PredictStreet, where the firm broadcast their prediction ads across pitch side as keen soccer fans tuned into each game.

Earlier this year Kalshi created an AI-generated ad showing the vast array of markets people can speculate on including egg prices and the amount of hurricanes to pass over the US.

Kalshi released a commercial starring NBA champion and Kalshi investor Giannis Antetokounmpo that played during the NBA Finals. (Supplied: Kalshi)

ASIC is urging consumers to check whether a financial services provider is licensed before investing and to verify whether an online platform appears on the Australian Communications and Media Authority's register of blocked gambling websites.

The new guidance also encourages Australians to consider whether they can afford to lose the full amount of any money they place on a prediction market before participating.

"We've been watching the hype that's been rising in Australia around prediction markets and the fact that they're being pushed by a number of YouTubers and other influencers," Mr Kirkland said.

Insider trading

ASIC is also concerned about the possibility of insider trading as several legal cases are underway in the United States on the matter.

"They're potentially just the tip of the iceberg," Mr Kirkland said.

"We really don't know how much insider trading might actually be happening on these platforms."

Foxtel owner partners with untested crypto betting product The backstory of the prediction markets' newest entrant has done little to calm concerns about the industry.

Among the more infamous cases is a US soldier allegedly wagering on the ousting of Nicolas Maduro from Venezuela, while being involved in the highly secretive operation.

" It is very difficult to detect and difficult for overseas regulators to enforce insider trading laws where they apply. "

Debating legal operation in Australia

There is an emerging debate about whether regulated versions should eventually be allowed to operate in Australia.

Financial futures trading house FEXGlobal has expressed a strong interest in becoming Australia's first licensed prediction market operator.

Daniel Crennan says prediction markets "are unable to be properly regulated as yet". (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

Group executive for the firm Daniel Crennan argues regulatory authorities are falling behind.

"It is unfortunate in the sense that prediction markets, which are rapidly expanding and are covering all sorts of possible future events, are unable to be properly regulated as yet," he said.

While there is no timeline on his company's push to run an operation, Mr Crennan says a regulated operator within Australia could solve the problem of meeting consumer demand in a safe manner.

"It will be a good thing for Australia to have a domestically licensed regulated market and prediction markets."

Mr Kirkland said no formal submission to hold a licence had been sent to ASIC.

"If somebody was to submit an application to operate a prediction market in Australia, then of course we would determine that under the law, but that's not the reality now," he said.

For now, the industry at large remains illegal in Australia.

World.title: Calls to scrap NSW emergency services levy as insurance costs rise
World.content:
Earlier this year, Hans received his annual home insurance bill, which had increased by nearly $1,000 from the year prior.

The total was $3,590, which included about $1,000 in government taxes and levies.

Hans, who asked to only use his first name for privacy reasons, is a pensioner from regional New South Wales whose home was impacted by Cyclone Alfred last year.

"The only option [to reduce the premium] was to increase the excess from $600 to $2,000, which is a pretty big excess," he said.

Insurance premiums rise 51pc in five years Home insurance premiums continue to rise, with properties in natural disaster-prone areas paying the most.

Because his premium increased, his government taxes also increased, as they are calculated as a percentage of the base premium.

For example, his emergency services levy (ESL) jumped to $362, up from $273 the year prior.

"I think the taxes need to be looked at," he said.

"Insurance is sort of treated as a lucrative revenue-raising source and that annoys me because it's not something that you can choose to have or not have."

NSW is the only jurisdiction to fund emergency services through a tax on insurance companies, which is then passed on to customers through premiums.

The state also levies local councils and foreign insured policy holders.

All other jurisdictions have moved to a property-based model or fund services from general revenue.

It also has some of the highest rates of non-insurance in the country, with about 36 per cent of homes holding no contents insurance.

A coalition of industry stakeholders — the Insurance Council of Australia, Strata Community Association NSW, Financial Rights Legal Centre, NSW Council of Social Service, Committee for Sydney and the National Insurance Brokers Association — are calling on the NSW government to scrap the insurance tax before the March 2027 state election.

NSW Premier Chris Minns has committed to removing the ESL since 2023 and "replacing it with a simple and transparent levy spread across all properties".

A NSW parliamentary inquiry into options for reducing insurance costs and changes to emergency services funding is underway.

Levy increases 54 per cent

The ESL has increased 54 per cent in the past six years, according to the Insurance Council of Australia (ICA).

The ICA said the ESL raises about $1.4 billion annually for government budgets, accounting for about three-quarters of NSW emergency services funding.

It estimated the ESL adds up to 18 per cent to household insurance premiums and up to 34 per cent to business premiums, before GST and stamp duty are applied on top.

Andrew Hall says households should not have to foot the bill for emergency services. (Supplied: Insurance Council of Australia)

"The cost of emergency services should not fall disproportionately on families and businesses that do the right thing by taking out insurance," said Andrew Hall, Insurance Council of Australia chief executive.

Modelling commissioned by the ICA found more than 2 million NSW households would be better off under a replacement property levy.

The average insured household would save $308 a year on insurance costs and be around $55 better off overall after paying a replacement levy, it found.

IAG warns severe weather will push up premiums A report from IAG and a scientific research centre finds escalating risk from severe weather events in south-east Queensland, New South Wales, and south-west Western Australia.

Households in disaster-prone regional areas would benefit the most, saving about $565 annually.

Financial Rights Legal Centre external relations and advocacy principal Julia Davis said the most vulnerable households get "pushed into the highest risk areas and the least resilient housing".

Julia Davis says home owners in disaster-prone areas are already paying more for insurance. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

"They are already paying more to protect their homes than households in less exposed regions," she said.

" They should not have to pay more for the same emergency services that are available to all households and businesses. "

The ICA also estimated that small businesses could save money under a replacement levy, from $105 for a bakery to more than $21,000 for a small livestock farm.

Climate concerns for insurance industry

Government levies are far from the only concern for the home insurance industry.

Industry stakeholders, including banks, are looking at how they can better respond to climate events in regional towns. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Industry stakeholders are also worried about other types of financial stress on towns impacted by climate change, including the future viability of bank loans.

Already, climate change has caused home insurance premiums to increase by more than 50 per cent.

Customer-owned banks have joined with actuarial and analytics firm Finity and Climate KIC Australia to look at how they can support communities through climate change.

Christopher Lee says communities can forward plan for disasters. (Supplied: Chris Lee)

Christopher Lee is chief executive of Climate KIC Australia, part of the University of Technology Sydney's Institute for Sustainable Futures.

He said the goal over the coming years was to equip regional towns with skills and tools to prepare and respond to climate events.

"That may be in strengthening their internal operations ... forward planning for particular disasters that may occur," he said.

Sharanjit Paddam says banks may be caught with losses if home owners are not insured. (ABC News: Dan Irvine)

Finity principal Sharanjit Paddam said this collaboration contributes to the future viability of communities.

"When [banks] lend you money for your home loan, [they] require you to have insurance," he said.

" If that insurance is out of reach for you and there is a disaster, then the bank will be stuck with the losses. "

Taskforce to tackle insurance unaffordability Industry experts warn we need to make homes more resilient in order to tackle unaffordable insurance premiums.

One of the ways to improve this, according to Mr Paddam, is for banks to continue offering "green loan products".

"So helping households get solar, helping households get batteries and electrify their homes, that allows households to insulate themselves," he said.

Uninsured homes on the rise

More households across Australia are experiencing home insurance stress, with the proportion of households facing unaffordable insurance climbing from 10 per cent in 2022 to 15 per cent in 2024.

More households across Australia are experiencing home insurance stress, as climate change disasters like flooding increase. (Supplied: City of Melbourne)

The financial regulator estimates one in seven Australian houses are currently uninsured, a figure that could rise to one in four by 2050.

Researcher Peter Kamstra from the University of Melbourne said there needed to be financial incentives for home owners to make their homes more resilient in the face of climate change.

"A lot of the people we've spoken to, they want to take action, but it's a difficult cost-benefit analysis to invest thousands ... unless there were lower premiums or sort of better insurance outcomes," Dr Kamstra said.

Retirements at risk The Australian retirement dream is being destabilised by the rising cost of home insurance, as retirees on fixed budgets find themselves unable to absorb skyrocketing premiums.

His research into flood insurance decision-making in Victoria found home owners understood the risk caused by certain weather events, but the system was "too complex" to navigate.

"Part of the flaw with communicating risk is there's no real engagement before," he said.

"It's a letter, it's sort of bad news, it's a text message that lets people know that they've been rezoned.

World.title: Why a teen Allegra Spender wore a hoodie to annoy mum Carla Zampatti
World.content:
As a child, Independent MP Allegra Spender spent her school holidays like many of us do: tagging along to her parents' work.

If she wasn't stuffing envelopes for her father John Spender, the Liberal MP for the federal seat of North Sydney, she was with her mum, famed businesswoman and fashion designer Carla Zampatti.

Watch Kitchen Cabinet on ABC iview Join Annabel Crabb for a brand new season as she breaks bread with six of the federal parliament's most fascinating and powerful figures from across the political spectrum.

"I remember when I was about 11 and [my sister] Bianca was 12, [Mum] wanted us to realise how hard you need to work to be successful. And so, we used to work in her office every single school holiday," the member for Wentworth told Annabel Crabb on ABC iview's Kitchen Cabinet.

Ms Spender said she loved her mum's business, but unlike Bianca, she never aspired to be a fashion designer.

"When I was a teenager, I was like 'Oh mum, it's so superficial' and I used to wander around wearing hoodies just to annoy her. And she literally threw out some of my clothes because she hated them."

Her mother made most of their clothes, while Spender begged her for a new pair of jeans.

Allegra Spender's job during the school holidays was to get everyone in her mother's office their tea and lunch. (Instagram: Bianca Spender)

"She made us wear these Victorian kind-of-dresses made of cords with big, white, fluffy collars — like we walked out of some Victorian paintings."

Despite this, nothing could prepare her for the awkwardness of going door knocking with her dad.

" I found it so embarrassing that he would walk up and knock on people's doors. I used to hide at the bottom of the garden path going, 'Oh my God …' "

Politics 'gives me a great deal of joy'

Politics, especially the Liberal Party, have loomed large in Ms Spender's life. Her father joined Malcolm Fraser's government in 1980 before serving under opposition leaders Andrew Peacock and John Howard.

Her grandfather, Sir Percy Spender, was a Liberal MP for Warringah who served under the Menzies government. He is known as the father of the Colombo Plan, which provided aid across South-East Asia, and negotiated the ANZUS treaty.

Yet when considering a career in politics, the Teal independent — who recently confirmed plans to form a new political party alongside fellow independent Zali Steggall — said she "didn't see anyone I would want to join".

Since becoming the MP for Wentworth, no Liberal leader has tried to lure her into the fold, either.

"I mustn't look like a Liberal to them," she said with a laugh.

Allegra Spender and Annabel Crabb getting ready to cook lunch. (ABC TV)

But what did her father, who lost his own seat to an independent, think of her decision to enter politics?

"I got this email at 3 o'clock in the morning, which was like, 'Darling, [these are] all the reasons why you shouldn't run.' But in the end, he was 100 per cent behind me."

Her father would pass away almost six months after her election win.

Ms Spender said politics was more enjoyable than she thought it would be.

"I like helping people when they get stuck in a bureaucratic system, and I love public policy and having the opportunity to help shape that, to help debate that, to push it as far as I believe it can go," she said.

"It gives me a great deal of joy."

Allegra Spender in parliament with fellow Teal and new party mate, Zali Steggall. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

'A proud migrant'

After Ms Spender graduated from Cambridge and the University of London, a stint advising banana growers in Kenya followed. As did a role with consulting giant McKinsey.

But despite her protestations about fashion as a teen, she eventually became the managing director of her mother's fashion label.

The legendary designer grew up in rural Italy during World War II and arrived in Australia when she was 11.

According to Ms Spender, her mother was a "very proud migrant" who was "incredibly grateful for the opportunities it gave to her".

Allegra Spender said the hardest thing about losing her mother Carla Zampatti was the "shock, because she was there and then she wasn't". (Supplied )

"She was a kid who got off a boat when she was 11 years old, didn't speak English, left school at 14. She ended up making a really big contribution to the country," she said.

Running for the seat of Wentworth shortly after her mother's death was the hardest decision Ms Spender's ever made.

"I thought a lot about Mum when I made it, because she said, 'I only regret the things I didn't do'.

"And I thought a lot about women, because one of the reasons why I stood was because I just believe you should have a parliament that reflects the country."

Allegra Spender said her mother Carla Zampatti was proud of multicultural Australia. (Getty Images: Gaye Gerard)

About the current immigration debate, Ms Spender believes there are "fair questions about the number of immigrants".

But she said it's challenging to "create a space where people feel that they belong and [there's] that sense of common ground, common values".

"I think it takes work," she said.

The 'greatest fear' realised

The seat of Wentworth stretches from picturesque Watsons Bay to Clovelly and includes Bondi Beach.

The MP and her family were at the beach on the day of the shooting in December 2025, leaving at about 5:30pm. Not long after, shots could be heard coming from the footbridge.

"I think it's the greatest fear that I had for the community, because we've had so many anti-Semitic attacks," she said.

"There was always a fear that there would be violence where people really got hurt."

Allegra Spender at the Bondi Pavilion memorial. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

So how did she approach this unthinkable situation?

"I think it's trying to be clear on what's your role. One is to hold the government to account on safety and security. The second piece is then about, what does the community need?" she said.

"And it can be things like psychological support. It can be victim support. It can be immediate practical things."

She said it's also thinking about rebuilding a sense of safety in the community.

"It's one of the reasons I was really pushing for a royal commission, so that we got the answers that lead us most likely to minimising chances of things like this happening again," she said.

"The country has changed, but it's up to us about how it changes us."

Watch Kitchen Cabinet tonight at 8:30pm on ABC TV or on ABC iview.

World.title: Indonesians mock Trump-style 'personality politics'
World.content:
Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Standing at a podium at a political party event in Jakarta, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto waved printed pages in the air.

"This is the prepared speech. Do you want me to read this speech?" asked Mr Prabowo.

"It could put me to sleep," he joked at the event last month.

Prabowo marks one year in office A year after Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto won the election, the families of Indonesians arrested in recent protests are expressing dissatisfaction with his leadership.

He later quipped that his advisors often reminded him not to go off script and to avoid using "wrong words".

"Today, I will be polite," he assured the crowd.

Moments later, the president was improvising again.

"In the past we called them 'londo ireng', those who fought alongside the Dutch against us. Those londo ireng still exist today," he said, adding that they could now be found among "journalists, reporters, analysts and NGOs".

The term londo ireng in Javanese has historically referred to Indigenous Indonesians accused of collaborating with Dutch colonial forces during the country's struggle for independence, according to some experts.

The insult prompted a backlash on social media, with some commenting that they were "ashamed" of the Indonesian president.

An Indonesian government official says Prabowo Subianto is committed to "fighting for the interests of the people". (Reuters: Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana)

The Indonesian Alliance of Independent Journalists and other media groups condemned the comment as "demeaning" and "dangerous for press freedom and democracy".

In the past few months, Mr Prabowo has also made headlines by telling people who thought rice was too expensive to "help grow it", dismissing expert critics by using the term "ndasmu", akin to "whatever", and suggesting that the rupiah's weakness against the US dollar did not matter because "people in villages don't use it".

On Friday, a live stream of Mr Prabowo speaking to business leaders was reportedly cut off and journalists ejected after he said "it is being said that Iran already has nuclear weapons", and that could lead to further proliferation in the region.

Iran's diplomats in the country were quick to reject the claim.

It has left many in Indonesia wondering how much impact Mr Prabowo's "wrong words" are having on voters' confidence and even the economy.

Prabowo likened to Trump

Student-led protests broke out across Indonesia in June. (Reuters: Claudio Pramana)

Ambang Priyonggo, a media and politics academic at Multimedia Nusantara University in Indonesia, said Mr Prabowo's communication style had undergone a "quite significant transformation" since the beginning of his political career.

Once strongly associated with the military, ahead of the 2024 election he recast himself as a cuddly grandfather figure.

Dr Priyonggo said Mr Prabowo's repeated controversial comments as president pointed to a broader "populist" pattern in his leadership communication style that relied on simple, direct and everyday language.

He said there were similarities between Mr Prabowo and United States President Donald Trump, whose political communication he described as "spontaneous, direct and often controversial".

He described both leaders' styles as examples of "personality politics", saying they also used nationalist rhetoric.

"This creates a risk of a cult of personality, where substantive criticism of policy can easily be seen as a personal attack on the leader," he said.

Ambang Priyonggo says Prabowo Subianto's communication style can be "spontaneous". (Supplied)

If this style continued to be used in the wrong way, it could make Mr Prabowo appear "insensitive" to public concerns and lead more people to question the president's authority, he added.

In June, students led protests across several cities in Indonesia over living costs and government spending priorities.

"What we are seeing now, for example, is the emergence of protests that reflect dissatisfaction with the government," Dr Priyonggo said.

Protesters in Jakarta faced with violence by police A 21-year-old has died after being struck by an armoured police vehicle during violent clashes at a Jakarta rally.

Fahd Pahdepie, from the Indonesian Government Communications Agency, said material for state speeches and official policy statements was prepared through a process involving ministries and government agencies.

However, he said Mr Prabowo's delivery, emphasis, choice of words and interaction with audiences reflected his personal style.

"There may be spontaneity, but it never departs from the president's authentic commitment to fighting for the interests of the people," he said.

He added that context was important when Mr Prabowo's statements circulated on social media, where short clips could strip remarks of their broader meaning.

Comments can be 'tone-deaf'

Satrio Wibisono (top left) poked fun at Prabowo Subianto's comments that Indonesians unhappy with the country should leave. (Threads: Satrio Wibisono)

Some Indonesians have responded to Mr Prabowo's populist turn with mocking humour.

In July, he said people who believed "Indonesia is bleak may look for another country".

Satrio Wibisono, a 30-year-old IT worker who moved to Kuala Lumpur last year, posted a photo on social media with two other members of the Indonesian diaspora and joked they were already in Malaysia.

'Let's just escape' hashtag goes viral in Indonesia Anger over slashed government budgets, poor quality of life, career stagnation and rampant official corruption is motivating many Indonesians to fantasise about "running away" from the country.

Mr Wibisono told the ABC that the government's comments were often insensitive to the public.

"There's something wrong about our government's statements … and they come across as tone-deaf," he said.

"I'm not questioning the president's capability; he is a legitimately elected leader, but his public speaking needs to be better managed."

Mr Wibisono said he disliked Mr Prabowo's leadership and communication style so much he would not return to Indonesia while he was president.

He is not alone in being dissatisfied with the government, although polling is inconsistent.

A January survey by Indikator found that 79.9 per cent of respondents were "satisfied" with his performance, up from 77.7 per cent in October.

However, a separate July survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting found that Mr Prabowo's satisfaction rating had dropped to 51.1 per cent, down from 81.2 per cent in November 2025.

Comments fuel social media chat

Experts say Indonesia's economy is influenced by a range of internal and international factors. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Mr Prabowo's comments about the rupiah and other economic topics have fuelled speculation on social media that they could be hurting the economy.

In July, social media users posted that the Indonesian rupiah and local share market weakened whenever Mr Prabowo delivered a speech.

Some posts called for the president's appearances to be cancelled or his microphone to be switched off.

However, Indonesia Stock Exchange president director Jeffrey Hendrik said politics had far less influence on share market movements than it did in the 1980s.

Speaking to media in Jakarta on July 13, he said markets were driven more by economic conditions and global uncertainty, including US tariffs and conflict in the Middle East.

Mr Pahdepie echoed Mr Hendrik's remarks, saying Mr Prabowo's speeches were not the only factor shaping public confidence or economic sentiment.

He said short-term market sentiment could also be influenced by global conditions and technical factors that lay beyond the control of government communications.

"We believe healthy optimism must be grounded in reality, not in image polishing," he said.

Kam Fong Chan says Indonesian investors react to both the content and delivery style of politicians' speeches. (Supplied: Kam Fong Chan )

Kam Fong Chan, an associate professor of finance at the University of Western Australia, said the economic impact of a leader's speech depended on whether markets were reacting to their speaking style or to the policy signals contained in their remarks.

He said remarks driven mainly by style or sentiment could move prices for one or two days before the market recovered.

"When the matter relates to trade or policy, the effect tends to persist for longer, because the market prices in a policy uncertainty premium," he said.

Dr Chan acknowledged similarities in the communication styles of Mr Prabowo and Mr Trump, but said foreign investors "hold dollars and US assets irrespective of President Trump's tweets, whether rants or trade threats".

"But they are willing to dump the rupiah and Indonesian assets on sentiment," he added.

World.title: The vulnerable workers bearing the cost of providing Australia with cheap food
World.content:
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide

Some days Gershom Isaac says he feels suicidal. He spends up to 12 hours a day climbing ladders to pick fruit or bent over pulling onions and pumpkins, sometimes earning less than $7 an hour.

At night, he returns to overcrowded, squalid accommodation. The relentless cycle has left him feeling exhausted and hopeless.

Gershom came to Australia from Papua New Guinea chasing the Australian dream. Instead, he became trapped in a system where labour hire contractors controlled almost every aspect of his life, his work, his pay and, ultimately, his future.

Now he is one of tens of thousands of migrant workers living in the shadows, and part of a much larger temporary migrant workforce vulnerable to exploitation.

"Even 40 degrees, you're still hanging there, picking oranges, trying to do as much as you can, and it's not easy. Sometimes you fall from those trees," he says.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Lifeline on 131 114

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

13 YARN on 13 92 76

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

If he gets sick or injured, he doesn't get paid. Without work, he says, he can't afford to eat.

He says the labour hire contractor controls every aspect of his working life.

Gershom's experience reflects a much bigger shift in Australian agriculture. Rather than employing workers directly, many growers rely on labour hire contractors to recruit and supply seasonal workers during harvest.

Australia's growing reliance on temporary migrant labour has fuelled a booming labour hire industry, with contractors sitting between growers and workers, often recruiting, transporting and housing them.

While some operate legally, others prey on vulnerable migrant workers, paying them cash, well below the minimum wage.

"I don't have any voice. I don't have any power," Gershom says.

"Every choice is with the contractor. They're the ones who make all the decisions, and the fruit pickers have to say yes to everything."

Gershom's story isn't unique. Across Australia's horticulture industry, workers described strikingly similar experiences: low pay, overcrowded and slum-like housing, labour hire contractors controlling where they lived and worked, and little power to complain.

It is part of an eight-month Four Corners investigation into whether Australians can trust the claims made about the food they buy.

Do you know more? Contact Adele Ferguson using ferguson.adele@abc.net.au and Chris Gillett on gillett.chris@abc.net.au

using and on If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The investigation tested supermarket food products, travelled to cocoa-growing communities in Ghana, and interviewed workers and industry insiders across Australia.

It found problems from food fraud and misleading claims to worker exploitation and child labour, as well as tomato products originating from China's Xinjiang region, which has been linked to allegations of forced labour.

It comes weeks after the Trump administration imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on certain Australian exports, arguing Australia does not effectively stop imports made with forced labour.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese rejected the criticism, saying Australia had "robust" modern slavery laws.

The chocolate industry's 'dirty secret' For decades, major chocolate companies have pledged to eradicate child labour. Four Corners discovered that in Ghana, the promises don't always match the reality.

In 2021, the US banned imports of products including tomatoes from Xinjiang over forced labour concerns, an allegation that China denies. Australia doesn't have an import ban.

As part of the investigation, Four Corners worked with Source Certain, an Australian forensic laboratory specialising in origin verification, which has done work for the FBI, Scotland Yard, Interpol and Australia's AFP.

Its scientists analysed hundreds of processed tomato products to see if they were really from Italy or Australia as stated on the labels.

One in four products had a problem. Those that failed came from China, with half linked to Xinjiang.

When 'Australian grown' is grown in China One of Australia's biggest tomato brands and two major supermarkets are selling products that exclusive forensic testing shows have misleading labelling.

For years, parliamentary inquiries, raids, and media investigations have exposed the exploitation of migrant workers in Australia's food industry. Governments have promised reforms, regulators have cracked down and companies have pledged to clean up their supply chains.

Four Corners reporters travelled to regional Australia, analysed payroll records, interviewed workers, unions, advocates, regulators and employers and examined how Australia's modern slavery laws operate in practice.

No sick leave, no pay slips, no super
