At a caravan park in the NSW Riverina, Pacific Islander workers broke their silence, many agreeing to be identified despite the risks.

They said they had left employers under Australia's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme after disputes over pay, working conditions or alleged mistreatment.

Under the PALM scheme, workers are tied to an approved employer. If they leave that employer, they are not allowed to take on new work and so many become "disengaged" from the scheme, leaving them with few lawful options to keep working.

Ken Dachi tries to give migrant workers a voice. (Four Corners: Rob Hill)

Ken Dachi worked for years in conflict-affected regions around the world. Now he helps vulnerable migrant workers here, through the Welcoming Australia organisation.

He says the PALM scheme was designed to connect Pacific Islanders with Australian employers and regional communities. But when workers aren't protected, labour hire contractors and other exploitative operators can fill the gap.

Dachi says many workers disengage from the PALM scheme without understanding that doing so makes them even more vulnerable.

He says the system is flawed.

"[They] are not numbers. They're people's lives. It's families, it's siblings, it's parents impacted … a long road without an exit sign."

They survive by finding labour hire contractors willing to pay them cash to pick fruit and vegetables destined for Australian supermarket shelves. They say they earn well below legal minimum wages, with no super, no sick leave and no pay slips.

Timothy earns less than $12 an hour. (Four Corners)

Timothy pays $280 a week to live in a tiny rented room in the caravan park.

"Just only this room. No kitchen, no bathroom," he says.

He collects bottles to earn extra money.

He says he works about 60 hours a week picking oranges for cash, earning about $700 a week — less than $12 an hour. "It's really hard," he says.

For Viona Obress, filling one bin with oranges can take three to four hours, equivalent to between $8.75 and $11.70 an hour.

If it is raining, it slows her down, so she says she earns even less and if she gets sick, she earns nothing.

"The fruit is so heavy and climbing a lot as a lady, it's really hard too," she says. "You feel exhausted when you finish work. You feel like you can't work another day, but what can you do? There's no options. You have to keep going."

Viona Obress works about 60 hours a week picking oranges. (Four Corners)

By going public, Viona hopes the conditions workers have endured will no longer remain hidden.

"The truth will finally come out," she says.

These workers do not receive pay slips, so the ABC has not been able to verify these workers' pay rates.

'I was treated more like an animal'

Across Australia's fruit and vegetable industry, Fair Work Ombudsman investigations have repeatedly uncovered widespread non-compliance.

In Coffs Harbour, 61 per cent of growers and labour hire companies inspected were found to be breaching workplace laws, including underpaying workers. The figure rose to 72 per cent in the Riverina and 83 per cent in Victoria's Mornington Peninsula and Yarra Valley.

In Coffs Harbour, local Raewyn Macky has become a lifeline for vulnerable workers.

She says she first noticed growing numbers of migrant workers seeking help while volunteering at a local second-hand clothes shop. She says they kept coming back with stories of unpaid wages, poor conditions and nowhere else to go.

Raewyn Macky heard about the experiences of migrant workers while volunteering at a local op-shop. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton)

Over the years she has built a detailed picture of a workforce falling through the cracks — workers reluctant to complain, uncertain of their rights and fearful of speaking up.

"They are exposed to dreadful working conditions, grossly underpaid, no pay slips and the pay can vary from day to day. They work … sometimes 10 plus hours and [in] summer it's pretty grim. There's not much shade on the farms. There's little sanitation," she says.

"It makes me angry. It makes me sad. It makes me sick to the stomach," she says.

Jin Lee had to work for a short period in regional areas as a condition of extending his working holiday visa.

He says he is still recovering from his time working on blueberry farms in Coffs Harbour.

"I wasn't being treated like a human being there," he says.

"I was treated more like an animal."

Jin Lee worked on blueberry farms in Coffs Harbour to extend his working holiday visa. (Four Corners)

Lee says some days he worked from 7:30am until 5pm for just $20.

"Some of us got diapers because they didn't provide bathroom breaks," he says.

They were also expected to pay for basic equipment themselves.

Lee says the labour hire company that recruited him — ECW Farming — controlled almost every aspect of his life — from where he worked to where he lived.

He says the company made a series of deductions from his wages, including $150 a week for accommodation and $10 a day for transport to and from the farm.

By the time those deductions were taken out, he says little was left.

"The accommodation had 18 people crammed inside of that house and each room had four beds as they call them and it was just mattresses that they took apart. They had four people in one room and that room had children's bunk beds so obviously not very comfortable for adults to sleep in," he says.

"There were roaches everywhere. There were broken doors, broken windows. And the air-conditioning unit was broken. So it was not livable."

The company that hired Lee is difficult to trace. Its registered address in Coffs Harbour was a backpacker's hostel that denied any connection to the business.

Documents obtained by Four Corners under Freedom of Information reveal the Fair Work Ombudsman investigated ECW Farming in 2024 after receiving a series of worker tip-offs.

The investigation was shelved in May 2025 after the ombudsman concluded it could not identify the "controlling minds" behind the operation.

For Lee, that is part of the problem. The workers are easy to find. The people profiting from them are not.

Lee says because his visa is due to end soon, he is unlikely to see any action against the company that recruited him before he departs Australia.

Raewyn Macky believes industry and government are not interested in combating worker exploitation. (Four Corners)

Determined to do something, Macky says she has repeatedly reported concerns to councils, police and regulators, hoping authorities would investigate.

Years later, she says little has changed.

"I just kind of think that everything boils down to … industry and government are not interested. They're not interested because otherwise it would have changed. It's not just happening here. It's happening all over the country."

'We have opened the door to crooks'

Macky's experience reflects a broader issue, according to NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner James Cockayne.

As an independent statutory officer, Cockayne's role is to monitor the effectiveness of anti-slavery laws and work across government, business and communities to address modern slavery. It gives him a rare view of how exploitation can fall in the cracks between agencies.

He says no single agency sees the full picture. Instead, each is responding to its own mandate, leaving no-one responsible for tackling exploitation as a whole.

"Each of them is holding a different part of the elephant," he says. "The challenge is to see the elephant as a whole and how it operates because these syndicates are very deliberate and intentional."

James Cockayne says the absence of a labour hire licensing regime in NSW has created opportunities for unscrupulous operators. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

"Right now our agencies are not working together in a trauma-informed and strategically intelligent way to see that big picture."

Through his work, which includes operating a confidential modern slavery hotline, Cockayne has spent years hearing from vulnerable workers, travelling to regional communities and building relationships with local advocates, whistleblowers and government agencies.

Cockayne says labour hire companies have become a critical link in Australia's horticulture workforce, connecting growers with the temporary migrant workers who harvest fruit and vegetables. But he says the same allegations keep surfacing: systemic worker exploitation, forced labour, debt bondage and, in some cases, human trafficking and servitude.

In NSW, labour hire companies don't need to be licensed. Cockayne says this has allowed unscrupulous operators to exploit vulnerable workers, recruiting through backpacker hostels, social media and migrant community networks.

"In NSW we have no labour hire licensing," Cockayne says. "There's no barrier to entry for any person to come and set up a labour hire company. So we have opened the door to crooks from NSW, from further afield in Australia, even from overseas, to come into that space and provide labour hire services in ways that rely on criminal methods and that amount in some cases we believe to be modern slavery offences," he said.

He says they do that by recruiting vulnerable workers.

"Working holiday-makers who they tend to recruit through local backpacker hostels [and] international students, many of whom are recruited through social media platforms and messaging apps, in the language that is spoken by the workers.

"The syndicates provide accommodation services, often overcharging the workers for substandard accommodation," he said.

Cockayne says he has visited a number of these places in NSW and further afield and some of them are hovels.

Worker accommodation in North Queensland. (Supplied)

"People living on top of each other with substandard sanitation, substandard fresh air, often cockroach infestations and being charged through the nose for these kinds of services," he says.

The labour hire syndicates rely on acquiescence by farmers, producers, and the companies that they sell onto not to ask too many questions, according to Cockayne.

Last week, the Fair Work Ombudsman and two other agencies went to 15 farms, most of them growing citrus fruit in the Riverina in NSW as part of a crackdown on rogue labour hire companies. In a statement, Fair Work said it was investigating businesses in the Coffs Harbour region.

A NSW government spokesperson said it had zero tolerance for worker exploitation and was working towards a Labour Hire Code of Practice, alongside stronger compliance through a supply chain program on NSW government construction projects.

Companies recycling reporting on modern slavery risks

The Modern Slavery Act, introduced in 2018, requires companies with annual revenue above $100 million to file a report each year, identifying the modern slavery risks in their operations and supply chains and what they're doing to address them.

It was designed to encourage transparency and improve corporate behaviour.

Four Corners used data analysis tools to analyse hundreds of annual modern slavery statements from 50 food companies between 2020 to 2025.

One in four contained sections that were more than 80 per cent identical to previous reports.

Chocolate maker Ferrero went even further, filing the exact same report two years in a row — even leaving the previous year's date unchanged.

Ferrero filed the same report two years in a row.

Coles and Woolworths removed references to cocoa as a modern slavery risk in their latest reports, despite selling chocolate including via their own brands.

Others watered down their promises year to year.

In 2023, Mondelēz, whose brands include Cadbury, said its Strategy to Help Protect Children had an "ultimate vision" to work towards a cocoa sector that was "free of child labour".

But in its 2024 Modern Slavery statement, this vision had disappeared. The same strategy was instead described as helping to "enhance child protection systems" and helping to "improve access to quality education".

Oz Group, a co-operative representing more than 140 berry growers across NSW's Mid North Coast, said in its 2020 statement it "does not accept any form of slavery-like practices within the co-operative or throughout its supply chain".

However, in its 2025 statement, the co-operative said, "addressing modern slavery requires ongoing effort and collaboration" and it remained "committed to continuous improvement".

Ferrero said its 2024 report remained valid for 2025.

Coles said its reports were not intended to be an exhaustive list of modern slavery risks, while Woolworths said its modern slavery risk profile was continually evolving, and it focused on the highest risks in its supply chain.

Mondelēz did not respond to specific questions about its modern slavery statements, but said it explicitly prohibited child labour. Oz Group did not provide a response.

Experts say the findings raise broader questions about whether some reporting has become a facile exercise in compliance rather than a genuine assessment of changing risks.

Former Australian Competition and Consumer Commission chairman Allan Fels has dedicated a lot of time to the plight of migrant workers.

He oversaw fixing the 7-Eleven wage fraud scandal, which paid out more than $150 million in back pay to underpaid workers on student visas and later authored a landmark report on modern slavery.

He describes the Modern Slavery Act as a symbolic and tokenistic law. "It's the sort of law you pass when you want to look as if you're concerned about something, but you don't intend anything to happen," he says.

An independent review of the Modern Slavery Act handed to the federal government in 2023 concluded Australia's framework should be strengthened.

"The report spells out what's obvious to regulators like me — that the law was never intended to be associated with any real action. It was just a law you put on the books as a sign of concern, but with no intent to take serious action," he says.

Allan Fels says the Modern Slavery Act has not produced real change. (Four Corners: Rob Hill)

The report recommended civil penalties for companies that fail to comply with reporting obligations, mandatory human rights due diligence, and lowering the reporting threshold from annual revenue of $100 million to $50 million.

The government accepted some of the review's recommendations and recently announced plans to introduce civil penalties and a new criminal offence for companies that fail to prevent modern slavery.

But some key reforms remain outstanding, including mandatory due diligence and lowering the reporting threshold.

After the Trump administration cited Australia's failure to ban imports made with forced labour as a reason for imposing tariffs on some Australian exports, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defended Australia's record, describing the country's modern slavery laws as "robust, comprehensive and world-leading".

Allan Fels disagrees. "Sorry, prime minister, you're wrong. Donald Trump is right. I thought I'd never say that," he says.

The PM declined to be interviewed. In a statement, the Attorney General, Michelle Rowland, whose department administers the Modern Slavery Act, said Australia had robust modern slavery laws and planned to introduce new criminal and civil penalties. Details are yet to be released.

Behind the fruit and vegetables on Australia's supermarket shelves are workers whose stories are rarely heard.

The cost of cheap food isn't borne equally. It falls hardest on the people harvesting it.

"Someone needs to talk about this," Jin Lee says. "So, I'm here and I'm talking about it because otherwise this might go under the radar for many more years."

"There needs to be change," says Gershom Issac. "We are struggling to survive."

Watch Four Corners' full investigation Duped: Food Exposed on ABC iview.

Notes on our data analysis:

The copy-paste statistic regarding Modern Slavery statements was calculated using code which measured the amount of shared text between consecutive Modern Slavery statements for each company.

The text from the Modern Slavery statements was standardised before the analysis for a more accurate comparison.

The ABC used AI to assist with scaling up the code, which then underwent manual checks.

World.title: Most older people are open to downsizing. So what are the barriers?
World.content:
As 78-year-old Eleanor Shearing looks over the cluttered boxes around the place she's lived in for 50 years, a mix of nostalgia and anxiety set in.

Seaford, a coastal suburb of Adelaide, is where she raised a family, formed a community and made a life.

But her three-bedroom home is now getting harder for her to live in, and on a single income, it's also becoming harder to pay for.

After four years of trying to downsize, Ms Shearing fears she might have to leave Seaford entirely.

Eleanor Shearing still has a photo of her home in Seaford when she bought it in the 1970s. (ABC News: Tim Morris)

She is not alone in wanting to downsize. Research has shown more than half of people over the age of 55 are open to it.

"This is home. It's very difficult when you're older to sort of start off anew," she said.

"I've thought about it, [but] you lose that connection with the community.

"I've got a lovely bunch of friends and people that I've known down here for a long time. So I really don't want to move too far away."

So what are the barriers?

The Productivity Commission has identified several factors, including planning laws, that are restricting housing supply and choice.

Those findings are laid out in its interim report into what governments can do to unlock more new homes.

Danielle Wood says planning rules are slowing development and making housing more expensive. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

While the full report is expected in March 2027, the interim report identifies several ways these barriers could be removed, including:

Allow up to three-storey developments across most residential land

Allow mid-rise or high-rise apartments in high-demand areas

Allow residential development in commercial zones, unless there is a clear rationale for excluding it

Reduce or remove minimum lot size requirements

Relax or remove built-form controls that limit flexibility and choice for households

Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood said poorly designed regulations made projects slower, more expensive and reduced the range of housing types available.

The real-life Utopia stories blocking new homes A new report from the Productivity Commission calls on governments to embrace a "build mindset" to make housing more affordable.

"The rules should allow us to build enough housing in the right places, while still protecting the things Australians value," she said.

Grattan Institute housing expert Matthew Bowes said many of the most desirable places to live, which often had aging demographics, were subject to restrictive zoning rules.

Those rules blocked housing supply by making it more difficult to build townhouses and low-rise apartments that might be most attractive to downsizers, he said.

"So, those kinds of homes are undersupplied," he said.

" Which makes it difficult for downsizers when they are trying to find a smaller home that still meet their needs in the community that they may have spent a lot of their lives in. "

Matthew Bowes says stamp duty has led to more older people staying in larger homes longer. (ABC News: Matthew Holmes)

Experts say most barriers for older people wanting to downsize sit at local and state government levels.

One barrier that sits at the state level is stamp duty, according to Mr Bowes.

In February, the South Australian government announced it would abolish stamp duty for people over the age of 60 who sell their homes to move into new builds.

Communities become developers amid downsize shortage In regional Australia, where baby boomers are being told to downsize to free up homes, country communities are having to become developers to build appropriate-sized housing.

The Australian Capital Territory plans to phase out stamp duty completely in favour of a universal land tax.

Mr Bowes said stamp duty was a tax on housing transactions that discouraged people from moving homes over time.

"In the case of downsizers, they may stay in a home that is larger than they need for a long period of time because if they had to move, they would have to pay stamp duty.

"So it acts as a disincentive on people choosing homes that best suit their needs at their stage in life."

Australian Housing Urban Research Institute managing director Tom Alves said an ongoing universal land tax paid by all landowners was more stable, efficient and fairer.

Tom Alves says any reforms to stamp duty need to be introduced slowly. (Supplied)

But there are challenges to implementing it, as two-thirds of properties are exempt from land taxes because they are the owners' main residence, he said.

"Politically, the impacts of moving from a stamp duty regime to a universal land tax is possibly more problematic as this tax change will affect all landowners, and not just investors," Dr Alves said.

"Reforms would need to be introduced incrementally."

Most older people want to age in place

Christine Toose is facing a range of these barriers in multiple states.

The grandmother in her early 70s wants to sell her four-bedroom Queensland house and move home to Victoria, where she purchased her "forever home" off the plan in May this year.

Christine Toose says she has been considering downsizing for the last year. (Supplied)

Ms Toose has grandchildren on the way in Melbourne, but the cost of stamp duty on her Queensland home has so far prevented her from putting it on the market.

"If the governments are really serious about getting baby boomers out of their big houses, then they need to be offering some sort of incentives," Ms Toose told the ABC.

"It's a big thing to move out of the place that you've been living in for some time.

" Downsizing is just an enormous feat in itself. "

The changes to stamp duty in South Australia have helped make it easier for Ms Shearing to downsize.

But she still is struggling to find a ground-floor two-bedroom home near her neighbourhood in Seaford.

"I manage the stairs okay now, but there's probably going to come a time later on down the track that I won't be able to," she said.

"If someone knocks down an old home in this area, they're going to put three and four townhouses on there.

"I don't want a townhouse. I want to go into something that's on one level."

Eleanor Shearing says she does not want to leave Seaford because it's all she's known for decades. (ABC News: Tim Morris)

She is among about two-thirds of older people who would like to age in place, which means to stay in your current home or neighbourhood as you age.

She does not want to leave the place where she raised her children.

But with tens of thousands of dollars left on her mortgage, the pensioner needs to find a solution soon.

"I've been down here since 1971 … everything's familiar," she said.

"The bus runs past my door. I've got a park across the road. The doctors are just across the park.

"As we age, you don't need as much either. But it's just knowing your community.

"So to me, everything is very convenient and very handy. To move, I won't have all that."

World.title: Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street. Sophie, Standing There

Meg Mason

Fourth Estate, $34.99, out now

Sorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques. Meg Mason’s third novel is more than a study of loneliness. James Brickwood Blackbirding

Ryan Butta

Simon & Schuster, $36.99, out now

The term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking. Time Travel for Beginners

Jaclyn Moriarty

Ultimo, $34.99, out now

Jaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.” Amy Remeikis decries civility politics in her new book. Screw Nice

Amy Remeikis

Hachette, $34.99, out now

Political analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”



Now, Autonomy

Max Easton

Giramondo, $32.95, out now

If you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria. Nuclear Archipelago

Elizabeth Tynan

NewSouth, $39.99, out now

The third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”. Mine

Adam Ouston

Transit Lounge, $$34.99, out now

Don’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide. Adam Ouston has written his new novel in one sentence. The Hurt

Catherine de Saint Phalle

Transit Lounge, $32.99, out now

When she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”. Realms of Gold

A.J. Mackinnon

Black Inc., $36.99, out August 4

Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A.J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice. Eye of the Needle

Christopher Raja

Text, $34.99, out August 4

The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

World.title: Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund
World.content:
Breaking CultureArt & designCity life Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund Chris Hook August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Sydney Opera House will receive an $120 million upgrade over the next four years to renew critical infrastructure, modernise ageing venue technology and replace 150 concrete beams, slabs and piers sitting in a tidal zone beneath the World Heritage masterpiece. In a second act of the Opera House’s major renewal, the Minns government will announce a four-year investment on Tuesday, with most works invisible to the public. Submerged structures beneath the Northern Boardwalk will be replaced. Steven Siewert The announcement was made just four years after the curtain was lifted on a $150 million refurbishment of the Concert Hall, and work will target the building’s smaller western venues and underlying marine structures. The announcement marks a final milestone for outgoing chief executive Louise Herron, who departs this week after 14 years at the helm to take on a Vice Chancellor’s Fellow role at the University of Sydney.



An executive search firm has yet to be appointed, and names thrown up as a possible replacement include Carriageworks’ Fergus Linehan, Sydney Theatre Company’s Anne Dunn and Brenna Hobson, the Opera House’s programming director. The investment was made possible under a new mechanism which quarantines the allocation to the Opera House for use for capital works only. After 14 years Louise Herron is leaving the Sydney Opera House. Steven Siewert “This funding will do wonders for the long-term future of a World Heritage masterpiece,” Herron said. “The area we are referring to is underlying marine structures on the northern side of the Opera House precinct, entirely facing the harbour and subject to the tides and wash of the passing heavy marine traffic. The work is going to tender by the end of the year and work will be staged in the Playhouse and Drama Theatre to minimise disruption.”



Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the $120 million injection, delivered over four years, would help the Opera House keep pace with modern visitor and performance expectations. Key features of the project include replacing 1970s-era theatre machinery and staging systems in the Playhouse, Studio and Drama Theatre – venues frequently used by companies including Sydney Theatre Company and Bell Shakespeare. The works will introduce automated stage draping, stage risers and acoustic curtains, allowing for faster and more efficient turnarounds between shows as the venue expands its program of contemporary music, talks, comedy, circus and cabaret alongside anchor residents such as the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Australian Chamber Orchestra and Sydney Philharmonia Choirs. The Drama Theatre relies on manual hand lines – a counter-weight and pulley system – and temporary chain motors. Installing cutting-edge theatre technology will improve safety while enabling greater performance range and complexity. Stage accessibility will also be upgraded, alongside event management and control systems across both indoor and outdoor venues to future-proof precinct-wide communications.



Work begins in 2027, focusing on reinforcing concrete piers and submerged structures of the Northern Boardwalk that have weathered more than 50 years of salt water, ferry wash and heavy foot traffic. Related Article Visual art David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’ The upgrades follow recent planning reforms that increased outdoor venue capacity and operational hours, Arts Minister John Graham said, important work for a building that was a “symbol of modern Australia”. The Sydney Opera House welcomes 11 million precinct visitors each year, with 1.4 million audience members attending its 1850 annual performances and more than 8000 people employed across the precinct. The former Coalition government contributed $234 million to the building’s decade-long renewal, its new Centre for Creativity, refurbished function and events centre and Joan Sutherland Theatre upgrades, with the Opera House contributing more than $50 million from its own cash reserves. It was the biggest capital investment in the Opera House since its opening. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist August 4, 2026 — 5:30am

August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The news that Collingwood and Geelong had reached agreements with Bobby Hill and Ty Stengle to depart the club was hardly a surprise. But that didn’t make hearing it any less disappointing as both were extremely talented players who starred on the biggest stages for their clubs. Premierships, All-Australian selection and a Norm Smith medal bear testament to the ability they possessed. Bobby Hill, pictured at training in June, parted ways from Collingwood. Getty Images More importantly they are also people who I care about having enjoyed the interactions I have had with them over the years. Like their teammates and coaches and fans, I only want the best for them in the next chapter of their lives.



But their untimely departures raise questions in my mind about whether we need to reevaluate the way we manage players as they learn what is required to be a professional athlete. Although ultimate responsibility sits with each individual, the game needs to have an honest look at what it can learn from such untimely departures. The first and most important question to consider is why the game seems to allow players to continue to make mistake after mistake without them being held accountable. That’s all players regardless of background, gender or talent. My impression is that the clubs, the AFL and the Players’ Association have become comfortable with a system which allows players too much protection the first time they commit relatively minor indiscretions.



If the offence enters the public arena they might receive a two-match ban. Otherwise the clubs, association and league are more inclined to keep the transgression behind closed doors to work with the player while they keep contributing to the business of winning. That approach sets individuals up for failure because they have the opportunity to move further and further away from meeting the standards required to be a professional athlete. It then becomes more difficult for them to adjust and reset themselves. I am not naive. Such an approach has been part of professional sport for aeons but in the era of unrelenting media coverage, wellbeing and personal issues are too often being used to protect individuals from unwanted scrutiny if they muck up.



Some argue that such a strategy has had successes no-one hears about. Tyson Stengle has left Geelong as a premiership player. Cameron Spencer But we also see the results of that approach when players gradually drift from the club and eventually train spasmodically. It is disappointing for all involved, particularly when you wonder if some tough love early would have set the players on a more realistic course. I suspect it would and if it didn’t it at least shows players what the expectations will be in the real world when skill at football means little and there is no-one to protect you.



Soon after I was charged with possessing cocaine in February 2010 (I eventually accepted a 12-month good behaviour bond) the club told me to go away for three months and work in a real job away from the team. It was hard work with no certainty as to what lay ahead. I learned that the privilege of being an AFL player could be taken from me instantly and I would need to work to win back the respect of the league, club, teammates and supporters. Such hard conversations would also force players to face the prospect that being a professional athlete might not be for them before clubs spend hundreds of thousands of dollars and expect teammates and coaches to speak in riddles about their absence from training or the club. Editor's pick Four Points

AFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation That doesn’t mean those in charge show no empathy for a player’s background or individual circumstances when developing them as a professional athlete. Not at all. Clubs must support people inside their environment.



Understanding players and building good relationships with them is an essential part of any successful club. I am arguing that all players have to meet a certain standard regardless of who they are, their life experiences, or where they come from. If they aren’t met, then the player faces consequences. I would expect clubs, the league and the players’ association to review the decisions which led to Hill and Stengle’s departures from their clubs. A mature conversation needs to be had about what happens if a player is not rocking up to training yet is still being rewarded with an income.



A conversation should also be held about the prospect of applying penalties to players who don’t meet required standards in real time to give them an incentive to lift their game. Such penalties could set them up for a life beyond the AFL rather than rationalising a reason for someone to play the week after a misdemeanour because they are talented. It will also reduce any disincentive a club might have in taking in players from various backgrounds or offering them long-term deals if they know they can deal with situations as they arise how they see fit. People in footy want the best for players but development can only occur when consequences result from behaviour. And the sooner that happens, the better. That’s the real world where the most important lessons are learned.



Mathew Stokes is a Larrakia man who played 200 games with Geelong and Essendon. He played in Geelong’s 2007 and 2011 premiership teams. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ASX set to dip, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation Stan Choe August 4, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are rallying to the edge of their all-time high after easing oil prices helped calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse. The S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and is just 0.1 per cent below its record set earlier this summer. It’s coming off a wild July, where it swung up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and other worries. The Dow Jones was up 649 points, or 1.2 per cent, as of 2:30 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.2 per cent higher. Wall Street has rallied to start the week. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 2 points at the open. The ASX jumped 0.5 per cent on Monday after President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. US stocks got a lift to kick off their trading week as the price for a barrel of Brent crude sank 5 per cent to $US83.52. Brent’s price careened between $US72 and $US102 last month as worries rose and fell about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide. The latest acquiescence by Trump helped to ease worries about the global flow of crude, and Treasury yields correspondingly fell in the bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.68 per cent from 4.75 per cent late on Friday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Home loans The path to first home ownership might be under a flight path Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Higher yields threaten to undercut prices for stocks and other investments, while slowing the economy by making borrowing more expensive for US households and businesses. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already leaped to its highest level in a year. Monday’s ease in oil prices helped airlines and other companies with big fuel bills lead the market. United Airlines flew 5.5 per cent higher, while American Airlines climbed 4.7 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 4.5 per cent higher. Boeing soared 7.2 per cent. US regulators certified its new 737 MAX-7 planes, clearing it for commercial service, following years of work to provide pilots with clearer information and warnings, along with other improvements.



Amazon rose as much as 5.8 per cent on Monday to touch an intraday high, becoming only the fifth company to ever cross the $US3 trillion ($4.3 trillion) market-cap threshold. Tyson Foods added 1.6 per cent after the meat company reported a slightly stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected. CEO Donnie King said strength is continuing in the company’s chicken business and its prepared foods, which include brands like Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm. It joined a lengthening list of big US companies to deliver a bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected. That’s imperative for Wall Street because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term, and worries were rising that US stock prices may have broadly already shot too high. Companies in the S&P 500 are on track to deliver earnings per share for the spring that are 47 per cent higher than a year before, according to FactSet, with more than half of the companies in the index having already reported. If that ends up being the case, it would be the strongest growth since the spring of 2021, when the economy was roaring out of the COVID pandemic. Also offering encouragement for profits was a report on Monday showing that growth for US manufacturing accelerated to its strongest level since 2022.



Keeping Wall Street unsettled, though, were swings for stocks of companies that make computer chips. They’ve been veering up and down for weeks on worries about whether their surging revenues because of the artificial-intelligence boom are sustainable. If AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than hoped, Big Tech companies could curtail their spending sprees on data centres that have helped chip stocks soar to tremendous heights. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Micron Technology went from a drop of 6.4 per cent to a gain of 1.7 per cent through the day before sitting at a gain of 1 per cent, for example. It’s still up roughly 190 per cent for the year so far. The manic swings for AI stocks have been most dramatic in South Korea, where the Kospi index is dominated by just two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.



Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.1 per cent Monday, coming off Friday’s 17.9 per cent surge that was its best day in history. In neighbouring Japan, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.9 per cent after the United States and Japan confirmed they had moved together to prop up the value of the Japanese yen against the dollar. A stronger yen would help to limit inflation in Japan, but it could also potentially hurt Japan’s exporters. AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading.
