"For mum and dad businesses that have got a mortgage, the house is on the line."

In welcoming the apology, Ingram said he would look forward to seeing what actions the government would take now to support small businesses going forward.

Overall Ingram said other parts of the discussion he "totally" agreed with, it was just the "whole parent-child narrative that came out that didn't really land very well".

The Rotorua mayor told RNZ the business community really appreciated having the prime minister in town.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tapsell was the National Party candidate for the East Coast electorate in 2020.

She acknowledged it was "tough times, and that was the context in which the question was answered".

She said Luxon didn't need to apologise because "he had a room full of people that was taking on his advice".

Tapsell, who wasn't at the event herself, was told that the feeling in the room afterwards was "definitely that they appreciated his thoughts on it".

"We need to get real in New Zealand," Tapsell said. "Sometimes it is us that actually needs to solve our own problems, and I feel like that's what he's doing not only in those comments but also actually in Parliament.

"So good on him."

Tapsell said Luxon was being honest, and that was "the best thing we can ask from people".

"At least he's not running us around in a circle, not answering the question, and honestly, that was appreciated and valued on the day in the room."

She said it was "very lovely" that he did apologise, and reflected Luxon's honesty and integrity, "he's being honest as he was in the room".

"It's a pretty big thing for a politician to apologise. This doesn't happen very often."

Tapsell said from the business perspective, he was answering a question in the context of difficult times.

"Yes, things are bad, but don't rely on government handouts - I can understand that as a mayor from a council as well.

World.title: Cost blowout puts fees for foreign PhD students under review
World.content:
Govt caps funding for foreign PhD students as costs surge Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A blow-out in the cost of treating foreign PhD students like locals has prompted a rethink of the long-standing policy and a cap on spending next year.

Since 2005 foreign doctoral students have paid the same tuition fees as local students (about $10,000 a year) with the government providing a tuition subsidy (starting at about $10,000 for the cheapest programmes) as if they were domestic students.

The policy pushed international PhD student enrolments nearly as high as domestic for most of the past decade but last year the cost of the scheme jumped by nearly a quarter to $69 million.

In response, this year's government Budget capped next year's funding at 2024's figure of $56m though the Education Ministry said it would be a "soft cap" used to calculate each university's funding rather than a benchmark or enrolment target.

Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds told RNZ the ministry was also reviewing the arrangement.

"The number of international PhD learners has increased quickly, and the cost of the current settings has grown by more than 20 percent a year over the past two years," she said in a statement.

"Our priority is to ensure New Zealand remains attractive to top international research talent, while maintaining opportunities for New Zealanders, and making sure that research is focused on our four national science, innovation, and technology pillars."

The government has capped next year's funding for foreign doctoral students paying the same tuition fees as local students at $56m. AFP

Ministry figures showed foreign PhD students accounted for about 48 percent of all PhD enrolments pre-Covid, dropping to a low of 43 percent in 2022 with 4310 enrolments before bouncing back to a high of 5265 or 49 percent of PhD enrolments last year.

During that time the cost of the scheme dropped from $55m in 2019 to a low of just over $43m in 2022 before rising to $56m in 2024 and about $69m last year.

Association of Scientists co-president Troy Baisden said the policy created a bigger population of research students which in turn increased the amount of research universities produced.

"That's been something that's really uplifted the reputation of our universities over the last two decades," he said.

But Professor Baisden said it seemed to have become successive governments' sole policy and other aspects of PhD study and early career research were neglected.

In particular, stipends for PhD students had not kept up with inflation and there was not enough funding for post-doctoral positions once they finished.

Baisden said those factors made it it increasingly difficult to persuade New Zealanders to embark on a PhD.

"They take a big hit to the money they would make for at least three years... and then have a very uncertain prospect of getting jobs out the end of their PhDs so there is a real problem there that has been building for many years," he said.

"The cap is a plaster on an issue that isn't fixed."

Association of Scientists co-president Troy Baisden. Waikato University

Baisden said reducing the number of foreign PhD students could incentivise people to create better conditions for New Zealand students.

Universities New Zealand chair Neil Quigley said officials were talking to universities but it was not yet clear what might change or when.

He said the sector could probably cope with a cut to its income from foreign PhD students because domestic enrolments were at all-time highs.

"We are in a situation where there's enrolment growth for domestic students across the country," he said.

"So probably at the moment we're in a period where the income from these students is not as big a concern as it might be in other situations."

However, he said the policy had been valuable for New Zealand's research effort.

Tertiary Education Union tiriti president Ti Lamusse said the union's members were worried about the policy's future.

"I just spoke to a member at Massey who all his PhD students are international students so they're at the core of advancing the most interesting and important research," he said.

Lamusse said any increase to international PhD students' fees would increase the cost of research because universities often covered students' fees from grants for specific projects.

"If you're going for a grant and that grant includes paying for a PhD student's scholarship it's a heck of a lot more expensive if you're paying for the international fees," he said.

Universities New Zealand chair Neil Quigley. Supplied

Where they come from, what they're studying

Education Ministry figures show there were 5390 domestic doctoral students last year, about 300 fewer than in recent years, and 5265 international PhD students, 80 percent of them from Asia.

China provided more PhD students than any other country with 1970 last year followed by India (350) and Sri Lanka (310).

Just over 60 percent of domestic PhD students (3305) and 55 percent of international PhD students (2870) were female.

Most PhD enrolments were in a handful of broad fields of study.

Society and Culture was the biggest area of PhD enrolment with 2155 students (including 790 foreign students) followed by Natural and Physical Sciences with 2045 students evenly split between domestic and international.

Engineering had 1690 students (1150 international) and Health 1565 (490 international).

In 2017, a Ministry of Education report said 75 percent of foreign PhD students had returned overseas five years after completing their studies, the highest percentage of any group of international students.

World.title: Death during brawl at league game in Samoa raises safety question
World.content:
By Talaia Mika, RNZ Pacific Samoa correspondent

There's been a call for police in Samoa to attend local sports matches after the death of a man during a rugby league game over the weekend.

The incident has raised questions about safety at community sporting events, but police say discipline cannot depend solely on officers being present.

A Marist Saints rugby league player, known as Saveatama Faamavaega Saveatama, died as a result of an altercation at the Vaiala Rugby Fields on Saturday during a match between Marist Saints and the Apia Barracudas.

Social media was flooded with footage of the brawl between players which continued in spite of the deceased lying flat on the ground, unconscious.

A local club rugby league match in Apia. August 2025 Facebook / Rugby League Samoa

Brawl on video

It was only until the altercation eased off that some people turned to the deceased and assisted although it was too late.

RNZ understands that these videos have all been reported to police as part of the collected evidence.

Acting Police Commissioner Leiataua Samelu Afamasaga said no one had been charged as investigators continued to gather evidence.

"The evidence needs to be beyond reasonable doubt before we can charge someone. We haven't found anyone yet," he said.

"So our investigation continues and we need to be satisfied that there is enough evidence to charge a certain suspect."

Leiataua said while tragedies cannot always be prevented, police remain focused on taking a proactive approach to law enforcement.

"The thing is, we cannot avoid what has already happened and the things that happen as part of life. However, we try and be proactive and preventive through our work as law enforcement."

'Refrain from retaliatory actions'

The Samoa Police, Prisons and Corrections Services (SPPCS) are continuing to investigate the incident and are appealing to members of the public who may have recorded videos or possess any footage to provide it directly to investigators or through the SPPCS' Facebook page.

"While videos are circulating on social media, the public is strongly urged to provide any such footage to the police, as it may assist significantly with the investigation," police said in a statement.

Authorities said public cooperation was vital in helping maintain peace and order at sporting events while supporting the pursuit of justice for the family of the deceased.

Police also urged those involved not to retaliate.

"We urge all parties involved to refrain from retaliatory actions. Such conduct will be dealt with swiftly and will face the full extent of the law."

The incident has also prompted calls for a stronger police presence at community rugby matches.

Attempts to get a comment from the mayor of Vaiala on how the village bylaws are handling the matter, were unsuccessful.

Village concern

A village meeting for Vaiala was expected to take place to discuss matters pertaining to the village including this incident.

Vaiala's female representative, Sileoleoga Patu Wilson, described the incident as deeply concerning and said it was the first time she had heard of someone dying in connection with games in Vaiala.

"This is the first time I have heard of someone dying from such games especially here in Vaiala so this is concerning and we need to make sure this doesn't happen again," she told RNZ Pacific.

"Part of that is making sure the police are present at these events to prevent such behaviour from taking place."

Wilson said she did not know the full circumstances surrounding the incident but believed it highlighted the need to encourage young people to stay away from violence.

"I don't have any specific information about what happened but for me as the female representative for Vaiala, it's important to encourage our young ones to stay away from such behaviours."

She said it remained unclear whether the victim was from Vaiala, who the young people involved were or exactly what had happened.

"We're not sure at the moment whether the victim is from Vaiala and who the kids involved are and what exactly happened and whether he was a player or whatever but it did happen."

Wilson said spectators needed to stop interfering with matches and allow referees to do their jobs.

"So it's important to advice our young ones to stop with this behaviour and stop interfering with the games. That's what the referees are for and I see a lot of this happen not just here in Vaiala but elsewhere too as there's a lot of rugby fields across the country now."

She added that while villages have councils, chiefs and bylaws to deal with such behaviour, police presence at games, as had occurred in the past, could also help deter violence.

"We have our village councils and chiefs and bylaws that deal with such matters within villages as well as the police and we would appreciate it if the police officers were to be present at the fields during the games like how it was back then."

Police can't be 'superman'

Responding to those calls, Leiataua said there was no law requiring police officers to be present at every rugby match.

"There is no law that states something like that, that we should be at all the games. There's more than 20 games happening at the same times as the others so we cannot be at all the games.

"We only do something like that when it's the international games. We also show support or attend when we're requested to by certain clubs and so forth."

Instead, he said discipline should already be embedded within rugby clubs and communities through the values of Fa'asamoa.

"So the discipline and that should already be instilled in any rugby union (or clubs) and the everyday Fa'asamoa that we're used to which is respect and everything else that comes with it.

"This mentality that discipline is only possible when police is around shouldn't be a thing. It should already be there everywhere with or without the police's supervision."

Asked whether police would review how officers are deployed following the incident, Leiataua said it was something authorities could consider but cautioned against assuming police presence alone would prevent violence.

"The only thing we can do is look into it. If a brawl or fight was to break out and there's four police officers present, they won't be able to prevent something like that from happening.

"So with or without police supervision, it'll still be the same if we all don't work together.

"It'd be nice if we had superpowers like Superman. But again, police or no police, nothing won't work if we don't work together."

World.title: Who's feeling job market recovery? And where has downturn hit hardest?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

It has been a tough few years to be a jobseeker. Data this week is expected to show the unemployment rate still hovering around the highest level it's been in a decade.

But fortunes have varied depending on where you are in the country, and the type of work you do.

The job market peak was reached in October 2023, when there were 2.395 million filled jobs nationwide. The trough was in October last year, when that had dropped to 2.337m.

Provisional estimates are that the number is now about 2.35m filled jobs.

Westpac chief economist on fuel prices and unemployment Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said from the peak of the market to the bottom, there were just under 60,000 jobs lost but since then, 17,575 have been recovered, leaving the country still 40,924 jobs short compared to the busiest time in the labour market.

Here are some of the winners and losers of the labour market both since the peak, and over the past five years.

Sectors

Since the job market peaked in October 2023, the biggest drop in jobs in percentage terms has been felt in the information media and telecommunications sector, down 11.2 percent or 3761 jobs.

Over five years, smoothing out the post-Covid high, job numbers in that sector are still down 5.6 percent.

Construction has also had a sharp fall from the peak, having lost 8.4 percent of its jobs, or 17,249, but the number is flat compared to 2021.

Some sectors have continued to grow since the peak, such as arts and recreation services, which is up 6.1 percent from 2023 and 16.2 percent over five years. Of this sector, the largest proportion of jobs is in sports and physical recreation, such as people working in gyms. Their numbers have lifted from 22,700 in 2023 to 24,400 last year. There has also been significant growth in businesses. Personal health and fitness training business numbers increased 112.5 percent between 2019 and 2025.

Healthcare and social assistance jobs have also increased since the job market peak, up 5.4 percent since 2023 and 12.7 percent from five years ago.

Education and training is up 4.4 percent from the peak and 6.6 percent over five years.

Eaqub said, on a per population basis, there had not yet been any real recovery. Data would show there were more hours being worked, he said, but the recovery in jobs so far had only kept pace with population growth. "It's not a high-quality recovery yet."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ

Construction's increase was the largest in number terms, followed by manufacturing down 11,822.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the strongest parts of the labour market were those that were tied to underlying population growth.

"It's the expansion of certain elements of public service-related industries as well, particularly in health, education… those sectors have grown a lot because the population has grown in the last five years. They've continued to grow, albeit at a slower rate since 2023, because that was when the population growth peaked… there's quite a few industries that are a lot more government or public sector dominated, and they just tend to not be really influenced by the cycle so much."

In contrast, sectors such as construction were much more closely tied to the fortunes of the wider economy.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said the October 2023 peak was exaggerated by the election, with a burst of short-term filled jobs in public administration. "Excluding that boost, jobs activity likely peaked around March 2024."

"The large increases in healthcare, public administration, and education and training reflect a growing population and of course one of the largest health-related events in memory.

"Further hiring in education is also likely due to retraining of people throughout the pandemic, and then as the unemployment rate increased, with more people looking at training options to re- or up-skill."

He said construction had gone through a significant period of change.

"At one point, residential construction intentions were the highest in half a century, fuelled by rocketing house prices and low interest rates, and the sector scaled up to meet that high demand. But when interest rates rose and house prices and activity dropped, construction activity pulled back too, having upped capacity to meet peak needs that just didn't, and were never going to, persist."

He said both admin and information media and telecoms jobs had been holding up for a while until the downturn became more pronounced.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

By age

Young people have experienced the biggest impact of the downturn.

There are now 61,009 fewer jobs held by people aged under 30 than there were at the peak, and 43,726 fewer than five years ago.

The number of people over 55 working has increased 9.7 percent over five years and the number aged 30 to 54 has increased 9.1 percent.

"It's definitely the younger people who had quite a big increase, particularly the 15 to 19-year-olds had a big increase in jobs or employment during that really tight labour market period, when there was a hiring frenzy during the Covid years, those numbers were unusually high.

"The cost of living particularly for necessities skyrocketed so a lot of young people, kids at school, started to work and that's kind of fallen off and hasn't really recovered."

Ministry of Social Development data shows the biggest increase in main benefit recipient numbers has been in the 25 to 39 age group where there are now 20 percent more people receiving a benefit than there were in June 2021.

Eckhold said it was a "no hire, no fire" market.

"We haven't necessarily seen enormous amounts of layoffs in aggregate across the economy, but it has become quite hard to find a job. And that's particularly impacted the younger age group, because they've got less skills and experience, so it's always just a bit harder."

Region

Canterbury has had some of the strongest job growth. Its job numbers are up 1.4 percent compared to the peak and 8.9 percent over five years.

Auckland is down 2.7 percent form the peak and 5.1 percent up over five years.

Wellington is down 3.8 percent from the peak and 0.3 percent up over five years.

Gisborne has been hard hit, down 4.2 percent from the peak and 1.5 percent over five years.

Wellington and Auckland have had the largest percentage increase in benefit recipients between June 2021 and June 2026, in percentage terms.

Eckhold said he expected to see a small increase in the unemployment rate this week and his current forecast was for that to be the peak.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"I will say though, we'll be doing a whole new set of forecasts this month. When we put in place our previous forecasts, it was in the context of a better outlook, because it looked like energy prices were quite a lot lower. It looked like we're going to have a period of more stability, and that seems to have tended not to be the case now that we've got a little bit further on. So, it may be optimistic to expect that the unemployment rate will be peaking now. Perhaps we might have to wait a bit longer for that."

He said the job market would be the last thing to pick up.

"GDP has actually been picking up now for three or four quarters or so. It looks like we had an interruption to growth in Q2, but three quarters before that we'd had some decent growth. But there's always a lag between when you actually see growth occur and then when hiring really picks up.

"Probably at the start of the year, we would have expected that hiring growth to really be starting to hit its straps now, in the second half of the year. But I think the Iran war has really just pushed that back."

World.title: Oranga Tamariki office blasted over baby's death also managed Tom Phillips case
World.content:
An Oranga Tamariki office whose handling of a baby's death was the subject of a scathing internal review also managed the Tom Phillips case, RNZ can reveal.

The agency says it's made a number of changes at both a site and regional level and has recently appointed a Waikato commissioner.

RNZ earlier revealed an internal Oranga Tamariki review found a series of failures in the agency's handling of Mustafa Ali before he was killed by his father in June 2024.

Mustafa was hospitalised about eight months before his death with serious injuries that his father, Mukzameel Ali, said were caused when he fell while carrying the baby down some stairs.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

A review found several failings in the agency's response including "minimal analysis" of risk and that the monitoring was not good enough.

It also said Oranga Tamariki staff reported there was a "lack of basic knowledge of practice and legislation" among some of the social workers and supervisors on site.

Tom Phillips (inset) with an image released by police of a campsite he used. RNZ / Supplied / Police

In response to questions from RNZ, Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan confirmed both Mustafa's case and the Phillips case were "managed by the same site for a time".

He said they were handled by different social workers.

A report of concern was first sent to Oranga Tamariki by a health staff member in October 2023 about unexplained injuries to Mustafa.

Phillips disappeared with his children in September 2021. He then reappeared and was the subject of criminal charges. Then in December he disappeared again with the children.

He died following a shoot-out with police in September last year. The children were located that day.

RNZ earlier reported it's understood Oranga Tamariki received several reports of concern about the children, both from family and police.

RNZ also asked about the agency's involvement with the Phillips children, including reports of concern.

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan. Supplied / Oranga Tamariki

"We acknowledge the understandable public interest in this case, but that does not outweigh our duty to protect these children's privacy.

"Further, there are suppression orders that apply and a Public Inquiry preparing to finalise their report."

Ronan said the agency was also bound by the Family Court Act.

He told RNZ that since 2024 the agency had made a number of changes at both a site and regional level to "ensure that our practice aligns with expectations and that kaimahi have the support they need to manage what is incredibly complex work".

It had also appointed a commissioner for the Waikato region.

Changes made at a site level included a new approach to intake and assessment work, additional practice support for the site and closer monitoring of non-accidental injuries and unborn/newborn baby monitoring by the practice leader.

The site risk register is reviewed weekly and the regional risk register reviewed fortnightly at a minimum, and staff now had a weekly meeting with senior site leaders to talk through case triaging and work load management and decision making.

At a regional level there had been ongoing training on child protection protocols and upskilling in other areas for staff who require it and strengthening professional supervision for staff and increasing oversight of cases.

The agency had also introduced new assessment and planning tools to support social work decision making alongside families and increased "collaborative ways of working across agencies and within communities to keep children safe".

Phillips inquiry

Former Attorney-General Judith Collins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The government earlier announced an inquiry into the handling of the Phillips case by authorities and whether all "practicable steps" were taken to ensure the safety and welfare of the Phillips children.

Former Attorney-General Judith Collins earlier said the decision to establish a public inquiry "reflects the significant public interest and concern for the children's welfare over the almost four years they were missing".

"It is important that we establish the facts and determine whether agencies could take steps to prevent, or resolve similar situations more quickly and effectively in the future," Collins said.

The terms of reference had been developed with the privacy and welfare of the children in mind. The inquiry would therefore be conducted in private and without public hearings.

Collins said the inquiry must also respect the independence of the courts and would not include findings on judicial decisions.

The Honourable Justice Simon Moore KC was appointed as the sole member of the inquiry.

The government received the final report on 21 July.

Justice Simon Moore KC. RNZ / Dan Cook

Attorney General Chris Bishop said last week the deadline for the inquiry had been extended by a month, in order to "clarify a matter".

He said the inquiry had provided a "thorough and exacting report" on the nature and extent of government agencies' involvement with Phillips and the children.

That included from before their disappearance through to when they were found.

"The inquiry has carefully considered suppression orders and the welfare of the children in its reporting.

"This aligns with the terms of reference's first principle, which ensures the children's welfare is not further threatened," Bishop said.

But he wanted an "issue" clarified, and intended to extend the inquiry's reporting date. No other aspects of the existing terms of reference would change.

World.title: 'Lot of nonsense': Dearden clears air on Cowboys future
World.content:
North Queensland co-captain Tom Dearden has cleared the air about his future and given the club a boost as he targets returning from injury to inspire a finals run.

At the end of the 2023 season Dearden, 26, signed a five-year contract extension through to the end of 2029.

But multiple reports in recent weeks linked him to an early exit for personal reasons due to his pregnant partner, Millie Over, living in Sydney.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Dearden fronted the media to refute the reports due to the impact they were having on his personal life.

"There's been a fair bit of speculation getting around at the moment. There's been a lot of suggestions that I wanted to move or leave the club," Dearden said.

"That's not the case at all. I don't feel like I should have to get up here and explain myself against speculation.

"It's just been a whole lot of nonsense. I've got my private life with a partner who's pregnant and I'd like for that all to be kept private.

"I'm committed to the Cowboys until the end of 2029 and I think it's a bit silly that you have to get up here and speak to a bit of nonsense that's going around."

Dearden made it clear that he was "not recommitting".

"I've always been committed to the Cowboys and none of that has ever changed, so it's a bit disappointing that my partner and family have had to deal with a lot of questions," he said.

Maroons dealt massive blow Queensland selectors have been forced to cope with the news one of their best playmakers will miss up to eight weeks with his ankle injury.

"It's had an impact on the personal life. I've got a pregnant partner and I think when there's speculation getting around like that, people are reading that and it gives them questions to ask and you always have to answer to people."

Dearden has played just once since suffering a syndesmosis and ankle fracture in round 10.

The injury ruled him out of the State of Origin series and he returned against the Dolphins in round 20 only to tear a muscle in his shin on the other leg.

Dearden played through the match but during the following week discovered the issue.

"It's been a frustrating year having to sit out because I love representing the Cowboys," Dearden said.

"It's a bit of a weird injury but it's tracking pretty well and hopefully I've only got a few more weeks [on the sidelines]."

Dearden and the club have targeted the round 26 home clash with Wests Tigers in Townsville as his return date, after the Cowboys' round 25 bye.

North Queensland is in ninth position and plays Gold Coast away on Thursday night before an away clash with Parramatta without its influential half.

AAP

World.title: Former Sea Eagle, ABC radio personality John Gibbs diagnosed with cancer
World.content:
Former Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles halfback and ABC Sport rugby league commentator John Gibbs has been diagnosed with cancer.

Gibbs, 70, has been part of the ABC Sport team since 2016 and has been a popular personality among listeners.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

He was on the ABC Sport call with Andrew Moore and Matthew Elliott on Sunday afternoon when the Parramatta Eels defeated Wests Tigers.

"Gibbsy", who played 81 first grade games for the Sea Eagles and represented New South Wales and Australia, announced his diagnosis on Monday, and that he would be stepping away from broadcasting to focus on his health.

Moore, ABC Sport's lead rugby league caller, said his friend Gibbs wanted listeners to know he was prepared for his upcoming treatment on NRL MONDAY.

"John Gibbs called me this afternoon to confirm something he had been fearing for a while. He's been diagnosed with cancer — Hodgkin's lymphoma," Moore said.

"He knows he's in for a fight, but he wants you to know he's up for it.

"We are family and, as I discovered a year ago, the wave of support from the ABC team, it's significant, it's powerful, it's amazing and it helps.

"Like so many of you, he's ready to kick cancer to the kerb and beat the mongrel."

The former international has been a constant on Sydney radio since the 1980s as a commentator, presenter, and host for 2UE, 2GB and ABC Sport.

World.title: Young Tiger banned as gut-punch crackdown continues
World.content:
Richmond defender Luke Trainor has received a one-match ban for striking as the AFL's crackdown on gut punches continues.

Trainor will miss the Tigers' trip to face Adelaide at Adelaide Oval on Saturday after punching West Coast forward Jack Williams in the stomach as the two were jostling in the goal square at the MCG on Sunday.

Williams dropped to the turf while Trainor jogged off.

Coach Adem Yze had hoped Trainor would only be fined for the second-quarter incident in the 11-point win over the Eagles.

But the match review officer took a dim view of the incident, assessing it as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which draws a one-match ban.

It leaves Richmond short of a tall defender against Adelaide's powerful forward line headlined by Riley Thilthorpe.

AAP

World.title: Wallabies to battle heat, typhoon in Japanese Test
World.content:
The Wallabies are not concerned Japan's searing heat and lingering typhoon will play a part in their preparation or Test match as they look to face old foes in Les Kiss's debut as coach.

Australia will take on Japan in the first of two Tests on Saturday night at Hanazono Rugby Stadium in Osaka, although conditions are not expected to be easy to play in.

Temperatures are tipped to stay in the high 20s to mid-30s degrees Celsius all week as the country grapples with a heatwave.

To make matters worse, Typhoon Dolphin is bringing wind gusts of up to 216kph and heavy rainfall ahead of hitting the Southern Japanese Ryukyu Islands on Friday, about 1,500 kilometres south of Osaka.

Wallabies thrash Italy as Schmidt era ends in triumph The Wallabies record a convincing 57-10 victory over Italy in Perth, as Joe Schmidt's coaching tenure finishes on a winning note.

But Queensland hooker Josh Nasser is treating the conditions as just another day in Australia.

"Obviously it's pretty warm over here, but I grew up in Brissy. We get some pretty hot summers as well. So humidity's up, temperatures up, but it's no different to some of the conditions we get back home," he told reporters on Monday.

"In the wet, the ball gets slippery, things tighten up a little bit. But I think we've got a big focus on just still trying to express ourselves.

"We play a fixture in Fiji each year, which we get pretty extreme conditions for.

"We're really not hyper-focused on it. We're just accepting that it will be hot, and then sticking to our processes."

Wallabies assistant coach Scott McLeod also warned of another typhoon that could affect Australia's clash.

"Is that Eddie Jones?" he joked when a journalist asked about Typhoon Dolphin.

Jones, who led Australia to a dismal Rugby World Cup showing in 2023 before resigning, will coach his second game against the green and gold with the Brave Blossoms.

Former Wallabies coach Eddie Jones will face Australia for the second time as Japan's coach. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

Nasser expects his presence to add extra spice to the fixture, especially as the master agitator took over the Japanese side just six weeks after resigning and was forced to deny that he had been in talks with Brave Blossoms officials during the World Cup.

Jones will not be the only Australian on the opposition, with former Queensland lock Harry Hockings along with Ben Gunter, Jack Cornelsen, Dylan Riley, Michael Stolberg and Tiennan Costley all options to play.

The Wallabies have been humbled by Australians featuring for different national teams in the past, most notably Canberra-born Mack Hansen when he scored a stunning first-half hat-trick to help Ireland win 46-19 last November.

"They'll be fired up to prove a point against us, I'm sure. [There's] nothing too strange about seeing them there, but it'll be a good battle," Nasser said.

"A couple of them are my good mates. Harry Hockings is one of my best mates.

"[I haven't spoken to him] on the rugby front, but I'm sure I'll catch up with him for a beer after the game."

The reunions will all culminate in Kiss's first match in charge of the national team since Joe Schmidt departed following the Wallabies' rousing 57-10 victory over Italy on July 18.

AAP

World.title: NRLW star in hot water for dangerous lifting tackle
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos NRLW star Ali Brigginshaw is facing the prospect of a lengthy stint on the sidelines after being referred straight to the judiciary for a lifting tackle during last weekend's Magic Round.

The Broncos remained unbeaten and on top of the ladder with a commanding 34-4 victory over the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, but the win was soured by Brigginshaw's first-half tackle on Bulldogs halfback Tayla Preston.

Brigginshaw was sent to the sin bin after her tackle on Preston, where the Bulldogs player was swung around and lifted before being driven into the ground head-first.

Preston avoided serious injury, and Brigginshaw was handed a grade three dangerous throw charge.

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has never missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

She will argue her case at the judiciary on Tuesday, where she could face a significant ban.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, where she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade three striking charge.

Brisbane, reigning NRLW premiers, faces Canberra this week, followed by a grand final rematch with the Roosters, then a derby against the Gold Coast Titans.

World.title: Canberra secures new NBL role amid expansion team hopes
World.content:
Canberra is one step closer to hosting an NBL team for the first time in more than two decades, the league's parent company chief executive has said.

The NBL's in-season competition, the Ignite Cup, will undergo a shake-up with the tournament's finals set to move from the Gold Coast to Canberra's AIS Arena.

It is the latest competition development in the nation's capital as speculation grows that the league is looking to expand into Canberra along with Darwin, the Gold Coast and a second Sydney team.

Ingles comes 'home' in coup NBL signing The legendary Boomers and NBA star will return to Australia's NBL for the first time since 2009, signing with Melbourne United for two years.

Competition executives have said they want to grow the current 10-team league, but new clubs will have to have the capacity to host at least 8,000 spectators.

With the ACT government announcing it will build the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct, hope remains the city can secure an NBL team for the first time since the Canberra Cannons were last involved in 2003.

The Cannons won three NBL titles before relocating to Newcastle, while the Sydney Kings now play some regular season matches at AIS Arena.

Admitting he would have loved to announce a Cannons rebirth on Monday, NBL Group CEO David Stevenson still gave every indication the league was eyeing the capital.

"We've got strong confidence that we can work together with Basketball ACT, with everyone involved in the sport to make sure that hopefully once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team," he said.

"What we're building is a really strong business case, and it's not just about what happens at the game; it's the economic contribution that's really important for us."

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr added that a minimum of 7,500 seats were planned for the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct.

"A key element of the business case is having a basketball team play there, or more than one basketball team, actually. But it's not just a basketball stadium, it's got to accommodate other uses as well," Barr said.

"The AIS Arena is a fantastic venue, but it sort of maxes out at about 5,000 people.

"It was very clear in talking both to live music promoters, to the major sporting organisations … that we were missing out because 5,000 was too small."

But before expansion, the nation's capital will have to settle for the midweek Ignite Cup, an NBL competition involving 20 games held on Wednesday nights.

The four most successful teams will compete for a share in $550,000 when they progress to the semifinals in Canberra on February 19 before the decider on February 21.

The NBL's MVP Awards are also moving from Melbourne for the first time in more than a decade and will be hosted at the Great Hall in Canberra's Parliament House.

AAP

World.title: McIlroy headlines summer of golf with DeChambeau targeted
World.content:
The return of grand slam winner Rory McIlroy and the first Australian PGA Championship in Sydney this century highlights a 19-event summer of golf starting this month.

With the global professional golf scene in a state of flux, the Australasian Tour has secured a record partnership and announced a jam-packed schedule with major championship and European Tour spots once again up for grabs.

McIlroy back gracing Melbourne fairways, this time at iconic Kingston Heath from December 3–6, and the PGA Championship at The Lakes possibly featuring big-hitting fan favourite Bryson DeChambeau, are the two hottest tickets.

McIlroy completes one of his missions Rory McIlroy's appearance at the Australian Open in Melbourne has gone a long way to restoring the prestige of the tournament.

Record crowds followed the Northern Irishman at last year's Australian Open at Royal Melbourne before McIlroy successfully defended his US Masters title at Augusta National in April.

Officials revealed they were also targeting two-time US Open winner DeChambeau for the PGA, which was last held in Sydney back in 1998.

The new season begins in the now traditional style with the PNG Open at Royal Port Moresby Golf Club on August 27–30 before visiting all mainland states in Australia, as well as New Zealand's north and south islands, across the 19-tournament schedule.

The centenary Queensland PGA Championship will take place on the Kurrai course at Nudgee Golf Club in Brisbane from November 19–22.

Boasting a past champions list that includes Australian greats Greg Norman, David Graham and Peter Senior, the event will be played immediately before the Australian PGA Championship.

Co-sanctioned by the European Tour, the Australian PGA Championship also marks the start of the Race to Dubai, the tour's season-long rankings competition.

The PGA Tour of Australasia will also feature two new tournament venues in 2026–27.

Secret Harbour Golf Links, south of Perth, will host the WA Open for the first time, while Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club becomes the new home of Players Series Victoria as a forerunner to hosting next year's Australian Open.

There is a switch of order for the three-leg New Zealand swing in February that proved to be a huge success in 2026.

The New Zealand Open will now be the finale, following the Japan-Australasia Championship that returns for its second year at Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club.

PGA Tour of Australasia schedule

PNG Open, Royal Port Moresby Golf Club, August 27–30

WA PGA Championship, Kalgoorlie Golf Course, October 8–11

WA Open, Secret Harbour Golf Links, October 15–18

Players Series SA, Willunga Golf Course, October 22–25

NSW Open, The Vintage Golf Club, November 12–15

Queensland PGA Championship, Nudgee Golf Club, November 19–22

Australian PGA Championship, The Lakes Golf Club, November 26–29

Australian Open, Kingston Heath Golf Club, December 3–6

Vic PGA Championship, Moonah Links Resort, December 10–13

Players Series Perth, Royal Fremantle Golf Club, January 7–10

Players Series Victoria, Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club, Jan 14–17

Vic Open, 13th Beach Golf Links, January 21–24

Players Series Murray River, Cobram Barooga Golf Club, January 28–31

Players Series Sydney, Castle Hill Country Club, February 4–7

NZ PGA Championship, Paraparaumu Beach Golf Club, February 11–14

Japan-Australasia Championship, Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club, February 18–21

New Zealand Open, Millbrook Resort, February 25–28

The National Tournament, The National Golf Club, March 18–21

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Delta stuns with Aussie classic, 76yo claims history-making gold
World.content:
Delta Goodrem belts out an Aussie classic, a 76-year-old makes Commonwealth Games history and a cycling star is proud to have not thrown up on the podium.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Delta makes it a hat-trick with Aussie classic

Delta Goodrem produced a breathtaking performance in the closing ceremony. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

It was a closing ceremony featuring some serious Australian star power, with Delta Goodrem headlining proceedings.

It was the third time, after Melbourne 2006 and Gold Coast 2018, that Goodrem had performed at a Commonwealth Games, and the Australian icon was in fine form at the Hydro indoor arena in Glasgow.

Goodrem was revealed to the crowd in dramatic fashion, lit by a spotlight and sitting at a grand piano, belting out her classic Born To Try, before rising from her seat and welcoming the athletes into the venue with an inspired medley of her hits.

And the performance reached a real crescendo when she welcomed Scottish pop star Cammy Barnes to the stage for a rendition of the most classic of Aussie classics, John Farnham's You're the Voice.

Goosebumps in Glasgow.

2. 76-year-old creates Games history

Louise Hoskins made history on the final day of competition. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Louise Hoskins, 76, made history on the final day of competition in Glasgow, becoming the oldest medal winner in Commonwealth Games history.

She, along with partner Serena Bonnell, won gold in the women's Para bowls, defeating New Zealand in a classic.

It was Bonnell who provided the winning moment for the Aussies, conjuring a sublime shot late in the second set to secure the win.

The oldest competitor in Glasgow, Hoskins was struggling to wrap her head around the enormity of the achievement.

"It is incredible. I'm still pinching myself," she said.

"I never thought I'd ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up."

Asked how she planned to celebrate, Hoskins noted Bonnell still owed her a few drinks.

What will it be then?

"Whatever Serena's going to give me," Hoskins laughed.

3. Cycling star proud not to spew on podium

Leigh Hoffman looked far from comfortable on the podium. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

Australian Leigh Hoffman won four medals in a packed track cycling program, including a gold on the final day of competition.

He was the second-last rider in the men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal.

And he looked far from comfortable on the top step.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but he says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years' time.

4. Aussie chef de mission gets ink

Loading...

Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas loves the Friendly Games — and understandably so.

She was a nine-time Commonwealth gold medallist during her decorated swimming career and has just overseen a Games in which Australia claimed 70 golds, 41 more than the next best nation, England.

On the final day of competition, Thomas was seen out in Glasgow getting herself a permanent testament to the event for which she has so much affection.

She said the Games have a special place in her heart, and now a special place on her body.

"I've thought about it for a long time and the Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics. So I thought why not get the Commonwealth Sport mark as well, and I'll wear it very proudly," Thomas said.

"The Commonwealth Games has played such an important part of my life and I wanted to get something to remember that."

5. Scottish athletes win fashion stakes

Scottish athletes had some fun at the closing ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

Scottish athletes were hard to miss at the closing ceremony.

The host nation's contingent wore traffic cones on their heads as they took part in the festivities inside The Hydro.

Loading Instagram content

It's common practice for Glaswegians to put traffic cones on the heads of statues around the city.

Arguably the most famous example is the Duke of Wellington statue outside the Gallery of Modern Art.

A statue in Boston could not escape the Glaswegian tradition during the FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Craig Williamson/SNS Group)

The ritual was celebrated at the recent FIFA World Cup, with Scottish fans decorating statues in Boston in their customary way.

You can never suggest Scots don't know how to poke fun at themselves.

ABC/AAP

Tech.title: Europe’s AI labeling and transparency rules are now in effect
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The European Union has ushered in some additional rules that aim to make it easier for people to identify chatbots and AI deepfakes online. The new transparency obligations under the bloc’s landmark AI Act came into effect on August 2nd, requiring companies to disclose when people are interacting with AI models, and if content has been generated or altered by them.

The transparency rules differ between providers (companies that develop and market AI systems) and deployers (platforms and services that use those AI systems), though some companies like Meta and SpaceXAI are classified as both.

If enough companies do adopt the EU’s AI icons then labels should look more consistent across online platforms. Image: The European Commission

Providers must design AI systems to explicitly notify users when they’re dealing with AI instead of a human, “unless this is obvious,” and include machine-readable marks on synthetic audio, image, video, and text so that it can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Likewise, deployers are required to label any AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, and video deepfake content that’s designed to look real.

“The rapid development of generative and interactive AI systems is making it increasingly difficult to distinguish AI interactions and AI-generated content from human-created and authentic content,” the European Commission said in its transparency guidelines. “People should know when they are interacting with AI or exposed to AI-generated content. This will help them make informed decisions, calibrate their trust and reliance on AI and avoid misinformation or deception.”

The Commission has also developed a set of AI disclosure labels that tech platforms can adopt in accordance with the AI Act rules, alongside examples of when they should be used. These mirror similar labels that have already been introduced by TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook. The EU-made icons have been introduced to prevent platforms from having to design their own, and while the EU examples are optional to use, the Commission pointedly notes that its labeling requirements “are not.”

Companies that fail to comply with these new transparency rules risk facing fines of up to €15 million (about $17.2 million), or 3 percent of their global annual turnover. While the new transparency rules are enforceable immediately for new AI systems, any models and services that launched before August 2nd have a four-month grace period until December 2nd to comply.

Tech.title: The first-gen Kindle Scribe is a big e-reader and digital notebook that’s $150 refurbished
Tech.content:
The Kindle Scribe is worth considering if you’re heading back to school, as its large 10.2-inch screen can display textbooks and ebooks, or let you jot down handwritten notes during class. Now through August 8th, the first-gen model (with a Premium Pen) is down to just $149.99 with 16GB of storage in refurbished condition at Woot when you apply the promo code KINDLE25 at checkout. That’s $220 off its original launch price from 2022 and even cheaper than the current Kindle Paperwhite, though you’ll only get Woot’s 90-day warranty. Woot doesn’t specify the exact condition of its refurbished devices, but it does offer a brief explanation here of what to expect.

The Kindle Scribe features a sharp 300ppi E Ink display that’s glare-free and supports adjustable color temperatures, making it easy to read whether you’re outside in the sun or studying late at night. Like all other Kindles, the Scribe gives you quick and easy access to Amazon’s massive store of digital books, so you can switch between assigned reading and your favorite novels without carrying multiple books or devices. It’s not waterproof like the Kindle Paperwhite, though, so you’ll want to keep it away from the pool and be careful when it rains.

It’s also a solid digital notebook, with the device offering a variety of pre-made templates for everything from lined paper and planners to to-do lists. After updating the software, the original Kindle Scribe also includes the same AI-powered note-taking features as the newer models, allowing you to jot down notes directly on compatible ebook pages, summarize and refine your handwritten notes, generate AI-powered summaries, and more.

Tech.title: Microsoft is bringing Xbox 360 games to PC
Tech.content:
Building on its recently announced plans to bring original Xbox games to PC, Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC as well, according to a leaked document, seen by The Verge, that was sent to developers recently. Xbox 360 games will be able to run on the next-gen Project Helix console, “Xbox PCs,” and handheld devices, the document says.

Microsoft has already said that Helix will play PC games, so making these older Xbox titles available on PC helps build a broader Xbox library that can travel between devices, similar to what’s already possible with Steam. Creating all these digital licenses also helps set up for a future of consoles without disc drives; Sony has already declared game discs dead, and Microsoft may follow.

With 360 games, developers can opt into making them backward compatible, and they will have control over things like a game’s price and if it’s available on Game Pass. The feature is expected to have a “gradual” rollout between 2027 and 2028 “across next-gen devices.” The “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC is also set for October 2026; the initial program announced in July included just four games.

The document also includes details about a way for players to get a digital version of a game that they already own on a physical disc, which The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on in July. The document says that if a player puts an Xbox One or Series game on disc into an Xbox One or Series X console with a disc drive, they’ll be granted a digital license that’s bound to “that disc and the player’s account.” The license will stay with a player across Xbox devices, but if the disc “changes hands,” the license will transfer to the new person. That should mean that gamers can still trade and sell discs; once the original owner of a disc does so, they can’t play the digital version they got from that disc anymore.

According to the document, a public beta for the disc-to-digital program was set for July with general availability set for August. We understand Microsoft had originally planned to test its disc-to-digital program with Xbox Insiders in July, but the beta was delayed. It’s unclear if the timeline of August general availability is still accurate.

The planned changes follow Microsoft’s major Xbox “reset” announced in July, which included thousands of layoffs and the company selling off four studios.

Tech.title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO.

This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder, because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all.

Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable.

But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop.

That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads.

This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it.

Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of BlueSky. Welcome to Decoder.

Thank you. Thanks for having me.

I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think BlueSky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are.

BlueSky today is really two things. There’s the BlueSky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath BlueSky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And BlueSky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol.

The whole point of BlueSky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app.

There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that BlueSky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of BlueSky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO?

It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why BlueSky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job.

I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. And so I agreed to be interim CEO initially because I was still a general partner at True and it’s a firm I helped build. It’s an amazing firm that I didn’t want to leave behind. But also, at True, we’ve had this model where we’ve moved back and forth between operator and investor. I did that while I was running Automattic.

So I stepped into it. After working on it hands-on for a few months, it just got more and more fun, more and more energizing. You just feel the momentum. Also, True just switched to a new fund. So actually the timing was good where I could say, “Okay, I will switch my true role to part-time, become a venture partner,” which is what I used to be when I ran Automattic, “and I’ll go all in at BlueSky.”

Tell me about the difference between being the interim CEO and the full-time CEO. When you’re the interim CEO, it feels like there are probably some boundaries in what you can do. And then the full-time CEO can obviously do everything that a full-time CEO can do. What did you feel like the boundaries were as interim CEO?

On the inside, it hasn’t felt very different. I actually think the move to drop the “interim” is more important on the outside, especially for the ATmosphere and the AT Proto community, and people building on this platform and in this ecosystem just to say, “No, I’m here for the duration. This isn’t just some interim gig and then somebody else is going to show up.” So I felt like, to the outside, that makes a big difference. On the inside, the job really hasn’t changed much..

So many of my conversations here in Decoder are really about the timescale of decisions. I’ll make the comparison to my newsroom because it’s easy and it’s easy to understand. Our reporters make decisions in like 30-minute increments. A story comes up, they write it, they publish it, they move on to the next thing. I make decisions maybe in like week- or month-long increments. What are we going to cover? Where are the resources going to go?

It seems like in the interim CEO role, the timescale of those decisions is necessarily short or it has the appearance of being short. And then I’m reading your note that you published when you became the full-time CEO. In the very beginning of it, you say we’re at the very beginning of the story with a decade of exciting work ahead. And I’m wondering if the timescale of the decisions you’re making now are a decade.

Yeah. It touches on something really fascinating with this project. In general with decision making, one of the frameworks I really like is the reversible and irreversible decisions. A lot of decisions we make are actually reversible. I like to optimize to just make those decisions quickly and then make sure you can undo the decisions if you need to change them.

And then there are a few decisions that really do have very long-term implications. They’re much harder to reverse. With this project in particular, there are decisions made at this protocol level that we’re going to have to live with for a long time. There’s a part of the company in this community that thinks very, very, very long term. This is a protocol that is going to be around for decades already. It’s in enough use that it’s going to be around for a long time. Those decisions you really need to be careful about. Then it goes all the way to things we try in the product that work or don’t work.

I wasn’t in the interim mindset as much because I am also an investor in the company, so I care very much about the long-term picture. What attracts me to this whole endeavor is that it can have a really important long-term impact. I always think about, okay, how will this play out? Does this truly serve the core mission? It’s okay to make some of these harder decisions now that won’t pay off for a long time because this is going to take a while.

It’s not just one company. It’s already thousands of others that are building together. That’s just a different timeframe and decision-making process than your typical just “go fast, scale as quickly as possible” [methodology]. I like it. I’m comfortable with it.

I just want to stick with BlueSky, the company that is both responsible for the standard and the protocol, and the product that a lot of end users love and sometimes hate. That is the core tension of the company. The user base of BlueSky is or is not interested in the development of AT Protocol, is or is not interested in the wider ATmosphere.

Under Jay’s tenure, the company was very focused on building out the protocol because the product literally could not exist unless the protocol was robust enough to stand up the product. You could see that back and forth. I have always felt that the company is far more interested in the protocol than the product, that the product was merely there to show what people could do.

But now the product is big. It might be waxing or waning. It will come to whether you need to turn it into TikTok or not. Tell me where you, as a CEO with a decade-long vision for all of this, see the balance inside of BlueSky between the product, the thing that looks like a Twitter app, and the protocol, the thing that should enable thousands upon thousands of other social experiences?

I see the BlueSky app and the product as enabling the ATmosphere. It’s an on-ramp, or maybe a lobby to the ATmosphere where it’s just a great way to get lots of people in, get people exposed to the idea, and then realize as you use the product, “Oh, there are other things here. This isn’t just a microblogging app.”

An example from the last couple of months that’s gone super well is this format called Standard Site that emerged. The history of that is that BlueSky’s a microblogging app. People are asking for longer-form posting. A bunch of other apps started popping up that were for newsletters and blogging. In particular, three apps called Leaflet, Pckt, and Offprint. They got together and said, “Hey, why don’t we define a format for all of us to work together on the ATmosphere for all of the posts that we publish?” We looked at it and said, “Great, we can now take that and surface it in our app.”

So now, if you’re posting a blog post on Leaflet, it just shows up in the BlueSky app and we can make that a seamless experience. This went over really well to the point where now WordPress is supporting Standard Site and lots of other publishing platforms. They’re realizing the benefit of, “If I just publish to this new format now, it’s going to show up and work across all these other platforms without me having to do anything.” It’s caused this really nice ripple effect throughout the ecosystem where people can work together just by using this format. Nobody has to do deals with each other. Nobody has to get permissions and no money has to change hands. And it’s just taken off.

I’m hoping more and more BlueSky users will see those kinds of integrations and go, “Oh, cool. I’m not just getting BlueSky content here. I’m getting content from all these other apps, all these other networks. And it just works. I don’t have to do anything. I don’t have to go 

You’re describing two different kinds of things. There’s a lot of work to be done at the protocol level. There’s a lot of work to be done to support new kinds of experiences like Standard Site. Then there’s BlueSky, a product which has 45 million people, and probably needs to be substantially bigger if it wants to be the aggregator for a massive network that can displace some of the other social products out there. That needs to be a lot of things to a lot of people. It needs to find different kinds of product market fit. How big is BlueSky the company now, and how is it structured to point in two different directions?

We’re now at 50 people, still very small. The biggest challenge is clearly trying to do everything you’ve described with a small team. We do have an ecosystem of hundreds and thousands of others working on it, so that helps. We do our best to coordinate everyone.

I would say we’re making good progress. We’re seeing good momentum, especially on the ATmosphere side. The things we look at are the number of daily active apps on the network, which has doubled since the beginning of the year. It’s about to hit a thousand. We look at SDK downloads for our tools that have tripled. It’s going to hit a million downloads a month by later this year. Those are the numbers that show that not only is it scaling, but we’re able to scale it with the team that we have.

How is that team structured?

About 50 people, all remote, structured into small teams. I’m a big believer that six to eight person teams, highly aligned, highly incentivized, and motivated are the way to get things done. Probably the only way to get things done. There are three core product teams. There’s the app team that deals with the BlueSky app. There’s the ATmosphere team that does all the developer-facing stuff. And then there’s a third product team called the exploration team, and that’s a new team that Jay has stood up and is running. We actually just launched a new version of the product they’re working on, Attie. Think of it as AI layered on top of the ATmosphere and what you can do with that.

Those are our three core product teams, and they’re each customer-facing. Consumer-facing, developer-facing, and then we’ll find out from the AI product what the market fit is there. We have a bunch of support teams that support those three core teams and that are pretty typical. We’ve got a legal team, et cetera, et cetera. I would say it’s a team that’s a very low ego, high agency. That is kind of the ethos. Low drama, just a lot of get-shit-done energy. Really collaborative.

Whenever I think about new social products and how they might scale, especially with explosive user growth – up until recently, the conventional wisdom is you’ve got to scale trust and safety and moderation linearly with the size of your user base. Maybe we’re going to add AI to this and that linear relationship will break, or maybe it’ll actually get even more costly because token spend will get more costly than having human moderators, or there’ll be more false positives and we’re going to be even angrier. So you have to have more humans in the loop.

It’s really unclear to me how that’s going to work. You’ve obviously been scaling BlueSky as a consumer social product. Then you have the complexity of, “We’re hooking onto lots and lots of other products that are putting content in front of people.” How does the moderation layer work? And have you seen it be a linear increase in cost with the size of the network and the user base?

Moderation is huge in any social product. In addition to our 50-person team, we do have contractors that help us with moderation. What we’ve done differently is that our whole moderation system is composable or pluggable. It’s not just us that can label content and moderate it. Anybody can do it and add labels. It’s part of the protocol. Anybody else who builds products can decide if they want to use those labels or not. So if somebody on our moderation team labels something as, let’s say, AI slop, everybody else who’s building in this ecosystem can take advantage of that piece of data. They don’t have to, but they can.

So what we’re seeing and what we’ve seen is we have our moderation team, but then there are other teams that have decided to moderate label content the way they want. For example, maybe the first non-BlueSky project on the protocol was Blacksky. And it’s now become a thriving company on its own. It’s a team building all kinds of interesting things. And they started out by saying, “Hey, we want to build a version of this network that is optimized for Black users and their needs. And we want to have our own moderation policies.” And they are able to do that and plug that in. But everything they’re doing is still part of the larger network. And now there are hundreds and thousands of these kinds of systems.

This has really helped where the moderation burden isn’t all on one team that has to scale and look at everything. There should be lots of different teams and lots of different systems because each network, each community has its own idea of what moderation should look like. So we feel like this kind of distributed moderation approach is more powerful. That said, yes, we’re continuing to scale up ours, but it’s manageable. It’s a lot of work, but it’s manageable. It’s worth it when the whole network can benefit from it.

The next part of that story that’s going to be really interesting is that the biggest thing we’re actually working on with AT Proto, the next evolution of the protocol, is private data. We all know that the public square, public social networking has reached a certain scale. And there are a lot of people who want to retreat into more private spaces. We’ve seen explosive growth in group chats. We’re all in a million group chats. This has been the number-one request from our community, from our developers: “Let us build more private, membership-based, various versions of private spaces on this protocol.”

We’re in the middle of building that. It’s a community effort. It’s rolling out very soon. Now, moderation moves and gets broken up into even more and smaller spaces. People can decide, “If I don’t like a network or I don’t like the way it’s moderated, [I can] go start my own.” Go start your own community. That’s the most interesting thing ahead of us, because right now everything on AT Proto is public. It can only be used for a completely public product. Once we enable private data, I think that it’s like 10 or 100X the number of use cases we can serve.

Not to be reductive, but I think it’s useful to talk about this in comparison to other social products people might be more familiar with. With AT Protocol right now and the ATmosphere, everything is very public. The models in my head are Twitter, and RSS, and massive broad-based publishing platforms, right? One-to-many. I think what you’re describing is much more like a Reddit style approach, where you have smaller, closed communities. Some of them can be totally private unless you’re invited in. And yet, they’re still on the ATmosphere in some way. Is that right?

That’s right. The trade-off has traditionally been that if you want to be on a launch network, you have to be on a public network. Or if you want to control, have ownership over your own community, you have to set up your own thing. You have to run your own server or you have to run your own forum. There’s clearly a need for that because there are lots of those out there. But the challenge is each one of those is now a little island. And you have to convince people.

We think we can pull off as the best of both worlds. When you build a community or private space on AT Proto, it’s absolutely 100% owned by you. It’s not owned by BlueSky or by any company. It’s just like everything else on a protocol. It’s owned by the users, not by the platform. So it’s really truly yours. You can move it around. You can make all the decisions. But because it’s on a shared protocol, all of these communities plug together. You can go to a place like BlueSky and get all your notifications in one place. You can see what’s going on across everything. You just need one login, one place to check, but you still have the independence and the identity of these individual communities.

That is something that no other platform can do right now. You’re either on the large platform owned and controlled place, or you run your own and you’re a little siloed. We think we can solve that. We see the energy behind this idea and the number of things people are already prototyping is very palpable.

I have to ask you the other Decoder question because I’m very curious where this idea came from and how you decided to bet on it. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for making decisions?

I already talked a little bit earlier about the reversible and irreversible decisions. The hardest thing about running any project is that, especially if it’s successful, it’s just an endless flow of things you have to prioritize and decide on. I find you could make that a lot less daunting and exhausting if you move a lot of decisions into this category of “they’re not that big a deal.” Let’s make it easy to experiment and reverse things, and really only focus on the truly long-term impactful things that we have to get right.

You have this lightness or almost playfulness about some of these things, where it’s just not that big a deal. Let’s just try something. Let’s be creative and improvisational about it. This is a lot of how Automattic runs. I actually credit a lot of that to Matt Mullenweg’s approach to first running an open-source project. Inside Automattic, there are a lot of jazz analogies because Matt started out as a jazz musician. Just this improvisational, “don’t take it so seriously if you don’t have to.”
